input.content:
The logo was **Google's Gemini wordmark** — another company's trademark serving as
this product's identity. The home hero was a photograph of an aircraft with "Gemini
Airways" painted along the fuselage. The tab icon was the Vercel triangle
`create-next-app` leaves behind. A shared link showed nothing at all.

This issue was parked because inventing a logo is design work rather than a code
change. Here is the design work.

## The mark

An **M drawn as one continuous path, split at its valley into two strokes** —
outbound saturated, return quieter. The monogram and a two-leg itinerary are the
same shape, and a leg is the object this application is built around.

Two decisions worth the words:

- **Square, and no wordmark.** The old asset was 344x127 requested at 20x20 and
  32x32, so Tailwind's `height: auto` painted it as a 7px sliver. Both call sites
  already name the airline in text beside the mark, so a wordmark in the asset would
  only repeat it — which is also why the header `alt` is now empty. It was reading
  "Mona Airways Mona Airways".
- **The legs differ by saturation, not brightness.** My first version dimmed the
  return leg with opacity. The reviewer measured that this inverts with the
  background: a paler stroke is the weaker one on black and the *stronger* one on
  white. Colour carries the hierarchy instead, so it survives the change of ground.

## The hero

A photograph cannot be redrawn, and a stock aircraft would say nothing about this
product, so the hero is **routes between places** — arcs, node dots, two glows.

Two bugs the review caught in my own work:

- **`.home` is the whole search page, not the hero.** Under `background-size: cover`
  the art grew with the results list, so a 16:9 canvas was blown up to twice the
  page width and its arcs ran across the filters and the result cards. It is bounded
  to one viewport now; below that the page is flat.
- **The node dots were landing inside the form controls.** A filled circle the size
  of a radio button was sitting in the FROM combobox on the value baseline. A line
  crossing a translucent card reads as atmosphere; a dot reads as a control. They
  are out of the band the centred card occupies.

On a phone the arcs magnify until they cross the search fields, so narrow screens
get the same light as CSS gradients and **do not fetch the artwork at all** —
verified: no request for `hero-routes.svg` at 390, 768 or 900, and it appears again
at 901.

## Icons and the social card

`app/icon.svg` puts the M on a gradient badge, because a tab strip is light in one
theme and dark in another. At 16px the two-tone split closed the counters and the
quiet leg smeared, so the badge glyph is solid white and larger — a 16px mark
carries one idea.

`app/favicon.ico` is hand-packed, and **I got it wrong the first time**: the
embedded PNG was RGB, Next's decoder requires RGBA, and it failed the build. There
is now a test asserting the ICO header bytes and the PNG colour type, because
`existsSync` is happy with a text file named `favicon.ico`.

The card renders **per request from the home page, not the root layout**.
`metadataBase` resolves when a page renders, and the auth routes are prerendered, so
a card declared at the root baked the build machine's address into every one of them
— `http://localhost:3000/img/og-image.jpg` in any container image, on exactly the
pages people paste into chat. Verified on a production server built with one URL and
started with another: `/` emits `https://mona.example.com/img/og-image.jpg`, and
`/login` emits no card and zero `localhost` references.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (575 unit + 21 database), `npm run
build`, a production server, the standalone server the Dockerfile actually runs, and
the full Playwright suite (28/28 on a clean database).

## The mark

An **M drawn as one continuous path, split at its valley into two strokes** — outbound saturated, return quieter. The monogram and a two-leg itinerary are the same shape, which is the object this whole application is built around, and the thing most of this session's bugs were about.

Two decisions worth naming:

**Square, and no wordmark.** The old asset was 344×127 requested at 20×20, so it painted as a 7px sliver. Both call sites already name the airline beside the mark — which is also why the header `alt` is now empty. It was reading "Mona Airways Mona Airways" to a screen reader.

**The legs differ by saturation, not brightness.** My first version dimmed the return leg with opacity. `ui-review` measured that this *inverts* with the background — a paler stroke leads on black and recedes on white. Colour carries the hierarchy instead, so it survives the change of ground.

## What the reviews caught in my own work

I was wrong about several things and the sub-agents were right:

- **`.home` is the whole search page, not the hero.** Under `cover`, the art grew with the results list — a 16:9 canvas blown up to twice the page width, arcs running across the filters and result cards.
- **The node dots landed inside the form controls.** A filled circle the size of a radio button was sitting in the FROM combobox on the value baseline. Lines read as atmosphere; dots read as UI.
- **My hand-packed `favicon.ico` embedded an RGB PNG** where Next's decoder requires RGBA — that 500'd every page. There's now a test asserting the header bytes and PNG colour type, because `existsSync` is perfectly happy with a text file named `favicon.ico`.
- **The social card baked the build machine's URL.** `metadataBase` resolves at render, and the auth routes are prerendered — so a card declared in the root layout shipped `http://localhost:3000/img/og-image.jpg` in any container image, on exactly the pages people paste into chat. It lives on the dynamic home page now. Verified on a production server built with one URL and started with another.

The verifier also corrected me on process: a bad ICO *does* fail `npm run build` — I only saw it at request time because dev compiles that route lazily.

## Also shipped

A gradient-badge favicon (solid white glyph — at 16px the two-tone split turned to mud), an Apple touch icon, and a 1200×630 social card set in the product's own typeface. ## The call I said you needed doesn't exist

When I filed #154 I framed it as a funnel decision: gating it means unauthenticated visitors can't see a seat map before signing in. **That framing was wrong**, and the code says so plainly.

`getOccupiedSeatsAction` has exactly two callers, and both already require a session:

- `app/checkout/page.tsx:93` — `/checkout` is in the `proxy.ts` middleware matcher **and** the page does its own `getServerSession` + `redirect('/login')` at line 37
- `components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx:139` — `/profile` is in the same matcher

There is no unauthenticated seat map anywhere in the app. Gating this costs zero funnel.

## Why it still needs the check

A server action is its own HTTP endpoint. Middleware protects *page navigations*; Next dispatches actions by header, so an action's authorization has to live in the action. AGENTS.md already states this principle for staff mutations — "a session alone is not enough."

The audit makes the outlier obvious. Of 18 exported actions, 15 check a session. The three that don't:

| Action | Public caller? |
|---|---|
| `searchFlightsAction` | Yes — the unauthenticated home page |
| `getFlightRoutesAction` | Yes — same |
| `getOccupiedSeatsAction` | **None** |

The first two are deliberately public and have a real reason. This one is ungated with nothing public that needs it.

## The one genuine decision, and it's narrow

**What scope of check?**

- **Any signed-in user, any `flightId`** — the only workable answer, and what I'd recommend. Checkout needs occupancy for a flight you don't yet have a booking on, so you can't scope it to "flights you're already on."
- Scoping to users with an existing booking would break checkout outright.
- Rate-limiting on top is possible (`lib/authRateLimit.ts` is the precedent) but I'd skip it — occupancy is low-sensitivity, and the value is that a signed-in identity is attached to the enumeration at all.

So: a plain `getServerSession` check, matching the 15 actions that already have one. If you disagree and would rather leave it open, the alternative is to say so in a comment at the call site so the next reviewer doesn't re-raise it — but I don't think that's the better call, since nothing public needs it.

Want me to take it? It's a small slice — the check, a test that an unauthenticated call is refused, and closing #154.
Yes take it on and lets go with your recommendation

input.content:
Found while gating `getOccupiedSeatsAction` (#154), and widened by it.

**Verification status:** the mechanism is confirmed by reading the source. The
display was not reproduced in a browser — reaching it needs a session that has been
invalidated while a page stays open.

## What happens

`components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx:139` loads seat occupancy for the seat-change
modal:

```ts
Promise.all(legs.map(leg =>
    getOccupiedSeatsAction(leg.flight!.id)
        .then(seats => [leg.id, seats] as const)
        .catch(() => [leg.id, [] as string[]] as const)
))
```

The `catch` turns *any* failure into "no seats are occupied", so the modal renders
**every seat as free**. It cannot tell "nothing is taken" from "I could not find
out", and neither can the customer.

## How it is reached

The session has to become invalid while `/profile` stays open. `lib/auth.ts:140`
returns a null session when `token.invalidated` is set, which happens on an
`authVersion` bump (a password reset), a deleted user, a cleared `emailVerified`,
or — the realistic one — an admin whose `staffMfaVerifiedAt` is older than
`STAFF_MFA_SESSION_MAX_AGE_MS`, which is **8 hours** (`lib/staffMfa.ts:19`).

So: sign in at 9am, leave the profile open, open the seat modal at 5pm.

## Severity, honestly

Bounded. **No wrong seat can be written.** `changeBookingSeatsAction`
(`app/actions.ts:483`) carries the same session gate, so in exactly the state that
produces the blank map the save is refused before touching the database. Two further
backstops hold even with a valid session and a stale map: the in-transaction check
under `lockFlightForUpdate`, and `@@unique([flightId, seatNumber])` on
`SeatAssignment`.

In that state the customer cannot save any seat, right or wrong. So this changes how
confusing the failure is, not what anyone can accomplish.

## Why #154 widened it rather than opened it

The `catch` predates that change and already swallowed a database error or a
validation failure the same way. Adding the session check gave it one more, more
reachable, trigger.

## Fix

Distinguish "could not load occupancy" from "nothing is occupied", and refuse to
render a seat map that could not be verified — an explanation and a retry, rather
than a grid that invites a choice the server will reject.

## Test it needs

`__tests__/components/ProfileClient.test.tsx` only ever calls
`mockGetOccupiedSeats.mockResolvedValue(...)` (lines 218, 266, 391, 418) — never
`mockRejectedValue`. The `catch` branch has no coverage at all, before or after
#154. That missing case is the one this fix turns on.

build`, plus `booking.spec.ts`, `multi-passenger.spec.ts` and
`booking-authority.spec.ts` against a freshly seeded database — 11 passed, re-run
clean with no order dependence.

The verifier ran the four new tests against the previous `actions.ts`: exactly the
two unauthenticated cases fail, the two characterization cases pass either way. It
also audited all 18 actions and confirmed no third gap, and confirmed no caller I had
missed — `__tests__/components/ProfileClient.test.tsx` mocks the action wholesale, so
it never touches this path.

## One regression, filed rather than fixed

**#175** — `ProfileClient` wraps this call in `.catch(() => [])`, so a failure
renders the seat map with **every seat free**. That `catch` predates this change and
already swallowed database and validation errors; the session check gives it one more
trigger.

I framed the trigger as session expiry, and the verifier corrected me: there is no
`maxAge`, so the NextAuth default is 30 days and that path is unrealistic. The real

that produces the blank map the save is refused before touching the database, with
the in-transaction check under `lockFlightForUpdate` and the

the failure is, not what anyone can accomplish. The fix belongs in `ProfileClient`'s
error handling and needs its own review.

I recorded it as not applicable because no reachable state renders differently. The
verifier's pushback is fair: #175 *is* a differing render, it just requires an
already-invalidated session. The accurate record is that the only differing render
requires an invalidated session and is tracked separately.

I claimed there that e2e bookings are never cleared between runs. They are —
`booking.spec.ts` and `multi-passenger.spec.ts` both delete their own in
`test.afterAll`. Only an interrupted run strands seats. I have corrected the issue.

input.content:
The boarding pass printed the raw cabin enum, so a customer's e-ticket read
`PREMIUM_ECONOMY` — underscore and capitals — on the artefact people keep and show
at a gate.

It was in **eight** places, not one:

- the seat step's `aria-label` and its visible "Class: X | Seat: Y"
- the review step's fare breakdown and its single-traveller line
- the boarding pass badge
- the staff passenger manifest
- the profile's seat-change modal, reading the cabin off the `SeatAssignment`
- the search picker — which was worse than raw

## The search picker was selling a different cabin by name

`flightBookingForm.tsx` kept its own map with `FIRST: 'First'`, while checkout, the
review and the ticket all said **First Class**. A customer picked one cabin by name
and was sold another. It now names cabins from the same helper, iterating
`SEARCH_CABINS` rather than four hardcoded `<option>`s.

## One helper

`cabinLabel()` lives in `lib/bookingItinerary.ts` beside `seatLabel` and
`legDirectionLabel`, since all three answer the same question: how a piece of an
itinerary reads to a customer. An unrecognised value is prettified rather than
passed through, so a cabin added to the schema before the map catches up still
cannot reach a ticket in snake case.

The picker keeps its surcharge, but derives it from `CABIN_FARE_PERCENT` instead of
writing it down — an option can no longer promise +50% while the fare charges
something else. Verified byte-identical to the strings it replaced, so that half is
a safety change with no visible effect.

## What the reviews caught

**I claimed a complete set twice and was wrong twice.** `ui-review` found the search
picker's competing map; the verifier then found that I had deleted the map feeding
the *unavailable note* but not the `<option>` elements the customer actually picks
from — so the disagreement had merely moved inside one component. It also found the
profile's seat modal, which reads the cabin off a `SeatAssignment` rather than a
`Passenger` and so escaped every grep I ran.

Both now have component tests. I also deleted a test of mine that the verifier showed
passes against the old code: it asserted a property of the helper, not of the search
form, while its comment claimed to cover the "First" vs "First Class" bug. A test
that cannot fail for the reason it names is worse than no test.

**The badge wrap was a real regression.** `ui-review` measured that "Premium
Economy" splits to two lines inside its pill at 390px — the enum was one unbreakable
token and never did. The badge is `nowrap` now; the carrier name takes the two lines
instead, which is a lockup rather than a broken word. Measured: badge 141px → 119px,
banner 67px → 63.4px.

**The `aria-label` I added was inert.** ARIA ignores `aria-label` on a bare `<span>`
— the role is `generic` — so it read as nothing. It is a visually-hidden "Cabin: "
in the reading order instead, which is what every other field on the pass has
visibly.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (586 unit + 21 database),
`npm run build`, and the full Playwright suite on a freshly reset database.

The verifier ran the changed assertions against the previous code: 5 fail, including
the new boarding-pass test. It flagged that in two multi-assertion tests the first
changed assertion masks the second, so a couple of the updated strings are carried by
their siblings rather than demonstrated independently — worth knowing rather than
counting as coverage.

It also confirmed the fallback branch is unreachable through the app, and for a
reason worth recording: `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` is `TEXT NOT NULL` with **no
check constraint and no Postgres enum**, so the guard is entirely Zod at the booking
boundary. The fallback is not defended by the schema.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#177** — two seat-validation error strings still interpolate the enum, one of
  them customer-reachable. Left out because error copy wants rewording, not a

#169 is closed and merged as `6701ff9`.

## What shipped

A cabin now reads as words everywhere a person sees one — via a single `cabinLabel()` in `lib/bookingItinerary.ts`, beside `seatLabel` and `legDirectionLabel`. It was in **eight** places, not the one the issue named.

The worst wasn't the shouting. **The search picker was selling a different cabin by name**: it kept its own map saying "First" while checkout, the review and the ticket all said "First Class". A customer picked one cabin and was sold another.

The picker also derives its `(+50%)` from `CABIN_FARE_PERCENT` now instead of hardcoding it, so an option can't promise one surcharge while the fare charges another. Verified byte-identical to what it replaced.

## I claimed a complete set twice and was wrong twice

`ui-review` found the search form's competing map. The verifier then found I'd deleted the map feeding the *unavailable note* but not the `<option>` elements the customer actually picks from — so the disagreement had merely moved inside one component. It also found the profile's seat modal, which reads the cabin off a `SeatAssignment` rather than a `Passenger` and escaped every grep I ran.

It also caught a test of mine that **passes against the old code**: it asserted a property of the helper while its comment claimed to cover the "First"/"First Class" bug. I deleted it and wrote real component tests for both missed sites. A test that can't fail for the reason it names is worse than none.

Two of my own fixes were regressions:

- The badge **wrapped** — "Premium / Economy" split inside its pill at 390px, which the unbreakable enum never did. Now `nowrap`; the carrier name takes the two lines instead.
- The `aria-label` I added was **inert**. ARIA ignores it on a bare `<span>`. It's a visually-hidden "Cabin: " in the reading order now.

## One thing worth knowing

`SeatAssignment.cabinClass` is `TEXT NOT NULL` with **no check constraint and no Postgres enum**. The four-cabin guarantee is entirely Zod at the booking boundary — the fallback branch isn't defended by the schema, which is exactly why keeping it was right.

- Two responsive measurements on **#79** (cabin select truncates below 390px; seat-step card wraps mid-value). Neither is a regression — both strings are shorter than the enum.

Ten merged this session. Remaining small and unblocked: **#175** (blank seat map), **#171**, **#165**, **#167**, **#173**, **#177**, **#178**.

Then it's the **Phase 2 chain** (#73 → #76 → #74 → #75 → #77), which is where the real product work is — and it's still waiting on the six decisions in #143: migration ownership across the overlapping schema changes, the cancellation policy table, hold TTL, authorize-vs-capture, and whether shared search URLs may 404. /**
 * When a seat counts as taken.
 *
 * One rule — a seat is held unless the booking holding it was cancelled — asked
 * by four queries: booking a flight, reading a seat map, changing a seat, and
 * editing a cabin layout. Each wrote the condition out again, so getting it
 * wrong in one place meant a seat that was free on one screen and taken on
 * another.
 *
 * It is stated here because three queued issues rewrite those same call sites
 * independently — inventory holds (#74), payments (#75) and cancellation rules
 * (#76) — and each would otherwise have to find all four and change them the
 * same way (#143).
 *
 * Note what this is *not*: `searchFlightsAction` filters cancelled **flights**
 * out of search results, which reads similarly and is a different question. A
 * cancelled flight is not a released seat.
 */

/**
 * The status a booking carries once it is cancelled.
 *
 * `Booking.status` is a bare `String` column with no enum and no check
 * constraint, so this literal is the whole definition. Typing those states in
 * the database is the remaining task of #73.
 */
export const CANCELLED_BOOKING = 'CANCELLED';

/**
 * A `where` fragment naming the seats that are actually held, to be spread
 * beside whatever else a caller is asking about:
 *
 *     where: { flightId, ...heldSeat }
 *     where: { flightId: { in: ids }, ...heldSeat, NOT: { leg: { bookingId } } }
 *
 * Spread rather than nested so a caller keeps its own conditions, with one
 * consequence worth knowing: a caller that also writes its own `leg` key will
 * overwrite this one and silently include cancelled bookings. Filter on
 * `booking` inside `leg`, or add to the `NOT`, rather than replacing `leg`.
 *
 * A cancellation leaves the seat row in place — it parks the seat under a
 * placeholder so the unique index stays satisfied — so this predicate is the
 * only thing that releases it.
 */
export const heldSeat = {
    leg: { booking: { status: { not: CANCELLED_BOOKING } } },
} as const;

const HELD_SEAT = {
    leg: { booking: { status: { not: CANCELLED_BOOKING } } },
} as const;

/**
 * Narrows a seat-assignment query to the seats that are actually held.
 *
 *     where: heldSeats({ flightId })
 *     where: heldSeats({ flightId: { in: ids }, NOT: { leg: { bookingId } } })
 *     where: heldSeats()
 *
 * A function rather than an object to spread, because the rule has to win.
 * Spread beside a caller's conditions it could be erased by one of them: a
 * `leg` key written *before* the spread is a TypeScript error, but the same key
 * written *after* it compiles cleanly and removes the booking join from the SQL
 * entirely — no cancelled bookings filtered, and nothing to grep for. Applying
 * the rule last means a caller cannot lose it by accident, only by editing this
 * file.
 *
 * What a cancellation does to a seat is worth being precise about, because it
 * decides which call sites this matters at. Cancelling renames the seat to a
 * `CANCELLED-<passengerId>` placeholder so the unique index stays satisfied,
 * and that rename is what frees the seat for anything comparing seat *numbers*.
 * This predicate does something narrower: it stops the placeholder row being
 * read back as an occupied seat, which matters wherever the stored seat number
 * is interpreted rather than matched — the cabin-layout check most of all.
 */
export function heldSeats<T extends object>(scope: T = {} as T): T & typeof HELD_SEAT {
    return { ...scope, ...HELD_SEAT };

#143 named this as the prerequisite before the Phase 2 chain:

> Extracting them into one `lib/seatOccupancy.ts` predicate first turns twelve lines
> in four files into one function.

Four queries each wrote out *a seat is held unless its booking was cancelled* —
booking a flight, reading a seat map, changing a seat, and editing a cabin layout.
Inventory holds (#74), payments (#75) and cancellation rules (#76) all rewrite those
same call sites, so each would have had to find all four and change them identically.

Nothing here needs a decision from anyone, which is why it goes first.

## A function, not an object to spread

I wrote it as an object first. The verifier found the hole: a caller's own `leg` key
written **before** the spread is a TypeScript error, but the same key written
**after** it compiles cleanly and removes the booking join from the generated SQL
entirely — no cancelled bookings filtered, and no inlined text for the grep guard to
find. Confirmed against real SQL:

```
WHERE ("j1"."bookingId" = $1 AND ("j1"."id" IS NOT NULL))
```

`heldSeats(scope)` applies the rule last, so it cannot be lost by accident — only by
editing this file. That is the whole point of the refactor, since three later issues
will be editing these call sites.

## The boundary

`searchFlightsAction` filters cancelled **flights** out of search results. It reads
almost identically and answers a different question — a cancelled flight is not a
released seat — so it is deliberately not folded in. My first pass at counting the
sites said five; it is four, and this is the one that isn't.

The verifier independently confirmed no fifth occupancy site, and that three other
`seatAssignment` reads are *deliberately* unfiltered: the admin manifest renders
cancelled bookings on purpose and labels their seats "Released", the profile shows a
customer their own cancelled bookings, and `FlightBookingService` has an
idempotency-replay read. Filtering any of them would be a regression.

## The site where it has teeth, which had no test

Everywhere else, dropping the predicate is invisible: a cancellation renames the seat
to a `CANCELLED-<passengerId>` placeholder that can never match a real seat id, so
seat-number comparisons are unaffected either way.

`FlightSeatLayoutService` is different — it feeds the stored seat number into
`assertSeatAvailableForCabin`, interpreting it rather than matching it. Without the
rule the placeholder reads back as an occupied seat and **every later layout change
on that flight is refused forever**. That case had no coverage, and
`seatLayoutGuard.database.test.ts` passed with the predicate neutered.

It now has a test that builds exactly the state `cancelBookingAction` leaves behind —
booking cancelled *and* seat renamed. Mutation-tested: neuter the predicate and it
fails with `Occupied seat CANCELLED-… is not available for ECONOMY in the requested
layout.`

That also corrected a sentence in my module doc. The rename is what frees the seat
for anything comparing seat numbers; the predicate's job is narrower — stopping the
placeholder row being *read back* as occupied.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (590 unit + 26 database), `npm run
build`, and the full Playwright suite (28/28, clean database, first run).

The verifier compared **generated SQL for all four sites**, inline versus extracted,
in one process against the same fixture: byte-identical query text, parameters and
rows. Including the two awkward ones — the nested `include` filter on the layout
edit, and the seat change where the rule sits beside a sibling `NOT: { leg: {
bookingId } }`. Those compose into separate joins (`j1`/`j2` for the rule, `j3` for
the exclusion) and still exclude only the caller's own booking.

It also proved the shared module-level object is never mutated, by wrapping it in a
recursive `Proxy` trapping writes and firing all four shapes concurrently. Worth
having checked: the spread is shallow, so every call site shares the same nested
`leg` object.

## Guard

`__tests__/lib/seatOccupancy.test.ts` fails if the rule is written out again, naming
the file and what to call instead. It is textual, with the limits that implies in
both directions — an equivalent re-inlining spelled `NOT: { status: … }` slips past,
and a future query legitimately filtering bookings by status would trip it. It
catches the copy-paste that actually happens; it is not a proof, and the test says so.

Rendered UI review is not applicable: no rendered output is touched, and the SQL
comparison above establishes the queries are unchanged.

## What shipped

No cancelled bookings filtered, and no inlined text for the grep guard to find. Applying the rule last means it can't be lost by accident — which is the whole point, given three later issues will be editing these call sites.

## Two corrections to what I told you

**I said five sites; it's four.** `searchFlightsAction` filters cancelled *flights* out of search — it reads almost identically and answers a different question. A cancelled flight is not a released seat. Folding it in would have been a false abstraction.

**My module doc overstated the rule.** I wrote that the predicate is "the only thing that releases" a cancelled seat. The *rename* to `CANCELLED-<passengerId>` does that for anything comparing seat numbers; the predicate's job is narrower — stopping the placeholder row being read back as occupied.

## The gap worth knowing about

That correction matters because it identifies where this rule actually has teeth. At three of four sites, dropping the predicate is invisible — the placeholder can never match a real seat id. But `FlightSeatLayoutService` *interprets* the stored seat number, so without the rule the placeholder reads back as occupied and **every later layout change on that flight is refused forever**.

That case had no coverage, and `seatLayoutGuard.database.test.ts` passed with the predicate neutered. It has a test now, built in exactly the state `cancelBookingAction` leaves behind, and mutation-tested to confirm it fails without the rule.

The verifier compared **generated SQL for all four sites**, inline versus extracted, in one process against the same fixture: byte-identical query text, parameters and rows — including the nested `include` filter and the seat change where the rule sits beside a sibling `NOT: { leg: { bookingId } }`. It also proved the shared module object is never mutated by wrapping it in a write-trapping Proxy, which mattered because the spread is shallow and every call site shares the same nested object.

## Status: steps 1 and 2 are complete, and the prerequisite is done

Recording this against the repo so the plan does not drift from it. This plan was written at `110cf2d`; `main` is now `ff2730d`.

### Step 1 — contract steps

Both closed before this run: #135 (drop the flight and schedule price strings) in #145, #137 (drop `Passenger.seatNumber`, `cabinClass`, `flightId`) in #147.

### Step 2 — cheap correctness fixes: **empty**

| Issue | Delivered |
|---|---|
| #142 Prisma error logs leak customer data | #164 |
| #140 logo asset carries the old identity | #174 |
| #152 round-trip review shows one leg | #161 |
| #153 `/flights` loads every flight row | #168 |
| #154 `getOccupiedSeatsAction` has no session check | #176 |
| #155 `seatAssignmentCoverage` flake | #166 |
| #158 boarding pass says GEMINI AIRWAYS | #170 |
| #160 third copy of the leg direction label | #172 |
| #169 raw cabin enum on the e-ticket | #179 |

Everything named in the "most-reported defect" and "other unverified findings" sections is now either fixed or filed. The round-trip review defect was real, and the e2e assertion covering it (`text=Seats: 11A, 12C`) had passed throughout its life — a pooled list reads the same whether or not the seats are paired with the right legs.

The one finding from this plan still unverified is **itineraries whose legs are out of order or do not connect**. Nobody has looked at it, so it is deliberately not filed.

### The prerequisite this plan named — done

> Extracting them into one `lib/seatOccupancy.ts` predicate first turns twelve lines in four files into one function.

Done in #180. One correction: it is **four** sites, not five. `searchFlightsAction` filters cancelled *flights* out of search results, which reads almost identically and answers a different question — a cancelled flight is not a released seat.

It landed as a function rather than an object to spread, because a caller's own `leg` key written after a spread compiles cleanly and silently removes the booking filter from the SQL. Applied last, the rule cannot be dropped by accident.

## #73 is much smaller than it reads

Five of its seven tasks are already delivered by work since this plan was written:

| Task | State |
|---|---|
| Airports with IATA code, country, IANA timezone | **Done** — `model Airport`, `lib/airports.ts` |
| Schedules separate from dated instances | **Done** — `FlightSchedule` + `Flight` |
| Itinerary and itinerary-leg models | **Done** — `ItineraryLeg` (#118) |
| Money as integer minor units | **Done** — `priceCents`, `totalPriceCents` (#134, #144, #145) |
| Traveler and seat-assignment records | **Done** — `Passenger`, `SeatAssignment` |
| **Typed cabin, fare, currency, booking, payment, flight, notification statuses** | **Not started** |
| Migration plan, rollback, recovery | Ongoing discipline |

`Booking.status`, `Flight.status`, `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` and `currency` are all bare `String`. `Role` is the only real enum in the schema. That is not abstract cleanup: verification during #169 established that `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` is `TEXT NOT NULL` with **no check constraint and no Postgres enum**, so the four-cabin guarantee is Zod at the booking boundary and nothing else.

## A correction to the ownership table's neighbourhood

I was about to recommend "typed statuses" as the next slice under #73. That would have walked into exactly the collision this plan exists to prevent — the table above assigns **`Booking.status` typing + status history to #76**, with #73 and #75 as consumers.

So the split is:

- **#76 owns** `Booking.status` typing. Leave it.
- **#73 owns** `Flight.from/to` → `Airport` FK. That one needs the decision below.
- **Nobody owns** `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` or `Flight.status` typing. Those are free to take now, and `cabinClass` has the evidence behind it.

## Decisions: take them just in time

Six are listed here, belonging to four different slices. Deciding all of them now means committing months ahead of the code, and this plan's own premises have already drifted in a fortnight. Only one is needed to start #73:

> must already-shared search URLs (`?from=Seattle%2C+USA`) keep working after the switch to IATA codes, or may they 404?

The cancellation policy table and staff-cancel behaviour belong to #76, hold TTL and timing to #74, authorize-vs-capture to #75, and document attestation to #77. Each is better answered by whoever opens that slice.

## Not in this plan, and worth adding to it

The test infrastructure is not ready for the volume. Four distinct shared-resource failures surfaced in one run: #155 (a parallel Jest flake which turned out to be a **vacuous** assertion — the scan it performed had been counting zero rows for its entire life), #173 (e2e seats stranded by an interrupted run), #178 (`booking.spec.ts:267` has ~12s of headroom and times out on a cold run), plus #165.

Phase 3 alone is ~40 PRs. Every one pays that tax, and every red run for an unrelated reason erodes the signal that tells you a real regression happened. Worth clearing before the volume rather than during.

## Filed along the way

Not part of any phase, all found by verification rather than by looking for them: #156, #159, #162, #163, #165, #167, #171, #173, #175, #177, #178.

-- request boundary. Everything that reaches the table another way -- a repair

-- the fare calculation, the seat map and the boarding pass would each read it
-- back and believe it.

-- is a constraint arriving late rather than a change of meaning.

--
-- `ALTER TABLE ... USING` fails on an unconvertible row by itself, but reports
-- only the first value it choked on, with no indication of how much of the
-- table is affected. An operator meeting this during a deployment needs to know
-- what is actually in the column before deciding what each value should become.
DO $$
DECLARE
    unexpected TEXT;
BEGIN
    SELECT string_agg(DISTINCT format('%L (%s rows)', "cabinClass", n), ', ')
    INTO unexpected
    FROM (
        SELECT "cabinClass", count(*) AS n
        FROM "SeatAssignment"
        WHERE "cabinClass" NOT IN ('ECONOMY', 'PREMIUM_ECONOMY', 'BUSINESS', 'FIRST')
        GROUP BY "cabinClass"
    ) AS outliers;

    IF unexpected IS NOT NULL THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION
            'SeatAssignment.cabinClass holds values outside the four cabins: %. '
            'Decide what each should become and update those rows before typing the column.',
            unexpected;
    END IF;
END $$;

    ALTER COLUMN "cabinClass" TYPE "CabinClass" USING "cabinClass"::"CabinClass";

input.command:
cd /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app
gh issue create --title "search e2e reads the return date between two effects and captures a stale value" --label bug --body "Found by the verifier during #73 work, on clean scratch databases. Not #173 or #178 — different mechanism.

**Verification status:** reproduced (1 failure in 3 full-suite runs); passes 3/3 in isolation. The arithmetic below confirms the mechanism.

## The failure

\`e2e/search.spec.ts:30\`

\`\`\`
- \"returnDate\": \"2026-08-17\"    (captured from the #return input)
+ \"returnDate\": \"2026-08-15\"    (what the URL carried)
\`\`\`

## Mechanism

\`components/ui/flightBookingForm.tsx:400-455\` splits the work across two effects. Choosing a new **From** fires one that calls \`setDepartureDate(route.nextOperatingDate)\`; a *separate* effect then recomputes \`returnDate = departure + 7 days\`.

The spec reads \`#return\`'s \`inputValue()\` between those two passes, so it captures a return date still derived from the **previous** route's departure:

- \`2026-08-15 = 2026-08-08 + 7\` — the New York route, the correct answer
- \`2026-08-17 = 2026-08-10 + 7\` — the previously selected route, what the spec captured

## Why \`expect.poll\` will not fix it

The expected value is captured once, before the assertion. Polling the URL against a stale expectation just polls for the wrong thing.

## Fix

Wait for the form to settle before reading it — assert the departure input holds the new route's date first, then read the return. Or collapse the two effects so a route change produces both dates in one pass, which would remove the intermediate state entirely rather than teaching the test to avoid it.

The second is the better fix: the intermediate state is briefly visible to a customer too."

gh issue create --title "admin e2e navigates before the status change has settled" --label bug --body "Found by the verifier during #73 work, on clean scratch databases. Not #173 or #178.

**Verification status:** reproduced (1 failure in 3 full-suite runs, then 6 consecutive isolated failures, then 3 passes). The database was polled during a failing run to rule out the write.

## The failure

\`e2e/admin.spec.ts:74\` — \`locator('table').locator('text=Delayed')\` not found on \`/flights\`.

## The write is not the problem

Polling during a failing run showed the row landed correctly:

\`\`\`
1629 | 2026-08-08 10:00 | DELAYED
\`\`\`

inside the board's \`now-2h .. now+7d\` window, with 29 rows in the window so \`take: 200\` never truncates. The board simply rendered before the write had committed.

## Mechanism

\`components/ui/FlightStatusSelector.tsx\` runs \`updateFlightStatusAction\` inside \`startTransition\` and then \`router.refresh()\`. Playwright's \`selectOption('DELAYED')\` returns as soon as the change event dispatches — it does not wait for the transition. \`e2e/admin.spec.ts:239\` then navigates straight to \`/flights\`, which is \`force-dynamic\` and renders whatever the database holds at that instant.

## Fix

Await the settled state before navigating — the select clearing its \`disabled\` state, or the row showing the new status on the admin page itself. Asserting the outcome on the page that performed the change is the more honest wait, since that is where the user would see it.

## Related

Same family as #173 and #178: the suite has several waits that assume an action is complete when the DOM event returns."

input.content:
Part of #73. `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` was `TEXT NOT NULL` with **no enum and no
check constraint**, so the four-cabin rule existed only in the Zod schema at the
request boundary. That was established during #169 verification, not assumed.

Anything reaching the table another way — a repair script, the seed, a service added
later — could write nonsense, and the fare calculation, the seat map and the boarding
pass would each read it back and believe it.

The four names are the ones already in use, so no row changes meaning. This is a
constraint arriving late.

## Scope: deliberately not `Booking.status`

#73's remaining task names seven typed statuses, but #143's ownership table assigns
**`Booking.status` typing + status history to #76**. Taking it here is precisely the
collision that plan exists to prevent. This takes the piece nobody owns and that has
evidence behind it.

## The migration

Hand-authored, per AGENTS.md. Three parts worth explaining:

**It says what is wrong before the cast does.** The bare `ALTER ... USING` reports
`invalid input value for enum "CabinClass": "STEERAGE"` — one value, chosen by scan
order, naming neither the table nor the column. The guard reports every offending
value with counts:

```
SeatAssignment.cabinClass holds values outside the four cabins:
'Premium Economy' (1 rows), 'STEERAGE' (2 rows), 'economy' (1 rows).
```

**It sets `lock_timeout`.** The verifier measured the rewrite at ~9.5s per million
rows and, more importantly, reproduced the lock queue: one open reader made the ALTER
wait 13s, and an ordinary `SELECT` arriving behind it blocked past its own timeout.
`docker-compose.yml` starts the one-shot `migrate` service *before* recreating `app`,
so on a redeploy the previous container is still serving seat maps from this table
while this runs. Failing fast and retryably beats freezing the table behind a lock
nobody chose to take.

**It documents its own reversal.** There are no down migrations in this repo, which
is consistent across all 28 — so the reversal is written into the header, along with
the fact that it needs no code/schema sequencing (the application only ever writes
the four names, so old code is fine against the enum and new code is fine against
TEXT).

## Verified against data, not just an empty database

Both directions, independently by me and by the verifier on separate scratch
databases:

- pre-change schema with `'STEERAGE'`, `'economy'` and `'Premium Economy'` rows →
  migration fails with the message above, and the failure **rolls back whole**: no
  orphan `CabinClass` type in `pg_type`, data untouched, retry clean
- clean data → applies, `udt_name` becomes `CabinClass`, existing rows preserved

`prisma migrate diff --from-migrations → --to-schema-datamodel --exit-code` reports
**no difference**, so the hand-authored SQL and `schema.prisma` agree exactly.

## What the verifier caught in my work

- **The enum stole the model's documentation.** I inserted it between
  `SeatAssignment`'s `///` block and the model with no blank line, so Prisma
  attributed the whole block to the enum and left the model — the one carrying the
  seat-uniqueness invariant — undocumented. Confirmed against the generated DMMF, not
  by eye. Moved.
- **One of my new assertions could not fail.** `cabinLabel` falls back to title-casing
  the enum, so "has a name, with no underscore" is satisfied by *any* enum-shaped
  input — deleting `FIRST: 'First Class'` would have printed "First" on the boarding
  pass and kept the test green. It now asserts the four words.
- **A bare `rejects.toThrow()`** would have gone green if a future constraint rejected
  that insert for an unrelated reason. Pinned to `/invalid input value for enum/`.
- **The database's own labels were unasserted** — the drift guard reads the generated
  client, i.e. `schema.prisma`. A second test reads `pg_enum` directly.
- **A cast in `FlightBookingService` is now provably redundant** and is removed; the
  verifier confirmed by probe that a genuine `string` would be a type error, so the
  type system is doing real work rather than silently widening.

## Recovery, which #73 asks for

A failed migration leaves Prisma refusing everything else with `P3009` rather than
the original error, and needs `prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back` before
retrying. That was undocumented, and this is the **second** migration here using a
`RAISE EXCEPTION` guard, so it is a recurring path rather than a one-off. It is now
in AGENTS.md's Gotchas along with the no-down-migrations convention.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (594 unit + 29 database), `npm run
build`, `migrate deploy` + seed on a fresh database, and Playwright.

The verifier confirmed no other read or write of the column behaves differently:
three write sites, all through schemas that narrow to the four; no raw-SQL write
outside the tests; no `orderBy`/`contains`/`startsWith` on the column, so the change
in sort semantics (alphabetical → declaration order) is unobservable today. Worth
knowing before someone adds a sort.

## Filed rather than fixed

Two pre-existing e2e flakes, each diagnosed to a mechanism and neither being #173 or
#178:

- **#181** — `search.spec.ts:30` reads the return date between two effects and
  captures a value derived from the previous route. The arithmetic confirms it:
  `2026-08-17 = 2026-08-10 + 7`, the route that was selected before.
- **#182** — `admin.spec.ts:74` navigates before the status change settles. The write
  lands correctly; the board just renders first.

gh issue create --title "Application types still say a cabin is any string" --label bug --body "Found while typing \`SeatAssignment.cabinClass\` in the database, and deliberately left out of that change because it is a chain rather than a line.

**Verification status:** the full narrowing was attempted and typechecked; the 15 resulting errors below are real, not predicted.

## What is loose

The column is now a Postgres enum. Three layers of application types still say \`string\`:

- \`lib/FlightBookingService.ts:23\` — \`PassengerInput.cabinClass: string\`, though \`cabinClassSchema\` has always enforced the four at the boundary and \`bookFlight\` re-parses through it
- \`lib/FlightBookingService.ts:79\` — a hand-written local type shapes \`passenger.seatAssignments[].cabinClass\` as \`string\`, shadowing what Prisma now generates
- a cast at \`lib/FlightBookingService.ts:~224\` exists only to bridge the first of these to \`calculateItineraryTotal\`, which correctly wants the union

## Why it was not folded in

Narrowing \`PassengerInput.cabinClass\` to \`CabinClass\` produces **15 errors across 4 files**: \`__tests__/app/actions.test.ts\` (2), \`__tests__/lib/FlightBookingService.test.ts\` (7), \`e2e/booking-authority.spec.ts\` (5), and the local type above (1). They are all the same shape — a fixture builds \`cabinClass: 'ECONOMY'\` inside a wider object literal, so the literal widens to \`string\` before it reaches the parameter.

None of that is hard, but it is a type refactor across the test and e2e suites, and folding it into a migration would have made a schema change hard to review.

## Fix

Narrow \`PassengerInput.cabinClass\` to \`CabinClass\` from \`lib/bookingPricing\`, let the local Prisma-shaped type use the generated enum, and give the fixtures \`as const\` or an explicit \`PassengerInput\` annotation. Then delete the cast.

Worth confirming while there that \`lib/bookingPricing.CabinClass\` and the generated Prisma \`CabinClass\` stay in step — \`__tests__/lib/cabinClass.test.ts\` already asserts they cover the same four, so the two can be reconciled rather than left as parallel definitions."

## The status update on #143

Recorded steps 1 and 2 as complete with the delivery table, the `seatOccupancy` prerequisite as done, and — the useful part — that **#73 is 5/7 already delivered**, so what remains is typed statuses rather than a phase of work.

It also carries a correction I nearly walked into: I was about to recommend "typed statuses" wholesale, but #143's own ownership table assigns **`Booking.status` typing to #76**. Taking it under #73 would have been exactly the collision that plan exists to prevent. The split is now written down: #76 owns booking status, #73 owns the Airport FK, and nobody owns `cabinClass` or `Flight.status`.

## The cabin enum

`SeatAssignment.cabinClass` was `TEXT NOT NULL` with no enum and no check constraint — the four-cabin rule lived only in Zod at the request boundary. Now the database says it.

The migration does three things beyond the cast: it names **every** offending value with counts before the cast can fail with one arbitrary one; it sets `lock_timeout`, because the verifier reproduced a rewrite waiting 13s behind a single open reader while `docker-compose` starts `migrate` with the previous container still serving seat maps; and it documents its own reversal, since this repo has no down migrations.

**The enum silently stole the model's documentation.** I put it between `SeatAssignment`'s `///` block and the model, so Prisma attributed the whole block to the enum and left the model undocumented. Caught against the generated DMMF, not by eye.

**The pre-push review blocked me, and its premise was wrong but its instinct wasn't.** It claimed the branch wouldn't build after I removed a cast; `tsc` exits 0, because the binding there is the Zod-parsed request rather than the DTO. But chasing its suggestion found real looseness — `PassengerInput.cabinClass` still says `string`, as does a hand-written type shadowing Prisma's. Narrowing them produces 15 errors across 4 files, almost all fixtures widening a literal. That's a type refactor across the test and e2e suites, so I restored the cast with a pointer and filed **#183** rather than smuggling it into a schema change.

Also filed **#181** and **#182** — two pre-existing e2e flakes, each diagnosed to a mechanism (a value read between two effects; a navigation before a transition settles), neither being #173 or #178.

Twelve merged this session. `Flight.status` is the other unowned enum and is the natural next slice — same shape, and I now have the migration pattern proven. After that it's the Airport FK, which needs your one decision: whether already-shared search URLs may 404 once routes move to IATA codes.

input.content:
-- Type whether a flight is running (#73).
--
-- `Flight.status` was `TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ON_TIME'` with no enum and no
-- check constraint, so the three-status rule existed only in
-- `flightStatusSchema` at the request boundary. A status written any other way
-- would be filtered on by search, counted by the admin board, and rendered to a
-- customer checking whether their flight is running -- where the board's label
-- lookup falls through to printing the raw value.
--
-- The three names are the ones already in use, so no row changes meaning. This
-- is a constraint arriving late.
--
-- To reverse:
--
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" ALTER COLUMN "status" DROP DEFAULT;
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" ALTER COLUMN "status" TYPE TEXT USING "status"::TEXT;
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" ALTER COLUMN "status" SET DEFAULT 'ON_TIME';
--     DROP TYPE "FlightStatus";
--     DELETE FROM _prisma_migrations WHERE migration_name = '20260807170000_type_flight_status';
--
-- Safe in either order against either version of the code: the application only
-- ever writes the three names, so old code is fine against the enum and new
-- code is fine against TEXT.

-- Fail fast rather than freeze the table.
--
-- The rewrite below takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on a table every search reads, and
-- `docker compose` starts the one-shot `migrate` service before recreating
-- `app`, so on a redeploy the previous container is still serving flight
-- searches while this runs. One open reader would otherwise hold the migration,
-- and the migration would hold everything queued behind it.
SET lock_timeout = '3s';

CREATE TYPE "FlightStatus" AS ENUM ('ON_TIME', 'DELAYED', 'CANCELLED');

-- Say what is wrong before the cast does.
--
-- `ALTER TABLE ... USING` fails on an unconvertible row by itself, but names
-- only the first value it choked on, and neither the table nor the column. An
-- operator meeting this mid-deployment needs to know everything that is in
-- there before deciding what each value should become.
DO $$
DECLARE
    unexpected TEXT;
BEGIN
    SELECT string_agg(DISTINCT format('%L (%s rows)', "status", n), ', ')
    INTO unexpected
    FROM (
        SELECT "status", count(*) AS n
        FROM "Flight"
        WHERE "status" NOT IN ('ON_TIME', 'DELAYED', 'CANCELLED')
        GROUP BY "status"
    ) AS outliers;

    IF unexpected IS NOT NULL THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION
            'Flight.status holds values outside the three statuses: %. '
            'Decide what each should become and update those rows before typing the column.',
            unexpected;
    END IF;
END $$;

-- The default has to go first and come back afterwards.
--
-- Postgres will not retype a column whose default it cannot cast, and the
-- existing default is a TEXT literal. Dropping it, retyping, then setting it
-- again is the whole reason this migration is three statements rather than one
-- -- and losing the last of them would leave every flight created without an
-- explicit status violating NOT NULL.
ALTER TABLE "Flight" ALTER COLUMN "status" DROP DEFAULT;

ALTER TABLE "Flight"
    ALTER COLUMN "status" TYPE "FlightStatus" USING "status"::"FlightStatus";

ALTER TABLE "Flight" ALTER COLUMN "status" SET DEFAULT 'ON_TIME';

gh issue create --title "The cabin-class migration's lock_timeout leaks into every later migration" --label bug --body "Found by the verifier while typing \`Flight.status\`, and proven with a probe migration rather than reasoned about.

**Verification status:** reproduced. A migration appended after \`20260807120000_type_cabin_class\` observed \`lock_timeout = 3s\` that it never set.

## The problem

\`prisma/migrations/20260807120000_type_cabin_class/migration.sql\` (#184) opens with:

\`\`\`sql
SET lock_timeout = '3s';
\`\`\`

A bare \`SET\` is **session**-scoped and commits with the migration. Prisma applies every migration in a deploy over one connection, so every migration authored after that one silently inherits a 3s lock timeout.

The consequence is a future migration doing legitimate long work on a busy table failing with \`canceling statement due to lock timeout\` for a reason nothing in its own file explains — and the failure then blocks the whole deploy until someone runs \`migrate resolve\`.

\`SET LOCAL\` is the fix, and it is safe because a Prisma migration file runs in one transaction (also verified: a deliberate error after the final statement rolled the whole file back).

## Why it cannot simply be edited

That migration is already applied. Prisma records a checksum per migration and \`migrate deploy\` refuses to run against a database whose applied migration file has changed, so editing it in place would break every environment that has already run it.

Options:

- A new migration that does \`RESET lock_timeout;\` — cheap, but it only helps deploys that reach it, and reads oddly out of context.
- Leave it and require every future migration needing a long lock to set its own \`SET LOCAL lock_timeout\` (or \`RESET\`) explicitly. Cheapest, and arguably right: a migration that cares about its lock behaviour should say so.
- Establish \`SET LOCAL\` as the convention so this cannot recur. \`20260807170000_type_flight_status\` already uses it.

I would take the second plus the third, and treat this issue as the place that records why.

## Related

Also worth writing down alongside it: a lock-timeout abort leaves the migration marked failed, so the next deploy reports \`P3009\` rather than the timeout. That is in AGENTS.md's Gotchas as of #184."

\`__tests__/lib/flightStatus.test.ts\` pins the Prisma enum against \`flightStatusSchema\`. These are not pinned:

Adding a fourth status to the enum and the Zod schema leaves all three silently incomplete **and the drift test green**, because a narrower union is assignable to the wider enum parameter.

\`components/ui/FlightStatusBoard.tsx:15\`, \`app/admin/flights/AdminFlightsTable.tsx:33\` and \`FlightStatusSelector\`'s \`currentStatus\` all declare \`status: string\`.

**Do not simply delete the default while the prop is \`string\`**: that trades an ugly label for a crash. Type the props as \`FlightStatus\` first, at which point both switches become exhaustive, the \`default\` branches can go, and adding a fourth status becomes a compile error at every rendering site rather than \`SCREAMING_SNAKE\` shown to a customer.

## Care needed

\`FlightStatus\` from \`@prisma/client\` used as a *value* (e.g. \`Object.values\` to build the \`<option>\` lists) is a runtime import, and these are client components — that is the trap #164 hit. input.content:
Part of #73, and the same treatment #184 gave `SeatAssignment.cabinClass`.
`Flight.status` was `TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ON_TIME'` with no enum and no check
constraint, so the three-status rule existed only in `flightStatusSchema` at the
request boundary.

A status written any other way would be filtered on by search, counted by the admin
board, and rendered to a customer checking whether their flight is running — where
the board's label lookup falls through to printing the raw value.

The three names are the ones already in use, so no row changes meaning.

## The difference from #184: this column has a default

Postgres will not retype a column whose default it cannot cast, so the migration is
**DROP DEFAULT → ALTER TYPE → SET DEFAULT**. Losing the last statement would leave
every flight created without an explicit status violating NOT NULL.

The verifier proved the whole file is one transaction by appending `SELECT 1/0;`
after the final statement: the column reverted to `text` with its original default
and no `FlightStatus` survived in `pg_type`. So a mid-file failure cannot leave the
column defaultless.

## `SET LOCAL`, not `SET`

A bare `SET lock_timeout` is session-scoped and commits with the migration, and
Prisma applies every migration in a deploy over one connection — so it silently
imposes itself on every migration written afterwards, which then fails for a reason
nothing in its own file explains. The verifier demonstrated this with a probe
migration that observed `lock_timeout = 3s` it never set.

`SET LOCAL` is safe here precisely because the file is one transaction. **#184
already shipped the leaking form**, and that migration cannot simply be edited —
Prisma checksums applied migrations — so that is **#185**.

## Verified against data, both directions

Independently by me and by the verifier, on separate scratch databases:

- `'DIVERTED'` ×2 and `'diverted'` ×1 present → migration fails naming both values
  with counts, `pg_type` has no orphan `FlightStatus`, column still `text`
- `migrate resolve --rolled-back` → fix the rows → `migrate deploy` applies, existing
  values preserved exactly
- default recast to `'ON_TIME'::"FlightStatus"`, and a **raw** insert omitting
  `status` gets `ON_TIME`
- lock timeout exercised: with an `ACCESS SHARE` lock held from another session the
  migration aborted after ~3s and rolled back cleanly

`prisma migrate diff` reports no difference between the migration chain and the
schema.

## The test that existed to protect the default did not protect it

The verifier deleted the third statement and my test still passed. Prisma
materialises `@default(ON_TIME)` client-side, so `flight.create()` sends the value
explicitly and never touches the column default — the assertion was testing
`schema.prisma`, not the migration.

It now asserts `information_schema.columns.column_default` directly **and** inserts
via raw SQL with the column omitted. Mutation-tested: dropping the default fails it,
restoring it passes.

## Also found

`satisfies Prisma.FlightCreateInput[]` on the seed fixtures is load-bearing, not
decoration — `prisma/seed.ts` passes them straight to `flight.create`, and without it
the literals widen to `string`, so a bad status would only fail when Postgres
rejected the insert. It also caught my own mistake: I put it on the wrong array first
(the file exports two), which type-checked `FlightScheduleData` against
`FlightCreateInput` and produced spurious errors. It is on `FlightData`;
`FlightScheduleData` is unconstrained.

The verifier confirmed nothing bypasses the boundary: every write is a Prisma call
with a literal, no raw SQL touches the column, reads are equality-only, and there is
**no `orderBy: { status }`** anywhere — which matters, because an enum sorts by
declaration order rather than alphabetically and that would have been a silent
behaviour change.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (597 unit + 33 database), `npm run
build`, `migrate deploy` + `db seed` on a fresh database, and the full Playwright
suite — **28/28 first run, no retries**, including `admin.spec.ts:74` and
`search.spec.ts:30`, so none of #173/#178/#181/#182 reproduced.

Rendered UI review is not applicable: the three values and their labels are
unchanged, no prop type or rendering path changed, and the admin spec that flips a
live status and re-reads the board passes.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#185** — the leaking `SET lock_timeout` in #184's already-applied migration, with
  the checksum constraint that stops it being edited in place
- **#186** — three more hand-maintained copies of the statuses (an action parameter
  type, the admin selector's cast and options, the board's options), plus the render
  props still typed `string`. That last part is what keeps `getStatusLabel`'s
  `default` branch from being provably dead; typing the props is the fix, and
  deleting the branch while the prop is `string` would trade an ugly label for a
  crash.

input.description: Check whether route strings map cleanly to airports

content.text:
## The premise in #143 is wrong — nothing 404s

`parseFlightSearchParams` returns `undefined` for anything it doesn't recognise, and `app/page.tsx:68` passes that straight to the form as `initialSearch`. So an unrecognised URL today doesn't error — **it silently renders the default search form**, discarding the visitor's intent with no explanation.

That reframes the choice. It isn't "keep working vs 404." It's "keep working vs silently show someone a blank search for the wrong route."

## Honouring the old form costs one lookup

The mapping is already total:

```
Airport.label   = 'Paris, France'   (matches the route string format exactly, @unique)
distinct route cities: 9    airports: 10    unmatched route strings: 0
```

Every city string in circulation resolves to exactly one IATA code. There's no ambiguity to resolve and no data to backfill.

## The codebase has already decided this exact question

In the same file, twelve lines above the `from`/`to` check:

> *An absent cabin is the default, not an invalid link: older shared URLs predate the parameter. An unrecognised one is invalid, because it would silently show a different cabin from the one the link named.*

The principle is already set: **fall back when the meaning is unambiguous, reject when it would silently mean something different.** `?from=Seattle,+USA` has exactly one meaning. Rejecting it would contradict a rule this file already states.

## Recommendation: read both, write one, redirect to canonical

1. **Accept** both `?from=SEA` and `?from=Seattle,+USA` when parsing, resolving the legacy form through `Airport.label`.
2. **Emit** only IATA from `buildFlightSearchUrl` — the app never produces the old form again.
3. **Redirect** a legacy URL to its canonical equivalent, so the old spelling stops propagating the moment someone follows a link.

That last step is what makes this a shim with a lifetime rather than a permanent second spelling. The legacy form only ever appears inbound, it disappears from anything shared onward, and you can delete the compatibility path later with evidence that it's gone quiet instead of a guess.

## What would change my mind

If the URLs genuinely aren't shared anywhere — no bookmarks, no external links, no traffic — the shim is dead weight and dropping it is right. I can't verify that from here; there's no share affordance in the UI and no analytics. But the cost of being wrong is asymmetric: the shim is ~10 lines and a redirect, while getting it wrong silently breaks every link that exists and gives the visitor no clue why.

## One real risk worth naming

City labels can change — renaming `'Rio de Janeiro, Brazil'` would break the legacy lookup for links using the old label. IATA codes don't change, which is itself an argument for the switch and for canonicalising aggressively rather than treating both spellings as equals.

Want me to take #73's Airport FK slice on that basis? It's the last piece of #73 that's actually owned by it, and this decision is the only thing blocking it.
Ok lets go with your Recommendations
Ok since we have not launched this yet there is no worry of links being shared anywhere

That's the fact I couldn't check, and it settles it the other way: **drop the shim entirely.** IATA only, no legacy spelling, no redirect. Maintaining compatibility with links that don't exist is pure cost.

What that removes is smaller than it sounds, though — it's the URL layer only:

- **Gone**: label→IATA resolution in the parser, the canonical redirect, and the tests for both
- **Unchanged**: the data migration itself. 1,414 flights still carry city strings in `Flight.from`/`to`, and those still have to become `Airport` foreign keys. That work is the same either way.

So the slice is now: convert the columns to FKs, switch the search URL to IATA outright, and update the seed and fixtures. No compatibility path anywhere.

Two things I'd want to settle before writing SQL, since this is the biggest migration yet:

**Do `from`/`to` become FK columns, or do the string columns stay alongside?** #143's table lists this as `Flight.from/to → Airport FK` with #84 and #78 as consumers, which implies replacement. But every read path — search, the status board, the boarding pass, `AdminFlightsTable` — currently renders those strings directly, so replacing them outright means each of those joins or denormalises a label. That's a wide change.

**One migration or two?** Add the FK columns and backfill first, cut the reads over, then drop the strings second — the pattern #135/#137 used and that this repo clearly favours. That keeps each PR reviewable and rollback-able, at the cost of two round trips.

My inclination is the two-step, following the precedent already set here. Shall I take the first step — add the FK columns, backfill from `Airport.label`, leave the strings in place and reads untouched?

-- Point a flight at the airports it touches (#73).
--
-- `Flight.from` and `Flight.to` carry free text -- 'Seattle, USA' -- which is
-- both the identity of the place and the words rendered to a customer. Editing
-- the prose therefore silently repoints the route, and nothing stops a flight
-- naming somewhere no airport exists.
--
-- This is the first of two steps. It adds the references and fills them; the
-- reads still render `from`/`to`, and dropping those columns is the second
-- step, once every read path has moved. Splitting it keeps each change
-- reviewable and each rollback a single statement, which is the shape #135 and
-- #137 used for the same reason.
--
-- To reverse:
--
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" DROP CONSTRAINT "Flight_toAirportCode_fkey";
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" DROP CONSTRAINT "Flight_fromAirportCode_fkey";
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" DROP COLUMN "toAirportCode";
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" DROP COLUMN "fromAirportCode";
--     DELETE FROM _prisma_migrations WHERE migration_name = '20260807210000_flight_airport_references';
--
-- Safe against either version of the code while `from`/`to` remain: nothing
-- reads the new columns yet.
--
-- If the guard below rejects the data, the migration is marked failed and no
-- later one applies until it is cleared:
--
--     npx prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back 20260807210000_flight_airport_references

-- LOCAL, so it lasts only this transaction rather than being inherited by every
-- migration written after it.
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s';

-- Nullable first, so the backfill has somewhere to write.
ALTER TABLE "Flight" ADD COLUMN "fromAirportCode" TEXT;
ALTER TABLE "Flight" ADD COLUMN "toAirportCode" TEXT;

UPDATE "Flight" f
SET "fromAirportCode" = origin."iataCode"
FROM "Airport" origin
WHERE origin."label" = f."from";

UPDATE "Flight" f
SET "toAirportCode" = destination."iataCode"
FROM "Airport" destination
WHERE destination."label" = f."to";

-- Say which places are unaccounted for, rather than which constraint failed.
--
-- A route naming somewhere with no airport row is a data question, not a schema
-- one: someone has to decide whether the airport is missing from the reference
-- data or the flight is wrong. NOT NULL would report neither the place nor how
-- many flights are stranded on it.
DO $$
DECLARE
    unmatched TEXT;
BEGIN
    SELECT string_agg(DISTINCT format('%L (%s flights)', place, n), ', ')
    INTO unmatched
    FROM (
        SELECT "from" AS place, count(*) AS n FROM "Flight" WHERE "fromAirportCode" IS NULL GROUP BY "from"
        UNION ALL
        SELECT "to" AS place, count(*) AS n FROM "Flight" WHERE "toAirportCode" IS NULL GROUP BY "to"
    ) AS gaps;

    IF unmatched IS NOT NULL THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION
            'No airport matches these places named by flights: %. '
            'Add them to the Airport table, or correct the flights, before referencing airports.',
            unmatched;
    END IF;
END $$;

ALTER TABLE "Flight" ALTER COLUMN "fromAirportCode" SET NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE "Flight" ALTER COLUMN "toAirportCode" SET NOT NULL;

ALTER TABLE "Flight"
    ADD CONSTRAINT "Flight_fromAirportCode_fkey"
    FOREIGN KEY ("fromAirportCode") REFERENCES "Airport"("iataCode")
    ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE;

ALTER TABLE "Flight"
    ADD CONSTRAINT "Flight_toAirportCode_fkey"
    FOREIGN KEY ("toAirportCode") REFERENCES "Airport"("iataCode")
    ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE;

CREATE INDEX "Flight_fromAirportCode_idx" ON "Flight"("fromAirportCode");
CREATE INDEX "Flight_toAirportCode_idx" ON "Flight"("toAirportCode");

input.content:
The last piece of #73 that #143's ownership table assigns to it. `Flight.from` and
`Flight.to` are free text that is simultaneously the identity of a place and the
words rendered to a customer — so editing the prose silently repointed a route, and
nothing stopped a flight naming somewhere no airport exists.

**Step one of two.** The references are here and filled; every read path still
renders `from`/`to`. Dropping the labels and moving the reads is step two. Splitting
it keeps each change reviewable and each rollback a single statement, which is the
shape #135 and #137 used.

Since the product has not launched there are **no shared search URLs to preserve**,
so the compatibility shim I had recommended is deliberately absent and the search URL
keeps using labels until step two.

## The migration

`SET LOCAL lock_timeout`, add nullable, two backfill `UPDATE`s joining on
`Airport.label`, a guard naming unmatched places with flight counts, then NOT NULL,
two foreign keys (`ON DELETE RESTRICT`) and two indexes.

The verifier threw twelve adversarial rows at it — leading and trailing whitespace,
both case variants, a bare city, an IATA code in the label column, an empty string,
an unknown destination — and every one was named with counts:

```
ERROR: No airport matches these places named by flights: ' Seattle, USA' (1 flights),
'' (1 flights), 'Atlantis, Nowhere' (2 flights), 'JFK' (1 flights), 'SEA' (2 flights),
'SEATTLE, USA' (1 flights), 'Seattle' (1 flights), 'Seattle, USA ' (1 flights),
'Toronto, Canada' (1 flights), 'seattle, usa' (1 flights)
```

Duplicate labels are unreachable — `Airport_label_key` is unique, so the backfill
cannot match two rows and pick arbitrarily. Failure leaves no columns behind, and
recovery via `migrate resolve --rolled-back` then retry backfills correctly. It also
aborted in ~3s when a lock was held from another session, which proves both the
transaction and `SET LOCAL`.

## A required key means every writer learns about airports

All four resolve through one function that refuses an unknown place rather than
guessing one. **Three fixtures turned out to be using IATA codes (`'SEA'`, `'JFK'`)
or bare city names (`'New York'`) where a label belonged** — the resolver caught
them, which is the point.

## The regression this introduced, and how it is fixed

`ui-review` and the verifier both landed on this. `saveFlightScheduleAction` resolved
the codes *inside the occurrence loop*, which runs **after** the schedule is written.
A typo therefore left the write standing and threw — and Next masks server-action
messages in production, so an administrator saw a generic failure for a save that had
succeeded. `flightScheduleForm.tsx` renders origin as free text with a placeholder
naming a *different* city, so `New York` is a plausible thing to type.

Now it resolves before the write and returns a validation failure, the way every
other fixable input in that action does. Three further things `ui-review` measured:

- **The `fields` payload was dead data.** The form kept only the summary message, so
  nothing reached the input — `aria-describedby` and `aria-invalid` were both null. I
  had claimed it was field-level; it was not. It is now, following the pattern
  `flightBookingForm.tsx` already uses.
- **The message rendered off-screen.** On phone the alert sat 232px above the
  viewport, so a rejected save looked like nothing happened. Focus now moves to the
  first field that needs changing, which fixes that and the next one together.
- **Focus was dropped to `<body>`** and Tab walked forward out of the form entirely.

Both ends are now reported at once — the short-circuit meant an unknown origin *and*
destination cost two round trips, with the second field left looking valid meanwhile.
That needed a multi-field `actionValidationFailures` helper, since the existing one
takes a single field.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (607 unit + 38 database), `npm run
build`, `migrate deploy` + `db seed` on a fresh database, and the full Playwright
suite — 28/28 first try, no retries, so none of #173/#178/#181/#182 reproduced.

The verifier confirmed: no fifth writer (`scripts/generate-inventory.ts` routes
through the service already changed, and nothing anywhere updates `from`/`to` after
creation, so labels cannot drift from codes); `ON DELETE RESTRICT` refuses removing
a referenced airport and `ON UPDATE CASCADE` is inert; the whole-table
label-equals-code assertion catches one wrong row in 1400; and no assertion was
weakened by the fixture edits — including one regex edit that hit a *search*
assertion, which I reverted.

New tests are mutation-tested: the schedule guard fails against the pre-fix code, and
the form tests fail without the `fields` wiring.

## Known limits, recorded rather than papered over

The whole-table equality assertion is stronger than any constraint and covers data it
does not own: renaming a city in `AirportData` and re-seeding updates `Airport.label`
while existing `Flight.from` keeps the old prose, and the test then fails on hundreds
of rows though nothing is broken. `ON UPDATE CASCADE` gives the mirror case. Both are
inert today and both disappear in step two.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#188** — admin types origins and destinations as free text over a ten-value
  domain, while the customer-facing form already uses a `<select>` over the same
  domain. A select makes this class of rejection unreachable. Includes the related
  finding that the form's "Edit" branch has no route into it.

That's now genuinely field-level, reports both ends at once instead of costing two round trips, and moves focus to the first thing to change. Three component tests pin it, mutation-tested against the unfixed form.

A useful side effect: the resolver caught **three existing fixtures** using IATA codes or bare city names where a label belonged.

## The CI failure was not mine

`npm audit` started failing every branch on a newly-published `nanoid` advisory reaching us via `next → postcss`. I split that into its own PR rather than bury a dependency pin inside a large migration — it unblocked every branch, not just this one — then rebased and re-verified.

## Where #73 stands

Its owned migration is done. Remaining under #73: `currency` and notification types, both smaller, and `currency` arguably belongs with payments (#75). `Booking.status` stays with #76.

Step two — dropping `from`/`to` and moving reads to the airport relation — is the natural next slice, and it's the one that also moves the search URL to IATA codes. Filed **#188** along the way: admin types origins as free text over a ten-value domain while the customer-facing form already uses a select over the same domain, which would make that whole class of rejection unreachable.
