input.content:
Step two of #73's route work, after #189 added the references. Every read of where
a flight goes now comes from the `Airport` rows it points at. The columns still
exist and still hold the same words, so **this is intended to be invisible** —
which is the point: it is what makes dropping them a migration rather than a
rewrite.

## What moved

`lib/flightRoute.ts` holds all of it, so no component learned about airports:

- `flightRouteInclude` — the relation a route-rendering query has to ask for.
  Spreads into a `select` as readily as an `include`.
- `withRouteLabels(flight)` — swaps the two columns for the airport labels, so
  every view keeps receiving a flight with `from` and `to` on it.
- `withLegRouteLabels(leg)` — the same for an itinerary leg.
- `flightRouteWhere(from, to)` — narrows a query by the airports rather than the
  prose.

Read sites migrated: search (both directions and the no-date branch), the
`/flights` status board, checkout, `/profile` history and points activity,
`/admin` recent bookings, `/admin/flights`, the booking-confirmation
notification, and the flight-status-change notification.

## The filter mattered as much as the render

`where: { from, to }` matched the label columns, so a search depended on two rows
spelling a place identically — and it kept the columns load-bearing long after
nothing rendered them. Those now filter on `fromAirportCode`/`toAirportCode`.

`flightRouteWhere` returns `null` when no airport answers to a name, and the
caller returns an empty result without querying. That is the same empty result
the label match gave, reached without a round trip — and `?from=` is a
user-controlled query parameter, so an unknown place is reachable.

`FlightSchedule.from`/`to` are deliberately untouched. That model has no airport
references; giving it them is separate work.

## Verification

The new database test writes a flight whose `from`/`to` columns say
`'Nowhere, Atlantis'` while its references say Seattle→Detroit, then searches. If
any read path still depends on the columns the flight either fails to come back
or comes back naming nowhere. Mutation-tested both ways: restoring the label
`where` fails two of the three cases, dropping `withRouteLabels` fails the third.

The status-notification unit test got the same treatment — its fixture's columns
now disagree with its airports, so the asserted message can only be right if the
code reads the references.

## What remains of #73

Step three drops `Flight.from` and `Flight.to`. The search URL still carries
labels; moving it to IATA codes is part of that step, and needs no compatibility
shim because the product has not launched.

gh issue create --title "Playwright silently reuses a stale dev server and reports a false failure" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Cost real time during #73 step 2a, and produced a **false regression signal** — verified against running code.

## Where

`playwright.config.ts:36-42`:

```ts
webServer: {
  command: 'npm run dev',
  url: 'http://localhost:3000',
  reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  ...
}
```

## What was observed

`e2e/admin.spec.ts:75` failed 3 runs out of 3 at line 244 — the flight was on the board but its status was never `Delayed`. The same spec passed on `HEAD`. That looks exactly like a regression in the branch, and I started bisecting the diff on that basis.

It was not a regression. A dev server left running from an earlier full-suite run was being reused, and it was serving stale output. After `pkill -f "next dev"`, the unchanged branch passed the spec 3 runs out of 3 and the full suite passed 28/28.

The bisect was worthless for a second reason that follows from the same line: because `webServer` runs `npm run dev`, `npm run build` before a Playwright run changes nothing about what is served. Reverting a file and rebuilding appeared to fix the failure when all it did was restart the server.

## Why it matters

Two failure modes, and the second is the dangerous one:

- A stale server makes a healthy branch look broken, which is where the time goes.
- A stale server can equally make a **broken branch look healthy** — the suite reports a pass against code that is not the code under test. `reuseExistingServer` is off in CI, so this is local-only, but local is where the pre-push decision gets made.

## Suggested fix

Either set `reuseExistingServer: false` outright, or keep the reuse and have the config assert the server is the current one — the runbook note alone is not enough, because nothing surfaces at the point of confusion. Related: #173, where the same line came up alongside e2e cleanup.
EOF

input.content:
Step two of #73's route work, after #189 added the references. Every read of where
a flight goes now comes from the `Airport` rows it points at. The columns still
exist and hold the same words, so **this is intended to be invisible** — which is
the point: it is what makes dropping them a migration rather than a rewrite.

## What moved

`lib/flightRoute.ts` holds all of it, so no component learned about airports:

- `flightRouteInclude` — the relation a route-rendering query asks for. Spreads
  into a `select` as readily as an `include`.
- `withRouteLabels(flight)` / `withLegRouteLabels(leg)` — swap the columns for the
  airport labels, so every view keeps receiving a flight with `from` and `to`.
- `flightRouteWhere(from, to)` — narrows a query by the airports, not the prose.

Read sites migrated: search (both directions and the dateless branch), the
`/flights` status board, checkout, `/profile` history and points activity,
`/admin`, `/admin/flights`, and both notification paths.

## The filter mattered as much as the render

`where: { from, to }` made a search depend on two rows spelling a place
identically, and kept the columns load-bearing regardless of what was displayed.
Those now filter on `fromAirportCode`/`toAirportCode`.

`flightRouteWhere` returns `null` when no airport answers to a name and the caller
returns empty without querying — the same result the label match gave. `?from=` is
user-controlled, so an unknown place is reachable.

`FlightSchedule.from`/`to` are untouched: that model has no references, and giving
it them is separate work.

## Verification, and what it caught

Two database suites write a flight whose columns say `'Nowhere, Atlantis'` while
its references say Seattle→Detroit — the only way to tell which source a page read,
since on every real row the two agree. Each of the seven converted paths was
mutation-tested by reverting it.

Three `verifier` rounds ran, and the first two found real holes rather than
confirming the work:

- **Five of the seven paths were covered by nothing.** They reverted cleanly with
  the entire suite green. That is the whole value of this change, so the page-level
  suite exists to close it.
- **My first version of that suite was vacuous for three of four cases** — the
  fixture departed outside the window `/admin/flights` renders, so assertions were
  passing on other seeded flights that happen to name Seattle. Fixed, with a
  flight-number assertion in every case as the non-vacuity guard (#155 again).
- **Asserting the route as text was still too weak.** A seeded reversed flight
  satisfies it on the fixture's behalf, and `/admin/flights` ships `FlightSchedule`
  prose carrying the same keys — that case was outright vacuous. The suite now
  finds the fixture's own flight object by flight number and reads the route off
  it.
- **The element walk was blind to host-element props**, so a column leaking through
  `title` or `aria-label` would have passed. It walks them now.
- Two further mutants survived and are now caught: dropping the `include` from the
  dateless search (a `TypeError` on every dateless search, reachable from the
  form), and re-attaching the relation objects to `updateFlightStatusAction`'s
  return value.

Final: `npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 608 unit + 48 database,
`npm run build`, and Playwright 28/28.

`ui-review` stood up a second server on the pre-change tree and diffed both:
text byte-identical across seven journeys at three viewports, 47 of 51 screenshot
pairs identical at 0.000% (the four are focus/hover timing).

One thing worth knowing: `admin.spec.ts` failed 3 runs of 3 and passed on `HEAD`,
which looked exactly like a regression. It was a stale dev server being reused —
filed as #196, because it can equally make a broken branch look healthy.

## Filed rather than fixed

#191 (the label→code and code→label mappings read different sources — the one
finding inside this slice's scope, and noted in `flightRouteWhere`), #192, #193,
#194, #195, #196, plus a note on #173.

## What remains of #73

Step three drops the columns. The search URL still carries labels; moving it to
IATA codes belongs there, and needs no compatibility shim because the product has
not launched.

input.content:
-- Stop storing a flight's route twice (#73).
--
-- `Flight.from` and `Flight.to` were free text that was simultaneously the
-- identity of a place and the words rendered to a customer. Editing the prose
-- silently repointed a route, and nothing stopped a flight naming somewhere no
-- airport exists.
--
-- The references arrived in #189 and every read moved to them in #197, so these
-- two columns have been write-only since. This removes the second answer to
-- "where does this flight go", which is what made the first one unreliable.
--
-- To reverse:
--
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" ADD COLUMN "from" TEXT, ADD COLUMN "to" TEXT;
--     UPDATE "Flight" f SET "from" = a."label"
--       FROM "Airport" a WHERE a."iataCode" = f."fromAirportCode";
--     UPDATE "Flight" f SET "to" = a."label"
--       FROM "Airport" a WHERE a."iataCode" = f."toAirportCode";
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" ALTER COLUMN "from" SET NOT NULL,
--                          ALTER COLUMN "to" SET NOT NULL;
--     DELETE FROM _prisma_migrations WHERE migration_name = '20260808120000_drop_flight_route_text';
--
-- The reversal reconstructs the labels from the airports, which is exactly what
-- the guard below proves they already are -- so nothing is lost that the
-- reversal cannot put back. It is safe against either version of the code:
-- old code reads columns that are there again, new code ignores them.
--
-- If the lock timeout aborts this, or the guard rejects the data, the migration
-- is marked failed and no later one applies until it is cleared:
--
--     npx prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back 20260808120000_drop_flight_route_text

-- Fail fast rather than freeze the table.
--
-- DROP COLUMN takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on a table every search reads, and
-- `docker compose` starts the one-shot `migrate` service before recreating
-- `app`, so the previous container is still serving searches while this runs.
-- LOCAL, so it lasts only this transaction: a bare SET commits with the
-- migration and would impose itself on every migration authored afterwards
-- (#185).
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s';

-- Prove the columns are redundant before destroying them.
--
-- Dropping a column is the one change no later migration can undo from the
-- data, so this refuses to run while either column still says something the
-- airports do not. A disagreement means a label was edited after the flight was
-- written, and an operator has to decide which of the two is right -- silently
-- keeping the airport's answer would discard the other one unrecorded.
DO $$
DECLARE
    disagreements TEXT;
BEGIN
    SELECT string_agg(
        format('%s: %L/%L vs %L/%L', "flightNumber", "from", "to", origin_label, destination_label),
        ', '
        ORDER BY "flightNumber"
    )
    INTO disagreements
    FROM (
        SELECT f."flightNumber", f."from", f."to",
               origin."label" AS origin_label,
               destination."label" AS destination_label
        FROM "Flight" f
        JOIN "Airport" origin ON origin."iataCode" = f."fromAirportCode"
        JOIN "Airport" destination ON destination."iataCode" = f."toAirportCode"
        WHERE origin."label" <> f."from" OR destination."label" <> f."to"
        LIMIT 20
    ) AS mismatched;

    IF disagreements IS NOT NULL THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION
            'Flight.from/to disagree with the airports these flights reference: %. '
            'Each is a route that reads one way and books another. Decide which is '
            'right and correct the row or the airport label before dropping the columns.',
            disagreements;
    END IF;
END $$;

ALTER TABLE "Flight" DROP COLUMN "from";
ALTER TABLE "Flight" DROP COLUMN "to";

import pathlib, re, subprocess

files = subprocess.run(['npx','tsc','--noEmit'], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
targets = sorted({l.split('(')[0] for l in files.splitlines() if l.startswith(('__tests__','e2e'))})

# Remove only a `from:`/`to:` pair that sits directly above an
# airportCodesForRoute spread inside a create -- the spread is what proves the
# lines belong to a Flight create rather than to a where clause or an assertion.
pattern = re.compile(r'^([ \t]*)from:[^\n]*\n[ \t]*to:[^\n]*\n(?=[ \t]*\.\.\.airportCodesForRoute\()', re.M)

for f in targets:
    p = pathlib.Path(f)
    if not p.exists(): continue
    s = p.read_text()
    new, n = pattern.subn('', s)
    if n: p.write_text(new); print(f'{n:2d} removed  {f}')

        FROM "Flight" f
        JOIN "Airport" origin ON origin."iataCode" = f."fromAirportCode"
        JOIN "Airport" destination ON destination."iataCode" = f."toAirportCode"
        WHERE origin."label" <> f."from" OR destination."label" <> f."to"

new="""    SELECT string_agg(
        format('%s: %L/%L vs %L/%L', "flightNumber", "from", "to", origin_label, destination_label),

        -- that row, and it is the one row whose label cannot be reconstructed

        -- cannot satisfy. Both foreign keys are validated and RESTRICT, so
        -- reaching this needs replication-role trickery; it is handled anyway
        -- because the cost of being wrong here is an unrecoverable reversal.

        LEFT JOIN "Airport" destination ON destination."iataCode" = f."toAirportCode"

input.content:
The last structural piece of #73's route work, after #189 added the references and
#197 moved every read onto them. `Flight.from` and `Flight.to` have been write-only
since, and this removes them along with the four writers that filled them.

They were free text that was simultaneously the identity of a place and the words
shown to a customer, so editing the prose silently repointed a route and nothing
stopped a flight naming somewhere no airport exists.

## The migration

`SET LOCAL lock_timeout`, a guard, then two `DROP COLUMN`s.

Dropping a column is the one change no later migration can undo from the data, so
the guard refuses to run while either column still says something the airports do
not. A disagreement means a label was edited after the flight was written, and an
operator has to decide which of the two is right — silently keeping the airport's
answer would discard the other one unrecorded.

Verified on scratch databases, by me and independently by the `verifier`:

- Two disagreeing rows and one agreeing: fails naming both bad ones and not the
  good one, columns survive, migration recorded failed, second deploy gives `P3009`
- `migrate resolve --rolled-back` → correct the rows → redeploy succeeds
- The reversal in the header reconstructs the labels exactly — 0 mismatches over 40
  rows
- From empty: `migrate deploy` + `db seed` gives 1412 flights, no orphan references,
  and `migrate diff` reports no difference
- Lock timeout applies: with a lock held from another session it aborts with `55P03`
  after ~3s and both columns survive, which also proves the file is one transaction
  and `SET LOCAL` is therefore not a silent no-op

The verifier found the guard's inner join let a flight referencing a **deleted**
airport slip past unchecked — and that row is precisely the one the reversal cannot
reconstruct, so it would fail on a `NOT NULL` it cannot satisfy. Reaching that state
needs `session_replication_role = replica`, since both FKs are validated and
`RESTRICT`, but the cost of being wrong is an unrecoverable reversal. It is a
`LEFT JOIN` with `IS DISTINCT FROM` now, and the message states the true total
rather than silently capping at 20.

## Removing the columns removed a cross-check

The whole-table invariant asserting the columns agreed with the airports is gone,
because the disagreement is now unstateable. That invariant was also what caught a
writer resolving a route to the *wrong* airports — and the verifier proved the gap
was real: reversing `airportCodesForRoute(from, to)` in `prisma/seed.ts` seeded 1412
flights onto backwards routes with all 608 unit and 48 database tests green.

The other three writers each fail a unit assertion on their create payload; the seed
was the only one without. It has one now, against the routes `FlightData` itself
names, covering 786 rows across both writers. Mutation-tested: the swap fails it.

## The two suites from #197 were rebuilt

Both were designed around a fixture whose columns contradicted its airports — the
only way to ask *which of two sources* a read used. That question is unaskable now,
so they assert the resolution itself: a page that forgets the relation gets
`undefined`, one that maps it wrongly gets the route backwards.

The fixture is Rio → Miami, because the seed flies Miami → Rio and not the reverse,
so no other row can satisfy the assertions on its behalf. The verifier confirmed
that against the seeded data (`GIG->MIA = 0`, `MIA->GIG = 157`) and re-ran the
mutation set: all 18 mutants killed, none that previously died now survives.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 608 unit + 49 database, `npm run
build`, Playwright 28/28 on a single cold run with no retries.

`ui-review` drove all eight journeys at three viewports, including creating a
schedule through the admin form — the path that writes new flights — and confirmed
the 30 generated occurrences render correctly, the unknown-place rejection is still
field-level and reports both fields at once, and no route renders `undefined`,
blank, or differently spaced.

## Filed rather than fixed

#198, #199, #200, #202, plus a comment on #193. And **#201**, which is not a
finding so much as a contradiction worth recording: `ui-review` measured focus
dropping to `<body>` after the schedule form rejects an unknown place, while the
jsdom test asserting that exact behaviour passes. Both can be true if a re-render
races the `requestAnimationFrame`. It needs a browser assertion to settle, and if
the browser is right then a test I added in #189 is asserting something
jsdom-specific.

## What remains of #73

The search URL still carries labels rather than IATA codes. That is the last piece,
it is independently shippable, and it needs no compatibility shim because the
product has not launched — so this PR does not close the issue.

def to_codes(m):
    global converted
    origin, destination = m.group(2), m.group(4)
    # Already a code (the new cases), or a place these fixtures never use.
    if origin not in CODES or destination not in CODES:
        return m.group(0)
    converted += 1
    return f'{m.group(1)}{CODES[origin]}{m.group(3)}{CODES[destination]}{m.group(5)}'

s = pattern.sub(to_codes, s)
print(f'param objects converted: {converted}')
p.write_text(s)

translation happens at the boundary. `buildFlightSearchUrl` writes codes,
`parseFlightSearchParams` reads them back as labels.

**No compatibility shim**, per the call that nothing has launched. An old-format
link is refused rather than accepted, so two spellings of the same link cannot both
survive.

## Refusing quietly was the harder half

`ui-review` blocked on this, and it was right: a rejected link fell back to the
default search in complete silence. The address bar said Seattle → Detroit, one-way,
20 Aug; the page showed Chicago → Paris, round trip, 10 Aug, with nothing to
distinguish it from a first visit. The no-shim decision *creates* that population —
old links are the expected path, not an edge case.

So the page now says the link was not used. Three things fell out of that, each
found by review rather than by me:

- **The notice never cleared.** Reading it straight from the prop meant it survived
  the traveller's own successful search, because the search rewrites the URL with
  `replaceState` and never re-renders the server component — a red banner sitting
  above results that contradict it, the mirror image of the bug being fixed.
- **A refused link still moved the booking window.** The origin is resolved before
  parsing, because the window is what parsing validates dates against; when parsing
  then refused the link, the selectable dates stayed in Tokyo while the form showed
  Chicago. It now comes back to the origin actually on screen.
- **Links refused for their date or cabin fell back silently**, because the check
  gated on `from`/`to` alone.

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 634 unit + 49 database, `npm run

booking-window timezone resolves identically from a code as it did from a label for
all ten origins — measured at 23:56 UTC, when zones straddle the date boundary and
the check is at its most discriminating.

The `verifier` then found **four mutations that survived the whole suite**: the
`?? ''` fallback reinstating the label format, `airportLabelFor` becoming tolerant
of case and whitespace (a shim by the back door), and two ways the refusal notice
could be wrong. The root cause was that `app/page.tsx` had no test, so the predicate
is now an exported function with direct coverage. All four are caught.

It also caught two decayed assertions in my own new e2e: one comparing against
`encodeURIComponent`, which writes `%20` where a query string writes `+`, so it
could never match; and a hard-coded date that would have started passing for the
wrong reason in twelve days.

## Filed rather than fixed

#204 (no visible focus indicator on the search selects), #205 (shared-link arrival
drops focus past the whole form), #206 (return date clipped to `08/17/202`). All
pre-existing, all made more visible by this change, none caused by it.

It finishes the `Flight.from`/`to` work. The issue's typed-statuses task remains:

content.text:
Six issues, and they group naturally. My plan is three slices, worst-first:

1. **Run isolation** (#196 + #173) — the two that make a run untrustworthy in both directions
2. **The two e2e races** (#181, #182)

Starting with the first. Reading the detail:

input.command:

gh issue view 173 --json body -q .body | sed -n 14,60p

result.output:
```

Seat 11A is already taken, so the seat map renders it as occupied and the selector
matching the *selectable* button finds nothing.

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM "SeatAssignment" WHERE "seatNumber" = '11A';  -- 2
```

## Why it is permanent once it happens

`e2e/global-setup.ts` truncates `authRateLimit` and nothing else. Bookings,
passengers, itinerary legs and seat assignments all survive between runs. So the
first run books 11A on the seeded flight and **every subsequent run of those three
specs fails on that database, forever**, until someone reseeds by hand.

This is why the suite passes in CI — CI migrates and seeds a clean database each
time — and rots locally.

## Options

- Have `global-setup.ts` clear the booking tables the way it already clears
  `authRateLimit`. Simple, and matches the existing intent of that file.
- Or have each spec pick a seat that is free at that moment rather than hard-coding
  `11A`, the way `booking.spec.ts` already does for the inbound leg
  (`locator('button[title^="Select Seat"]').nth(1)`).

The first is the better fix: three specs hard-code `11A` today, and a seat chosen at
random makes a failure harder to read.

## Related

This is adjacent to #155, which was the same class of problem inside Jest — tests
sharing one database and interfering with each other. That one was solved by
serialising; this one needs cleanup rather than ordering, because the interference
is between *runs* rather than within one.

content.text: Confirmed pre-existing — it fails on unmodified `main` too, so I didn't cause it. But it makes the suite red, and it's one of the six issues in this cleanup, so I'll fix it here rather than open a PR I know CI may reject:

gh issue view 182 --json body -q .body | sed -n 12,50p

result.output:
```
1629 | 2026-08-08 10:00 | DELAYED
```

inside the board's `now-2h .. now+7d` window, with 29 rows in the window so `take: 200` never truncates. The board simply rendered before the write had committed.

## Mechanism

`components/ui/FlightStatusSelector.tsx` runs `updateFlightStatusAction` inside `startTransition` and then `router.refresh()`. Playwright's `selectOption('DELAYED')` returns as soon as the change event dispatches — it does not wait for the transition. `e2e/admin.spec.ts:239` then navigates straight to `/flights`, which is `force-dynamic` and renders whatever the database holds at that instant.

## Fix

Await the settled state before navigating — the select clearing its `disabled` state, or the row showing the new status on the admin page itself. Asserting the outcome on the page that performed the change is the more honest wait, since that is where the user would see it.

## Related

Same family as #173 and #178: the suite has several waits that assume an action is complete when the DOM event returns.

Found by the `verifier` while checking #195's fix. **Introduced by that fix**, and recorded rather than widened into it.

## Where

`components/ui/titlebar.tsx:37-50`. The poll suppresses `console.error` when the rejection's message is one a browser produces for a torn-down request.

## Why the set is not enough

Those strings are correctly identified, but they are not exclusive to navigation. Verified in real Chromium, none of these involving a navigation:

| Scenario | Message |
|---|---|
| server unreachable | `TypeError: Failed to fetch` |
| connection reset before response | `TypeError: Failed to fetch` |
| server dies mid-body | `TypeError: Failed to fetch` |
| response stream fails mid-read (how React's Flight client consumes a server action) | `TypeError: network error` |

So a crashed, killed or restarting dev server now produces **no console output at all**, where it previously printed every 3 seconds.

input.content:
First of three slices clearing the test-infrastructure tax before Phase 3's ~40 PRs.
Four issues, all of them ways a run could lie about the code under test.

## What each one was

**#196 — a reused dev server.** `reuseExistingServer` borrowed whatever was on the
port. That made a healthy branch fail three runs of three, and the bisect that
followed was worthless: with `webServer: npm run dev`, rebuilding between steps
changes nothing, so every "fix" was really just a server restart. The mirror case is
worse — a stale server can report a pass for code that is not under test. Playwright
now starts its own.

**#173 — seat 11A, held forever.** The suite booked it and nothing released it, so
the seat map rendered it taken and three specs failed on that database from the
first run onwards. CI never saw it because CI seeds a fresh database each time.
Global setup now clears what a previous run booked.

**#182 — navigating before the write landed.** `selectOption` returns on the change
event, not on the server action committing, and `/flights` is `force-dynamic`. The
spec now waits for the change to settle on the page that made it.

**#195 — an aborted poll reported as a failure.** The notification bell polls every
3s; a navigation tears that down. It was the only console error the suite ever
produced.

## Verified by reproduction, not by reading

- Planted the exact leftover #173 describes — 11A held on a seeded flight by a stale
  booking — and the three named specs **failed without the cleanup and passed with
  it**.
- #182 failed 3/3 before the wait and passed 3/3 after. I checked it against
  unmodified `main` first, because I had changed how the server starts and needed to
  rule myself out: it fails there too.
- Two consecutive full green runs, 30/30 each.

## What review caught

`ui-review` found a real defect in my #195 fix. The original matched by regex, and
`/aborted/i` as a substring silenced PostgreSQL's *"current transaction is aborted,
commands ignored until end of transaction block"* and Prisma's *"Transaction
aborted."* — in development Next forwards a server error's message to the client
verbatim, so exactly the failures a developer most needs arrive at that `catch` as
written. It now matches whole messages against a closed set of what browsers
actually say. Whole-message equality is what makes it safe.

The `verifier` then found the new test **green against code that does not do the
job**: it inlined `booking.deleteMany()` rather than calling the function, so
deleting the call from `global-setup.ts` left it passing. Its "seeded inventory
survives" assertions were vacuous too — `flight.count() > 0` is guaranteed by the
fixture the test creates itself. It now imports the real function, counts before and
after, and asserts to the row. Both mutants die.

It also caught that the config assertion pinned source text, so reintroducing reuse
*conditionally* slipped past. It reads the loaded config now.

I removed one of my own tests outright: it asserted a property of whatever the
database happened to hold, and failed when a Playwright run was in progress — a
flake, in a PR about removing flakes.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 643 unit + 51 database, `npm run
build`, and Playwright 30/30 twice.

## One behaviour change worth knowing

A dev server already on port 3000 now **stops** the suite instead of being borrowed:

```
Error: http://localhost:3000 is already used, make sure that nothing is running
on the port/url or set reuseExistingServer:true in config.webServer.
```

It exits in ~2.9s rather than hanging. `AGENTS.md` is updated, since it still said
Playwright auto-starts the server. Note the message advises the setting the config
now forbids — the reason is in the comment beside it.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#212** — the #195 fix means a *dead* dev server now fails silently too. The
  message cannot carry the signal; an `AbortController` in the effect cleanup can.
  Recorded rather than widened into this slice.
- **#213** — `travelguide.spec.ts` leaks a user, review and favorite per run; 37
  accounts had accumulated. Same class as #173, not covered by it.
- **#208, #209, #210, #211** — pre-existing notification-bell findings from
  `ui-review`: the drawer is clipped to 16 visible pixels on phone, the empty state
  claims "You're all caught up!" when loading failed, the unread count is invisible
  to assistive tech, and `next-auth`'s own session poll still logs on hard
  navigation.

## Still to come

#181 (search e2e reads a stale return date) and #178 (round-trip e2e headroom) are
the next slice; #165 is housekeeping after that.

cd /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app
gh issue create --title "Database test serialisation depends on how Jest is invoked, not on the config" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Found while addressing Codex review on #214 — by tripping over it repeatedly.

## Where

`package.json:15` — `"test:database": "npx jest --selectProjects database --runInBand"`.

`jest.config.js` splits the projects and documents at length why the database files must not run beside each other, but the config itself does not enforce it. `--runInBand` in the npm script is the only thing that serialises them.

## What was observed

Running `npx jest --selectProjects database` directly — which looks equivalent, and which the config's own comment does not warn against — runs those files in parallel. That reproduces exactly the interference #155 was filed for:

```
● the route a page renders › comes from the airports on the admin dashboard
  Expected substring: "RTE-66f9eabc"
```

`runIsolation.database.test.ts` calls `clearPreviousRunBookings()`, which deletes every booking by design, while `routeRenderSources.database.test.ts` is holding a fixture booking open. Intermittent: it passed on the immediately following run.

Verified: `npm run test:database` passes 3 runs of 3.

## Why it matters

The split exists so a whole-table assertion cannot count another file's fixtures. That guarantee currently holds only if you type the right command — and the wrong command is the shorter, more obvious one. It cost me several confusing failures in one session, each of which looked like a real regression in the code under review.

`jest` does not support a per-project `maxWorkers`, so the fix is not a one-liner. Options worth weighing: a `globalSetup` for the database project that refuses to run when it detects parallelism; a top-level `maxWorkers: 1` (correct but slows the 64-suite unit project); or a `testSequencer`/wrapper that makes the direct invocation fail loudly with a pointer to the script.

Related: #155 (the original collisions), and the note in `AGENTS.md` under Gotchas that already tells agents to use the scripts.
EOF
)" --label roadmap 2>&1 | tail -1

content.text:
The loop works. **PR #214: 👍 from Codex, all threads resolved, CI green, `MERGEABLE / CLEAN`** — and still unmerged, waiting on you.

## The mechanics, as observed

- Reactions live on the **PR itself** (`issues/<pr>/reactions`), not on a comment. 👀 while reading; it's *removed* and replaced with 👍 when clean.
- Findings are **inline review threads**, invisible to `gh pr view --json comments`. They need `pulls/<pr>/comments`, or GraphQL `reviewThreads` for the IDs to resolve.
- **Every push re-triggers it** — your description was right and the bot's own docs are incomplete (they only mention open/ready/`@codex review`).
- One trap: replying to a thread creates review objects **under your name**, so a naive "review count went up" check fires on your own replies. Only a review by the bot *on the current head SHA* is a verdict. My first poll got this wrong.
- Round trip was ~3–6 minutes.

## Three rounds, and it was right every time

It rejected each of my fixes for a concrete reason, and each rejection was correct:

1. **P1** unguarded `booking.deleteMany()` — a misaimed `DATABASE_URL` wipes every booking. Plus two P2s: my message-matching abort suppression, and a leaking session mock.
2. My host allowlist → **`localhost:5432/production` passes**. Plus: `pagehide` fires for the back-forward cache, so one Back would have silenced errors permanently.
3. Host **and** name → **`db/travel_app` is what Compose gives the application**, so no address can distinguish a dev database from a deployment.

That last one changed the design: the environment now declares itself with `DATABASE_IS_DISPOSABLE=true`, set in `.env.example` and CI and nowhere that deploys. It has teeth — my own `.env` predated it and the suite refused to run until I added the line. It also caught an IPv6 bug (`URL.hostname` returns `[::1]` with brackets, so the entry meant to allow it never matched).

Notably, its P2 on abort suppression pushed me to fix #212 properly rather than deferring it, which was the better call.

## Workflow update — drafted, deliberately not in this PR

I wrote step 8's Codex loop and made 👍 a merge gate in step 11, then **backed it out of #214** to keep that PR a coherent test-infra slice. It's saved and ready to go as its own small PR.

Two things I'd flag before you merge: this PR grew from two issues to four (#182 and #195 made the suite red once servers were always fresh), and **every existing checkout now needs `DATABASE_IS_DISPOSABLE=true` added to `.env`** or the tests refuse to start.

Want me to merge #214, and open the workflow-docs PR?
Yes merge 214 then open the workflow doc pr. That will be a good test of the updated workflow

**#214 merged** (`10f1187`), closing #196, #173, #182, #195.

**#216 is green and unmerged**: 👍 on the current head, zero unresolved threads, CI pass, `MERGEABLE / CLEAN`.

## The doc got better by being reviewed six times

The bot reviewed the description of itself and found four real defects in it:

- **The merge gate could pass on an unreviewed commit** — a 👍 survives a later push.
- **My fix for that was also wrong** — matching a bot review to the head SHA doesn't establish a *clean* verdict, since a head review can be one that carried findings; resolve those and every condition passes without approval ever being given.
- **The loop said "address the findings, run the tests, push"** — which pushes nothing, because the fixes are still uncommitted. It now routes back through steps 6–9.
- **REST can't answer the merge question** — it carries neither `isResolved` nor the thread ID.

The second one is my favourite, because fixing it made the rule *shorter*: it collapsed to **"only a 👍 you watched arrive counts."** That drops the SHA matching, the author filtering, and the caveat about your own replies creating review objects. It's also what the loop had actually been doing all along — the text was describing a more elaborate check than the practice.

Net effect of "don't overcomplicate": the section went from 30 lines to 18, and is more correct.

## One finding I declined

It asked me to document the `@codex review` fallback for a quiet PR. I'd observed exactly that — #216 was ignored for ten minutes after opening, then reviewed within a minute of being asked — and had written it up. You told me to drop it, so I did, and replied on the thread explaining why rather than resolving it silently: every push since has been picked up automatically within a minute, so one docs-only PR is thin grounds for a permanent extra step.

Worth knowing it happened, in case a PR ever does sit quiet — the fallback works, it's just not in the workflow.

=== issue 181 ===
Found by the verifier during #73 work, on clean scratch databases. Not #173 or #178 — different mechanism.

**Verification status:** reproduced (1 failure in 3 full-suite runs); passes 3/3 in isolation. The arithmetic below confirms the mechanism.

## The failure

`e2e/search.spec.ts:30`

```
- "returnDate": "2026-08-17"    (captured from the #return input)
+ "returnDate": "2026-08-15"    (what the URL carried)
```

## Mechanism

`components/ui/flightBookingForm.tsx:400-455` splits the work across two effects. Choosing a new **From** fires one that calls `setDepartureDate(route.nextOperatingDate)`; a *separate* effect then recomputes `returnDate = departure + 7 days`.

The spec reads `#return`'s `inputValue()` between those two passes, so it captures a return date still derived from the **previous** route's departure:

- `2026-08-15 = 2026-08-08 + 7` — the New York route, the correct answer
- `2026-08-17 = 2026-08-10 + 7` — the previously selected route, what the spec captured

## Why `expect.poll` will not fix it

The expected value is captured once, before the assertion. Polling the URL against a stale expectation just polls for the wrong thing.

## Fix

Wait for the form to settle before reading it — assert the departure input holds the new route's date first, then read the return. Or collapse the two effects so a route change produces both dates in one pass, which would remove the intermediate state entirely rather than teaching the test to avoid it.

The second is the better fix: the intermediate state is briefly visible to a customer too.

What changed, in `components/ui/flightBookingForm.tsx`: choosing a new origin or destination used to set the departure date in one effect, and a *second* effect then derived the return date from it (departure + 7 days, clamped to the booking window). That committed a render in between showing the new route's departure beside the **previous** route's return date — briefly wrong on screen. Both dates are now set together in one pass, and the derivation is shared in a new `defaultReturnDate` helper so the two places that set it cannot drift.

This is #181. It was found because an e2e spec reading both inputs in that gap captured the stale value, but the intermediate state was visible to a customer too, which is why it is fixed in the component rather than in the test.

The risk I need you to probe is that collapsing the two passes broke one of the other paths that set these dates. Exercise, at phone, tablet and desktop:

1. Change origin, and change destination, several times in a row. Confirm the departure and return always agree — the return is exactly a week after the departure shown beside it — and that you never catch a mismatched pair mid-update.
2. Switch between Round Trip and One Way, in both directions, and confirm the return date clears and comes back correctly, including after a route change while on One Way.
3. Edit the departure date directly and confirm the return still re-derives.
4. Edit the return date directly and confirm a later route change overwrites it as expected.
5. Pick a route whose departure is near the end of the booking window, so departure + 7 days would fall outside it, and confirm the return is clamped to the last selectable date rather than exceeding it.
6. Arrive via a shared link (`/?from=SEA&to=DTW&depart=...&return=...&trip=round-trip`) and confirm the restored dates are not overwritten by the new one-pass effect — this is the path I am least sure of, because the effect now claims the return-date guard.
7. The nearest-operating-date suggestion path: search a date with no flights, click a suggested date, and confirm both dates update coherently.

Also worth checking: whether the departure and return inputs' `min`/`max` attributes still track the origin's booking window when the origin changes.

Kill any existing dev server before you start — `playwright.config.ts` sets `reuseExistingServer: false`, so a server you leave running will make a later Playwright run fail to start.

Report every actionable finding with the concrete route/selector/viewport, and say explicitly which of the seven checks you exercised versus could not reach.

Found by the verifier while checking #169, on a clean database — so this is **not** #173.

**Verification status:** reproduced once, then timed across four runs to establish the mechanism.

## The failure

```
✘ e2e/booking.spec.ts:267 › User can book a round trip and both legs are seated and persisted (30.3s)
    Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded.
    Error: page.goto: Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded.
      - navigating to "http://localhost:3000/profile", waiting until "load"
      at e2e/booking.spec.ts:358:16
```

## Why

The test carries a two-leg checkout, a confirm, a profile load and a seat change inside one fixed 30s budget, against a dev server that compiles routes on demand. Measured:

| condition | duration |
|---|---|
| warm server, in-file | 10.6s |
| warm server, isolated | 24.9s |
| cold server (`rm -rf .next`), isolated | 17.8s |
| second full run, same cold conditions | 10.6s, suite 28/28 |

So headroom on a cold server is roughly 12s, and the first Playwright run of a session — cold OS page cache over the Next toolchain — can eat it. It passes on re-run, which is exactly what makes it easy to wave through.

## Fix

`test.slow()` on this one case triples its budget and is the smallest honest change. Splitting it — book the round trip, then change a seat — would be better, since one test currently covers four distinct outcomes and a timeout tells you nothing about which.

## Related

Same family as #173 and #155: shared-resource timing rather than a defect in the application.

parallel and serialised projects (#155). Both pre-date that change; neither has a

live Postgres, and the warning read off ordinary run output.

## 1. Two database test files never `$disconnect`

`__tests__/lib/authTokens.database.test.ts` and
`__tests__/lib/passengerDataProtection.database.test.ts` have an `afterAll` that
cleans up rows but never calls `prisma.$disconnect()`. The other seven database test
files do.

This mattered less when every test file ran in its own worker and the process exited
after it. Now that the database project runs `--runInBand`, all nine files share one
process, so those clients stay connected for the remainder of the run.

Measured impact today: **none**. Peak connections during an in-band run were 5 of
`max_connections=100`, and `--detectOpenHandles` reports nothing. It is worth fixing
before the database project grows, not because it is currently hurting.

## 2. Haste module naming collision on every Jest run

Every run prints:

```
jest-haste-map: Haste module naming collision: travel-app
```

from `package.json` colliding with `.next/standalone/package.json`. It is noise on
every invocation, which is the kind of thing that trains people to skim past output
that might one day say something useful.

`modulePathIgnorePatterns: ['<rootDir>/.next/']` in `jest.config.js` should clear
it — worth confirming it does not disturb the `next/jest` transform setup, which is
why this is filed rather than folded into the #155 change.

**#178** — measured before changing anything: 21.6s against a 30s budget on a cold run, so ~8s headroom rather than the ~12s originally recorded, because #196 means every run is now cold. `test.slow()` triples it, and I proved the budget actually moved: a 33s delay inside the test passes with it and fails without.

**#165** split in two:
- The `$disconnect` half was real and is fixed in both files. Since nothing noticed for as long as it was wrong, it's now a test that scans every database suite rather than a convention.
- **The haste collision doesn't reproduce.** With the colliding manifest on disk and both names genuinely `travel-app`, four invocations produced zero warnings, and the resolved config shows nothing suppressing it. I drafted the suggested `modulePathIgnorePatterns` and then removed it — it changes module resolution under `.next/` to silence a warning nobody can produce. Evidence and the one-line fix are on the issue if a Jest upgrade brings it back.

**Both review rounds caught the same mistake twice from me:** I wrote the guard to match where the database tests happen to live rather than what the config actually runs. First it matched only `.ts` when the project accepts `.ts/.tsx/.js/.jsx`; then it rooted at `__tests__` when the project's pattern is repo-wide. Each time I verified with a throwaway probe file — a `.tsx` suite, then one colocated under `lib/` — and each time it failed the guard as it should.

**Three related issues remain open**, all filed during this work rather than pre-existing:

- **#215** — serialisation depends on typing `npm run test:database` rather than on the config; `npx jest --selectProjects database` silently runs them in parallel. This one bit me repeatedly.
- **#213** — travelguide e2e leaks a user, review and favorite per run.
- **#212** — a dead dev server now makes the notification poll fail silently; needs an AbortController rather than the teardown flag.

#215 is the one I'd take next if you want to keep going on test infrastructure — it's the one that actively misleads. }

Roughly **130 pull requests** across Phases 2–5. Phase 3 alone (#78–#82) is ~40. This is not a backlog that closes in a sitting.

Six schema changes were independently proposed by two or more areas. Each needs a single owner or they will collide:

| `Booking.status` typing + status history | #76 | #73, #75 |

2. **Cheap correctness fixes** — six PRs, one day each, blocking nothing. Includes #142 and the round-trip defect below.

5	/**
6	 * The dev server compiles a route the first time something asks for it, and
7	 * `app/api/auth/[...nextauth]` is expensive enough to cost more than the default
8	 * budget of the assertion that waits for a sign-in to land. Whichever test signs
9	 * in first against a server that has not compiled it yet pays that bill and can
10	 * fail on it (#121).
11	 *
12	 * The symptom moves around, which is what made it look like cross-spec
13	 * interference: what matters is whether the server being used has already
14	 * compiled the route, not which test or how many are running. `reuseExistingServer`
15	 * means a re-run against a still-warm server passes, so re-running a failure
16	 * "proves" nothing.
17	 *
18	 * Paying it here puts the cost outside every test's budget.
19	 */
20	async function warmAuthRoutes(baseURL: string): Promise<void> {
21	  const deadline = Date.now() + 30_000;
22	
23	  // Playwright starts the web server before this runs, so one attempt is
24	  // normally enough; the loop only covers a server still finishing its boot.
25	  while (Date.now() < deadline) {
26	    try {
27	      // One GET of the NextAuth handler compiles the whole route module, which
28	      // is what the sign-in POST would otherwise wait for. The login page is
29	      // warmed too because every sign-in starts by loading it.
30	      const responses = await Promise.all([
31	        fetch(`${baseURL}/login`),
32	        fetch(`${baseURL}/api/auth/csrf`),
33	      ]);
34	      // Drain the bodies rather than leaving sockets open for the whole run.
35	      await Promise.all(responses.map(response => response.arrayBuffer()));
36	      return;
37	    } catch {
38	      await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 500));
39	    }
40	  }
41	
42	  // Not fatal: the suite still works, it just goes back to paying the compile
43	  // inside whichever test signs in first. Say so loudly, because the failure
44	  // that follows will look like an unrelated flake.
45	  console.warn(
46	    `[global-setup] ${baseURL} was unreachable for 30s; auth routes were not warmed. `
47	    + 'Expect the first sign-in to be slow and possibly flaky (#121).'
48	  );
49	}
50	
51	/**
52	 * Everything a previous run booked.
53	 *
54	 * The suite books seat 11A on a seeded flight, and nothing removed it, so the
55	 * seat map rendered 11A as taken and three specs failed on that database from
56	 * then on -- permanently, until somebody reseeded by hand. CI never saw it
57	 * because CI seeds a fresh database every time; a developer's database rotted
58	 * after one run (#173).
59	 *
60	 * `Booking` is the only delete needed: `Passenger`, `ItineraryLeg` and
61	 * `SeatAssignment` all cascade from it, and a held seat is what the next run
62	 * needs back.
63	 *
64	 * Deliberately not `User`, and deliberately not `Notification`: the seed
65	 * creates neither, so every row belongs either to a previous run or to whoever
66	 * is developing here, and this cannot tell them apart. Leftover accounts and
67	 * notifications are harmless -- the specs mint fresh emails and assert against
68	 * their own rows -- while deleting someone's manual test login is not.
69	 *
70	 * The trade this does make, and it is a real one: a booking made by hand in the
71	 * development database goes too, and it goes before the specs run rather than
72	 * after, so it is gone quietly. Nothing here can tell that booking from the
73	 * one a previous run left holding 11A.
74	 */
75	/**
76	 * Hosts a suite is allowed to destroy data on.
77	 *
78	 * `localhost` is a developer's machine and CI's service container; `db` is the
79	 * Compose service. Anything else is somebody's real database.
80	 */
81	const DISPOSABLE_HOSTS = new Set(['localhost', '127.0.0.1', '::1', 'db']);
82	
83	/**
84	 * The environment stating, of itself, that its data is expendable.
85	 *
86	 * Host and name cannot carry this. `db/travel_app` is what `docker-compose.yml`
87	 * gives the *application*, so a checkout pointed at a running deployment --
88	 * or at its published Postgres port -- looks exactly like a developer's own
89	 * database. The difference is not in the address; it is in whether whoever set
90	 * that environment up considers the contents disposable.
91	 *
92	 * So it has to be said, in the environment rather than on the command line: a
93	 * flag on the invocation is set by whoever runs the tests, and the question is
94	 * about the database, not about them. `.env.example` and CI set it; nothing
95	 * that deploys this application does.
96	 */
97	const DISPOSABLE_MARKER = 'DATABASE_IS_DISPOSABLE';
98	
99	/**
100	 * Database names this suite owns.
101	 *
102	 * A host on its own is not identity: `postgresql://…@localhost/production` is
103	 * local, and so is a production database reached through an SSH tunnel or a
104	 * proxy. The name has to say what it is.
105	 *
106	 * `travel_app` is the only name the repository configures -- `.env.example`,
107	 * `docker-compose.yml` and CI all use it. Anything else has to be named
108	 * `*_test`, or added here deliberately where the addition is reviewed.
109	 */
110	const DISPOSABLE_DATABASES = new Set(['travel_app']);
111	const DISPOSABLE_DATABASE_PATTERN = /_test$/;
112	
113	/**
114	 * Refuse to delete anything on a database this suite does not own.
115	 *
116	 * The deletion below is unqualified by design -- it has to be, since it cannot
117	 * tell a previous run's booking from any other. That makes a misaimed
118	 * `DATABASE_URL` catastrophic and silent: point it at staging, run `npm test`
119	 * or `npx playwright test`, and every booking is gone with nothing asked and
120	 * nothing recoverable.
121	 *
122	 * So the check is on the destination rather than on intent, and it fails closed:
123	 * an unparseable or absent URL stops the run too.
124	 */
125	function assertDisposableDatabase(): void {
126	  const databaseUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
127	  if (!databaseUrl) {
128	    throw new Error('Refusing to clear bookings: DATABASE_URL is not set.');
129	  }
130	
131	  if (process.env[DISPOSABLE_MARKER] !== 'true') {
132	    throw new Error(
133	      `Refusing to clear bookings: ${DISPOSABLE_MARKER} is not set to "true" in this `
134	      + 'environment. This suite deletes every booking in the database it is pointed at, '
135	      + `so the environment has to say the data is expendable. Add ${DISPOSABLE_MARKER}=true `
136	      + 'to the .env you use for development and testing -- and never to one that deploys '
137	      + 'this application.'
138	    );
139	  }
140	
141	  let host: string;
142	  let name: string;
143	  try {
144	    const parsed = new URL(databaseUrl);
145	    // Node returns the IPv6 literal with its brackets, which would never match
146	    // a bare `::1`.
147	    host = parsed.hostname.replace(/^\[|\]$/g, '');
148	    name = parsed.pathname.replace(/^\//, '');
149	  } catch {
150	    throw new Error('Refusing to clear bookings: DATABASE_URL is not a URL this can check.');
151	  }
152	
153	  if (!DISPOSABLE_HOSTS.has(host)) {
154	    throw new Error(
155	      `Refusing to clear bookings: DATABASE_URL points at host "${host}", which is not one `
156	      + `this suite may destroy data on (${[...DISPOSABLE_HOSTS].join(', ')}). `
157	      + 'Point DATABASE_URL at a local or Compose database before running the tests.'
158	    );
159	  }
160	
161	  // Being local is not the same as being disposable. A tunnel or a proxy puts
162	  // any database on localhost, so the name has to identify it too.
163	  if (!DISPOSABLE_DATABASES.has(name) && !DISPOSABLE_DATABASE_PATTERN.test(name)) {
164	    throw new Error(
165	      `Refusing to clear bookings: DATABASE_URL names database "${name}", which this suite `
166	      + `does not own. Expected ${[...DISPOSABLE_DATABASES].join(', ')} or a name ending in `
167	      + '"_test". Being reachable on localhost is not enough -- a tunnel or a proxy puts a '
168	      + 'real database there too.'
169	    );
170	  }
171	}
172	
173	export async function clearPreviousRunBookings(): Promise<void> {
174	  assertDisposableDatabase();
175	
176	  await prisma.booking.deleteMany();
177	}

179	async function globalSetup(config: FullConfig): Promise<void> {
180	  loadEnvConfig(process.cwd());

182	  const baseURL = config.projects[0]?.use?.baseURL ?? 'http://localhost:3000';

## What the change is (issue #213)

Three Playwright specs leaked rows into the development database on every run. Measured before the fix: 25 `guidetest-*` users + 25 Reviews + 25 UserFavorites (`travelguide.spec.ts`, no cleanup at all), 42 users from `auth.spec.ts` (`test-*` and `login-test-*`, no cleanup at all), and 20 `VerificationToken` rows from `auth-abuse.spec.ts` (it deleted the user and rate limits but not the token). Only the first was in the filed issue.

The slice:
1. `e2e/helpers/rowSnapshot.ts` (new) — snapshots row identifiers for User, VerificationToken, Review, UserFavorite, Notification; `rowsAddedDuringRun(before, after)` diffs them; `describeLeakedRows` builds the failure message.
2. `e2e/helpers/runBaseline.ts` (new) — module-level carrier for the baseline between global setup and teardown.
3. `e2e/global-setup.ts` — records the baseline before it changes anything.
4. `e2e/global-teardown.ts` — throws after clearing rate limits if rows survived the run.
5. `e2e/travelguide.spec.ts`, `e2e/auth.spec.ts`, `e2e/auth-abuse.spec.ts` — each now deletes what it creates in `test.afterAll`.
6. `__tests__/e2e/rowSnapshot.test.ts` (unit) + `__tests__/e2e/rowSnapshot.database.test.ts` (database project).
7. One AGENTS.md Gotchas bullet.

Each spec now deletes what it created, which is what its neighbours already did. The
review and the favorite cascade from the account, so `travelguide` needs one delete;

accounts because it cannot tell a run's account from a developer's — that is why 67 of

at the end appeared while the run had the database to itself.

and leave the specs wrong, and the next spec to leak would be just as invisible.

content.text:
Read #76 and the code behind it. The most useful thing to know first: **#76 isn't greenfield — cancellation already ships**, and two of its parts are live defects rather than missing features.

`app/actions.ts:428` already cancels transactionally: locks flights in ascending order, releases seats, sets status, notifies, deducts status points. What it has no concept of is *eligibility*. So today:

- A customer can cancel a booking **after the flight departed** — releasing a seat on a flown flight and deducting points for a trip they took.
- Staff can set a flight to `CANCELLED` (`actions.ts:986`) and the bookings **stay `CONFIRMED`, still holding seats**. The only consequence is a notification. Customers keep a boarding pass for a flight that isn't operating.
- `Booking.status` is a bare `String` with no enum and no check constraint — `lib/seatOccupancy.ts:27` says so explicitly, and the literal in that file is the entire definition.
- Seats are released by renaming them to `CANCELLED-<passengerId>` to dodge the unique index, which is why `bookingItinerary.ts:82` has to translate that back into the word "Released" for display.

## My recommendation on the two decisions

**Staff-cancelled flight → `DISRUPTED`, not auto-cancel.** This is the clearer call of the two. Auto-cancel forecloses the rebooking that the issue's own acceptance criteria ask for; it releases seats you may want to hold while rebooking; it would deduct status points for something the customer didn't do; and it's a one-way door — a staff misclick then reversed leaves bookings destroyed and seats resold. Keeping the paths separate also buys the thing that matters most: **an involuntary cancellation is refunded in full, bypassing fare rules and the cut-off entirely**, because the airline caused it. That distinction is impossible if both paths converge on `CANCELLED`.

One nuance: if a round trip has one leg cancelled, the whole booking goes `DISRUPTED`. A half-itinerary isn't a usable trip.

**Cancellation policy — cabin-tiered, percentage fee, 24h cut-off:**

| Cabin | Before 24h | Inside 24h | After departure |
|---|---|---|---|
| First, Business | Full refund | Cancel, no refund | Refused |
| Premium Economy, Economy | Refund minus 20% | Cancel, no refund | Refused |
| Any, flight `DISRUPTED` | Full refund, no fee, no cut-off | | |

Three points of reasoning:

**Percentage, not flat.** `Booking.currency` already exists on the model. A flat fee is wrong the moment a booking isn't USD, and it needs FX to stay right. A percentage of `totalPriceCents` needs neither. Specify the rounding direction in the policy (floor, in minor units) so tests can pin it rather than inheriting whatever the first implementation did.

**Cancel inside 24h, but don't refund.** Refusing outright strands the customer with a booking they can't act on and keeps a seat held that could be resold. Allowing it with zero refund releases the inventory and is honest about the fare rules.

**Refuse after departure.** Not a policy choice so much as an integrity one — cancelling a flown flight rewrites history, corrupts the points ledger, and frees a seat that was used.

I'd deliberately keep every cabin refundable rather than making Economy non-refundable. A non-refundable Economy means the most common path never exercises the refund calculation, and the e2e coverage the issue asks for gets thin exactly where the traffic is.

**On money:** #75 (real payments) comes *after* #76 in the plan, so I'd have #76 **calculate and record** the refund — an amount plus an immutable status-history row — and not attempt a money movement. That keeps #76 shippable standalone, and gives #75 a recorded figure to actually refund against.

## How I'd slice it

Five PRs, in this order — the first two are the migrations #143 says other issues are waiting on:

1. Type `Booking.status` as an enum + add the status-history table. Behaviour-neutral; unblocks #74 and #75.
2. Replace the `CANCELLED-<passengerId>` rename with `releasedAt` + a partial unique index — the issue's "release seats without rewriting seat identifiers", which also deletes the display hack.
3. Eligibility and refund calculation (the table above).
4. Staff cancel → `DISRUPTED`, plus the customer's refund-or-rebook choice.
5. E2E for the self-service and staff-assisted paths.

input.content:
-- Type what state a booking is in, and record every move between them (#76).
--
-- `Booking.status` was `TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'CONFIRMED'` with no enum and no
-- check constraint. Unlike `Flight.status` there was not even a Zod schema at
-- the boundary: the whole definition of the domain was a string literal in
-- `lib/seatOccupancy.ts`, whose own comment said so. That literal decides
-- whether a seat is held -- `heldSeats()` filters on `status != 'CANCELLED'` --
-- so a status written any other way sells a seat that somebody is sitting in,
-- or holds one nobody paid for.
--
-- `DISRUPTED` is created here although nothing writes it yet. This migration is
-- where the domain of booking states is decided, and #76 has decided it: a
-- flight cancelled by staff moves its bookings to `DISRUPTED` rather than
-- cancelling them, so the customer keeps the choice between a refund and a
-- rebooking. Adding the value later is not free either -- Postgres will not let
-- a value added by `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` be used in the same transaction,
-- and Prisma applies each migration in one, so it would take two migrations to
-- add the value and start writing it.
--
-- The status history is the other half. Cancellation, disruption and refunds
-- all have to be auditable, and a single mutable column cannot say what a
-- booking used to be, when it changed, or who changed it.
--
-- To reverse:
--
--     DROP TABLE "BookingStatusChange";
--     ALTER TABLE "Booking" ALTER COLUMN "status" DROP DEFAULT;
--     ALTER TABLE "Booking" ALTER COLUMN "status" TYPE TEXT USING "status"::TEXT;
--     ALTER TABLE "Booking" ALTER COLUMN "status" SET DEFAULT 'CONFIRMED';
--     DROP TYPE "BookingStatus";
--     DELETE FROM _prisma_migrations WHERE migration_name = '20260810040000_type_booking_status';
--
-- Dropping the table discards the audit trail it exists to keep, so reversing
-- this is a decision about the history rather than about the column. The column
-- half is safe in either order against either version of the code: the
-- application only ever writes the names below.
--
-- If the lock timeout aborts this, or the guard rejects the data, the migration
-- is marked failed and no later one applies until it is cleared:
--
--     npx prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back 20260810040000_type_booking_status

-- Fail fast rather than freeze the table.
--
-- The rewrite takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on a table read by every profile page and
-- every seat-occupancy check, and `docker compose` starts the one-shot
-- `migrate` service before recreating `app`, so the previous container is still
-- serving from it while this runs. LOCAL, so it lasts only this transaction
-- rather than being inherited by every migration authored after it (#185).
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s';

CREATE TYPE "BookingStatus" AS ENUM ('CONFIRMED', 'CANCELLED', 'DISRUPTED');

-- Say what is wrong before the cast does.
--
-- `ALTER TABLE ... USING` fails on an unconvertible row by itself, but names
-- only the first value it choked on, and neither the table nor the column. An
-- operator meeting this mid-deployment needs to see everything that is in there
-- before deciding what each value should become.
DO $$
DECLARE
    unexpected TEXT;
BEGIN
    SELECT string_agg(DISTINCT format('%L (%s rows)', "status", n), ', ')
    INTO unexpected
    FROM (
        SELECT "status", count(*) AS n
        FROM "Booking"
        WHERE "status" NOT IN ('CONFIRMED', 'CANCELLED', 'DISRUPTED')
        GROUP BY "status"
    ) AS outliers;

    IF unexpected IS NOT NULL THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION
            'Booking.status holds values outside the three statuses: %. '
            'Decide what each should become and update those rows before typing the column.',
            unexpected;
    END IF;
END $$;

-- The default has to go first and come back afterwards: Postgres will not
-- retype a column whose default it cannot cast, and the existing default is a
-- TEXT literal. Losing the last statement would leave every booking created
-- without an explicit status violating NOT NULL.
ALTER TABLE "Booking" ALTER COLUMN "status" DROP DEFAULT;

ALTER TABLE "Booking"
    ALTER COLUMN "status" TYPE "BookingStatus" USING "status"::"BookingStatus";

ALTER TABLE "Booking" ALTER COLUMN "status" SET DEFAULT 'CONFIRMED';

-- One row per move between states.
--
-- `from` is null for the row that records the booking coming into existence,
-- which is the only status a booking has ever had that was not a change from
-- something. `actorUserId` is the person who caused it and is null for a
-- customer acting on their own booking or for a change nothing attributes.
CREATE TABLE "BookingStatusChange" (
    "id" TEXT NOT NULL,
    "bookingId" INTEGER NOT NULL,
    "from" "BookingStatus",
    "to" "BookingStatus" NOT NULL,
    "reason" TEXT,
    "actorUserId" TEXT,
    "createdAt" TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,

    CONSTRAINT "BookingStatusChange_pkey" PRIMARY KEY ("id")
);

-- The history of a booking that no longer exists has no subject, so it goes
-- with it. That is also what keeps the immutability rule below implementable:
-- a rule that blocked deletes would block the cascade, and both the e2e harness
-- and deleting a flight rely on it.
ALTER TABLE "BookingStatusChange"
    ADD CONSTRAINT "BookingStatusChange_bookingId_fkey"
    FOREIGN KEY ("bookingId") REFERENCES "Booking"("id") ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE;

-- Losing the account does not lose the fact that somebody did it; it loses only
-- which account, which is the same trade `Booking.userId` already makes.
ALTER TABLE "BookingStatusChange"
    ADD CONSTRAINT "BookingStatusChange_actorUserId_fkey"
    FOREIGN KEY ("actorUserId") REFERENCES "User"("id") ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE;

CREATE INDEX "BookingStatusChange_bookingId_createdAt_idx"
    ON "BookingStatusChange"("bookingId", "createdAt");

-- A history that can be rewritten is not one.
--
-- In the database rather than in the application, because the value of an audit
-- trail is precisely that it does not depend on every future caller choosing to
-- respect it -- a repair script, a psql session or a service added later all
-- reach this table without passing through any code this repository owns.
--
-- UPDATE only. Deletes are left to the cascade above: blocking them would make
-- a booking undeletable, and a row whose booking is gone is not evidence of
-- anything.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION "refuse_booking_status_change_update"()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
BEGIN
    RAISE EXCEPTION
        'BookingStatusChange is append-only: row % belongs to booking % and cannot be '
        'modified. Record a new change instead.',
        OLD."id", OLD."bookingId";
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER "BookingStatusChange_is_append_only"
    BEFORE UPDATE ON "BookingStatusChange"
    FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION "refuse_booking_status_change_update"();

-- Give every existing booking the row it would have had.
--
-- Without this, "a booking always has at least one status change" is true only
-- of bookings made after today, and every reader would need a fallback for the
-- others -- which is the shape of two-sources-of-truth this issue is removing.
-- `from` is null and the timestamp is the booking's own, because what is known
-- is the state it is in now and when it was made, not the path it took there.
INSERT INTO "BookingStatusChange" ("id", "bookingId", "from", "to", "reason", "createdAt")
SELECT
    gen_random_uuid()::TEXT,
    b."id",
    NULL,
    b."status",
    'Recorded when the status history was introduced; the path to this state was not kept.',
    b."createdAt"
FROM "Booking" b;

content.text: My own fixture exposed the flaw: `prisma.booking.create` without the nested write produces a booking with no history. An invariant that depends on every caller remembering isn't one — same reason the append-only rule lives in the schema. Moving the write into a trigger:

input.old_string:
-- Give every existing booking the row it would have had.
--
-- Without this, "a booking always has at least one status change" is true only
-- of bookings made after today, and every reader would need a fallback for the
-- others -- which is the shape of two-sources-of-truth this issue is removing.
-- `from` is null and the timestamp is the booking's own, because what is known
-- is the state it is in now and when it was made, not the path it took there.
INSERT INTO "BookingStatusChange" ("id", "bookingId", "from", "to", "reason", "createdAt")
SELECT
    gen_random_uuid()::TEXT,
    b."id",
    NULL,
    b."status",
    'Recorded when the status history was introduced; the path to this state was not kept.',
    b."createdAt"
FROM "Booking" b;
input.new_string:
-- The history writes itself.
--
-- The first version of this had the application insert the row beside the
-- change, nested in the same statement so the two could not come apart. The
-- test fixture that came next created a booking without it and got a booking
-- with no history -- which is the whole objection: "every status change is
-- recorded" was true only while every caller remembered, and callers include a
-- repair script and a psql session.
--
-- So the trigger is the only writer of the automatic rows, and there is no way
-- to change a booking's status without one appearing.
--
-- `reason` and `actorUserId` are the parts a trigger cannot know, so the caller
-- leaves them where it can be read: transaction-local settings, which is why
-- both `set_config` calls must pass `true`. Transaction-local matters more than
-- convenience here -- a session-scoped setting would survive the commit, and
-- the next booking to use that pooled connection would be attributed to
-- whoever set it last.
--
--     SELECT set_config('app.booking_status_reason', 'Cancelled by customer', true);
--     SELECT set_config('app.booking_status_actor', '<user id>', true);
--
-- Both are optional and both default to null. `current_setting(..., true)`
-- returns null for a setting that was never set, and the empty string for one
-- set to it, so `nullif` covers the second.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION "record_booking_status_change"()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
DECLARE
    reason TEXT := nullif(current_setting('app.booking_status_reason', true), '');
    actor TEXT := nullif(current_setting('app.booking_status_actor', true), '');
BEGIN
    IF TG_OP = 'INSERT' THEN
        INSERT INTO "BookingStatusChange"
            ("id", "bookingId", "from", "to", "reason", "actorUserId", "createdAt")
        VALUES
            (gen_random_uuid()::TEXT, NEW."id", NULL, NEW."status", reason, actor, NEW."createdAt");
    ELSIF NEW."status" IS DISTINCT FROM OLD."status" THEN
        INSERT INTO "BookingStatusChange"
            ("id", "bookingId", "from", "to", "reason", "actorUserId", "createdAt")
        VALUES
            (gen_random_uuid()::TEXT, NEW."id", OLD."status", NEW."status", reason, actor,
             CURRENT_TIMESTAMP);
    END IF;

    -- AFTER trigger, so the return value is discarded.
    RETURN NULL;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- `UPDATE OF "status"` narrows this to statements that mention the column at
-- all; the `IS DISTINCT FROM` above then drops the ones that set it to what it
-- already was. Neither is redundant: the first keeps every other update off the
-- trigger entirely, the second keeps a no-op write out of the history.
CREATE TRIGGER "Booking_records_status_changes"
    AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OF "status" ON "Booking"
    FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION "record_booking_status_change"();

-- Give every existing booking the row it would have had.
--
-- Without this, "a booking always has at least one status change" is true only
-- of bookings made after today, and every reader would need a fallback for the
-- others -- which is the shape of two-sources-of-truth this issue is removing.
-- `from` is null and the timestamp is the booking's own, because what is known
-- is the state it is in now and when it was made, not the path it took there.
INSERT INTO "BookingStatusChange" ("id", "bookingId", "from", "to", "reason", "createdAt")
SELECT
    gen_random_uuid()::TEXT,
    b."id",
    NULL,
    b."status",
    'Recorded when the status history was introduced; the path to this state was not kept.',
    b."createdAt"
FROM "Booking" b;

input.old_string:
-- UPDATE only. Deletes are left to the cascade above: blocking them would make
-- a booking undeletable, and a row whose booking is gone is not evidence of
-- anything.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION "refuse_booking_status_change_update"()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
BEGIN
    RAISE EXCEPTION
        'BookingStatusChange is append-only: row % belongs to booking % and cannot be '
        'modified. Record a new change instead.',
        OLD."id", OLD."bookingId";
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
input.new_string:
-- UPDATE only. Deletes are left to the cascade above: blocking them would make
-- a booking undeletable, and a row whose booking is gone is not evidence of
-- anything.
--
-- One update is allowed, because refusing it would make a *user* undeletable:
-- `actorUserId` is ON DELETE SET NULL, and setting null is an update. So
-- forgetting who did it is permitted -- the same trade `Booking.userId` already
-- makes -- and nothing else is.
--
-- The comparison is against the whole row with that one field cleared, rather
-- than a list of the columns that must not change. A list would go stale the
-- day somebody adds a column, and it would go stale silently, leaving the new
-- column quietly mutable through this path.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION "refuse_booking_status_change_update"()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
DECLARE
    forgotten_actor "BookingStatusChange" := OLD;
BEGIN
    IF OLD."actorUserId" IS NOT NULL AND NEW."actorUserId" IS NULL THEN
        forgotten_actor."actorUserId" := NULL;
        IF NEW IS NOT DISTINCT FROM forgotten_actor THEN
            RETURN NEW;
        END IF;
    END IF;

    RAISE EXCEPTION
        'BookingStatusChange is append-only: row % belongs to booking % and cannot be '
        'modified. Record a new change instead.',
        OLD."id", OLD."bookingId";
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

Two findings from slice 1's verification that belong to later slices rather than to it.

## Two changes in one transaction share a timestamp, with no tiebreaker

`record_booking_status_change` stamps `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, which is transaction start
time, so three status changes in one transaction all carry the same instant:

```
 from      | to        | createdAt
           | CONFIRMED | 2026-08-10 03:53:34.791
 CONFIRMED | DISRUPTED | 2026-08-10 03:53:34.791
 DISRUPTED | CANCELLED | 2026-08-10 03:53:34.791
```

`@@index([bookingId, createdAt])` cannot order those, and `id` is a random uuid, so
"the latest status change" is not answerable by `ORDER BY`. The order is recoverable
only by chaining `from` to `to`.

Nothing does two status changes in one transaction today, so this is harmless now.
**Slice 3 records a refund against a history row and slice 5 shows a timeline** — both
will want a monotonic column. Adding one is a small migration; noting it here so it is
a decision rather than a rediscovery. Verified against running code.

## The backfill is only exercised by a database that predates the migration

`prisma/seed.ts` creates no bookings, and dev and CI databases are built from empty by
`migrate deploy` or `migrate reset`. So when the "has an entry for every booking"
assertion runs, the only bookings present are ones the trigger already covered:
deleting the backfill `INSERT` from the migration leaves the suite green everywhere it
normally runs.

The verifier did exercise it by hand — a pre-migration database holding two bookings,
migrated over, produced exactly one history row each with `from` null and the booking's
own `createdAt`, zero orphans — and the guard was confirmed in the same way, rejecting
`'REFUNDED'` and `'pending'` and rolling back whole.

The assertion is kept because the invariant it protects is real going forward. The gap
is that the only database where the backfill matters is a deployed one, which nothing
tests against. Worth remembering for any later migration in this issue that backfills.
EOF
