refund and a rebooking. This migration is where the domain is defined, and Postgres
will not let a value added later by `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` be used in the same
transaction that adds it — Prisma applies each migration in one, so deferring costs two
migrations rather than none.

`heldSeats()` deliberately does not treat `DISRUPTED` as released: that booking keeps
its seat until the customer chooses.

## The history writes itself

The first version had the application insert the row nested in the same statement as
the change, so the two could not come apart. **The next test fixture I wrote created a
booking without it and got a booking with no history** — which is the whole objection.
"Every status change is recorded" was true only while every caller remembered, and the
callers include a repair script and a psql session.

So a trigger is the only writer, and there is no way to change a booking's status
without a row appearing. The two things a trigger cannot know — why, and who — are read
from transaction-local settings:

```sql
BEGIN;
SELECT set_config('app.booking_status_reason', 'Flight cancelled', true);
SELECT set_config('app.booking_status_actor', '<user id>', true);
UPDATE "Booking" SET "status" = 'DISRUPTED' WHERE "id" = 1;
COMMIT;
```

Transaction-local matters: a session-scoped setting would survive the commit and
attribute the next booking on that pooled connection to whoever set it last. There is a
test for exactly that.

## Append-only, with one deliberate hole

A history that can be rewritten is not one, so the rule is a trigger rather than a
convention. One update is allowed: `actorUserId` may go from a user to null, because
that is what `ON DELETE SET NULL` does and refusing it would make **any user who ever
acted undeletable** — which the e2e harness and account deletion both need.

The carve-out compares the whole row with that one field cleared, rather than listing
the columns that must not change. A list would go stale silently the day somebody adds
a column. Its limit is documented: row equality needs an equality operator, which
`json`, `xml` and `point` lack — `jsonb` is the answer for an audit payload.

## What review caught

The `verifier` found **the documented reversal was wrong and left the database
unusable**. Run verbatim it fails at the third statement — Postgres refuses to retype a
column a trigger mentions — and with no `BEGIN`, the first two have already committed,
leaving `status` as the enum with no default. Every booking insert then violates NOT
NULL, and since the `_prisma_migrations` row is never reached, `migrate deploy` reports
nothing pending and will not heal it. The header now drops the triggers first and wraps
the whole thing in a transaction, and that form was run end-to-end: reversal → old
schema works → re-applied with the backfill.

It also found the carve-out's central claim untested — a naive `if the actor went to
null, allow it` passed the entire suite while permitting
`SET actorUserId=NULL, to='CONFIRMED', reason='tidying up'`. There is a test for that
now, and it kills the naive version. Same for the GUC channel and the no-op
suppression, neither of which had any coverage.

Two findings are [recorded on the issue](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/76#issuecomment-5235702982)
for later slices rather than fixed here: changes made in one transaction share a
timestamp with no tiebreaker (slices 3 and 5 will want a monotonic column), and the
backfill is only exercised by a database that predates the migration, which is not one
CI or a developer ever has.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 682 unit + 72 database, `npm run build`,
Playwright 30/30, and `prisma migrate diff` reports no drift.

The verifier additionally applied the migration to a **pre-migration database holding
bookings**, which is the only way the guard and the backfill run: the guard rejected
`'REFUNDED' (2 rows), 'pending' (1 rows)` and rolled back whole, and after fixing the
rows the backfill wrote exactly one row per booking with `from` null and the booking's
own `createdAt`.

Mutations that now die: dropping either trigger, widening the carve-out either way,
omitting `DISRUPTED`, and removing the backfill (against a populated database).

input.content:
-- Release a seat by saying so, not by renaming it (#76).
--
-- Cancelling a booking overwrote each seat number with
-- `CANCELLED-<passengerId>`. Nothing wanted that string: it existed only to
-- stop `UNIQUE (flightId, seatNumber)` from holding the seat forever, since the
-- index could not tell a held seat from a released one. So the fix for an index
-- that was too strict was to destroy the data it indexed.
--
-- What that cost:
--
--   * The seat number is gone. Which seat somebody was in before they cancelled
--     is not recoverable from this table, and this migration cannot put it back
--     -- the value was overwritten in place. Rows released from here on keep it.
--   * Every reader had to know the convention. `seatLabel` translated the
--     placeholder back into the word "Released" so it never reached a customer,
--     and a `CANCELLED-` prefix check stood between the two.
--   * "Is this seat taken" needed a join to the booking's status, because the
--     seat row itself could not say.
--
-- A partial unique index answers all three: uniqueness applies to held seats
-- only, so a released row can keep its real seat number and a new customer can
-- take that seat.
--
-- Note the index is invisible to Prisma, which cannot express a `WHERE` clause
-- on `@@unique`. That is why `@@unique([flightId, seatNumber])` is gone from
-- the schema rather than replaced: leaving it would have Prisma recreate the
-- unconditional index, which is the constraint being removed. `migrate diff`
-- reports no drift -- it ignores what it cannot represent -- so this index
-- lives and dies with this file, and a later migration that means to change it
-- has to say so here.
--
-- To reverse:
--
--     BEGIN;
--     UPDATE "SeatAssignment" SET "seatNumber" = 'CANCELLED-' || "passengerId"
--         WHERE "releasedAt" IS NOT NULL;
--     DROP INDEX "SeatAssignment_flightId_seatNumber_held_key";
--     CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "SeatAssignment_flightId_seatNumber_key"
--         ON "SeatAssignment"("flightId", "seatNumber");
--     ALTER TABLE "SeatAssignment" DROP COLUMN "releasedAt";
--     DELETE FROM _prisma_migrations WHERE migration_name = '20260810050000_release_seats_without_renaming';
--     COMMIT;
--
-- The first statement is not optional and it is lossy: the old index cannot be
-- recreated while two rows on a flight share a seat number, which is exactly
-- what this migration allows, so the reversal has to reimpose the placeholder
-- and discard the real seat numbers again. Reversing therefore destroys data
-- that reversing cannot restore -- unlike every other migration here.
--
-- If the guard below rejects the data, the migration is marked failed and no
-- later one applies until it is cleared:
--
--     npx prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back 20260810050000_release_seats_without_renaming

-- Fail fast rather than freeze the table.
--
-- Dropping and creating an index takes locks on the table every seat map reads,
-- and `docker compose` starts the one-shot `migrate` service before recreating
-- `app`. LOCAL, so it lasts only this transaction rather than being inherited
-- by every migration authored after it (#185).
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s';

ALTER TABLE "SeatAssignment" ADD COLUMN "releasedAt" TIMESTAMP(3);

-- When the seat was let go.
--
-- For rows already carrying the placeholder this is an approximation, and the
-- best one available: the booking's move to CANCELLED, which for a booking
-- cancelled before #228 is itself the backfilled row carrying the booking's
-- creation time. The alternative was CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, which would claim every
-- historical cancellation happened during this deployment.
UPDATE "SeatAssignment" sa
SET "releasedAt" = COALESCE(
    (
        SELECT max(c."createdAt")
        FROM "ItineraryLeg" l
        JOIN "BookingStatusChange" c ON c."bookingId" = l."bookingId"
        WHERE l."id" = sa."legId" AND c."to" = 'CANCELLED'
    ),
    (
        SELECT b."createdAt"
        FROM "ItineraryLeg" l
        JOIN "Booking" b ON b."id" = l."bookingId"
        WHERE l."id" = sa."legId"
    )
)
WHERE sa."seatNumber" LIKE 'CANCELLED-%';

-- Every placeholder has to become a released row, or it stays held forever
-- under a seat number no customer can be given.
DO $$
DECLARE
    stranded bigint;
BEGIN
    SELECT count(*) INTO stranded
    FROM "SeatAssignment"
    WHERE "seatNumber" LIKE 'CANCELLED-%' AND "releasedAt" IS NULL;

    IF stranded > 0 THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION
            'Refusing to change the seat index: % placeholder seats could not be dated, so '
            'they would stay held under a seat number nobody can be given. Their legs have '
            'no booking, which should be impossible.', stranded;
    END IF;
END $$;

DROP INDEX "SeatAssignment_flightId_seatNumber_key";

-- Strictly weaker than the index it replaces, so no existing row can violate
-- it: the old one held across every row, held or not.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "SeatAssignment_flightId_seatNumber_held_key"
    ON "SeatAssignment"("flightId", "seatNumber")
    WHERE "releasedAt" IS NULL;

-- Reading "which seats on this flight are taken" no longer joins to the
-- booking, so the column it filters on is worth an index of its own.
CREATE INDEX "SeatAssignment_flightId_releasedAt_idx"
    ON "SeatAssignment"("flightId", "releasedAt");

content.text: Four database tests fail because they cancel by writing the status — and a seat no longer releases as a side effect of that. That's a real gap: a `CANCELLED` booking still holding seats is now representable and always wrong. Enforcing it where slice 1 put the other invariant:

input.old_string:
-- Reading "which seats on this flight are taken" no longer joins to the
-- booking, so the column it filters on is worth an index of its own.
CREATE INDEX "SeatAssignment_flightId_releasedAt_idx"
    ON "SeatAssignment"("flightId", "releasedAt");
input.new_string:
-- Reading "which seats on this flight are taken" no longer joins to the
-- booking, so the column it filters on is worth an index of its own.
CREATE INDEX "SeatAssignment_flightId_releasedAt_idx"
    ON "SeatAssignment"("flightId", "releasedAt");

-- A cancelled booking never holds a seat.
--
-- Splitting the release out of the status makes the two capable of disagreeing,
-- which the old join made impossible: a booking could now read CANCELLED while
-- its seats stayed held, and the seat map would keep showing them taken with
-- nothing to point at. That is not a state anything should be able to reach, so
-- it is not left to the caller that happens to know both facts.
--
-- Only on the way *into* CANCELLED. `DISRUPTED` deliberately keeps its seats:
-- a flight the airline cancelled leaves the customer choosing between a refund
-- and a rebooking, and the seat is theirs until they do (#76). And a seat
-- released for some other reason is not un-released by a booking that was
-- already cancelled.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION "release_seats_on_cancellation"()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
BEGIN
    UPDATE "SeatAssignment" sa
    SET "releasedAt" = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
    FROM "ItineraryLeg" l
    WHERE l."id" = sa."legId"
      AND l."bookingId" = NEW."id"
      AND sa."releasedAt" IS NULL;

    RETURN NULL;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER "Booking_releases_seats_when_cancelled"
    AFTER UPDATE OF "status" ON "Booking"
    FOR EACH ROW
    WHEN (NEW."status" = 'CANCELLED' AND OLD."status" IS DISTINCT FROM 'CANCELLED')
    EXECUTE FUNCTION "release_seats_on_cancellation"();

Review the rendered UI impact of branch `refactor/seat-release` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app (AGENTS.md step 6). Postgres and Mailpit are running. Playwright's config refuses to reuse a dev server, so if you want the app running, start `npm run dev` yourself on port 3000 and stop it when done — and do not run `npx playwright test` while a dev server of yours is up.

## The change, and its only rendered surface

Cancelling a booking used to overwrite the seat number with `CANCELLED-<passengerId>`; `seatLabel()` in `lib/bookingItinerary.ts` recognised that prefix and printed "Released". Now the assignment row keeps the real seat number and carries `releasedAt`, and `seatLabel` reads the release instead of the prefix. Its signature changed from `seatLabel(seatNumber)` to `seatLabel(seat)`.

The rendered consequence is the seat cell in the bookings table of `components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx` (around line 339), fed by the query in `app/profile/page.tsx` which now selects `releasedAt`. The visible string should be unchanged: "Released" for a released seat, the seat number otherwise, "Not assigned" when there is none.

## What I want checked

1. **The seat cell still reads correctly in a browser** at phone, tablet and desktop widths, for a booking with a released seat and one without. Sign up, book a flight, view `/profile`, cancel the booking, and look at the seat cell before and after. Confirm the real seat number is never shown for a released seat — that is the part that newly matters, because the row now holds a number that looks exactly like a live seat rather than an obviously-fake placeholder.
2. Whether "Released" is adequate for a customer, or whether it reads as an error state — and whether a cancelled booking's row communicates its status clearly enough that a bare "Released" in the seat column is not confusing.
3. Any accessibility problem in that cell specifically: is "Released" conveyed to a screen reader as seat information, and does the cancelled-booking row have a non-colour indication of its state?
4. Whether the boarding pass / e-ticket view shows a seat for a cancelled booking, and what it shows.

Keep the scope to that. Do not review the wider profile page unless something you find is caused by this change. Capture screenshots or equivalent evidence at each viewport, and if a finding is not applicable say concretely why.

Verify branch `refactor/seat-release` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app (AGENTS.md step 7). Slice 2 of 5 for #76 — `gh issue view 76 --comments` has the plan. Postgres and Mailpit are running; port 3000 is free. A `ui-review` agent may also be running and may start a dev server on port 3000 — if the port is busy, wait rather than killing it, and do not run Playwright concurrently with it.

## What the change is

Cancelling a booking used to overwrite each seat number with `CANCELLED-<passengerId>`, purely so `UNIQUE (flightId, seatNumber)` would stop holding the seat. The fix for an index that was too strict was to destroy the data it indexed — the seat somebody sat in before cancelling is unrecoverable for every booking cancelled before this.

New migration `prisma/migrations/20260810050000_release_seats_without_renaming/migration.sql`:
1. `SeatAssignment.releasedAt` added; existing `CANCELLED-%` rows dated from the booking's move to CANCELLED (via the `BookingStatusChange` table added in #228), with a guard that fails if any placeholder could not be dated.

content.text:
Slice 2 is implemented and green locally; `ui-review` and `verifier` are running now.

**What changed.** Cancelling used to overwrite the seat number with `CANCELLED-<passengerId>` — the fix for an index that was too strict was to destroy the data it indexed. A partial unique index on `(flightId, seatNumber) WHERE releasedAt IS NULL` says the same thing honestly: uniqueness applies to held seats only, so a released row keeps the seat the traveller actually sat in and the seat is free for the next customer.

That let three things collapse. `heldSeats()` is now a column check instead of a join to the booking status. `seatLabel()` reads the release instead of sniffing a string prefix. And `cancelBookingAction` no longer touches seat assignments at all.

**Two things worth flagging from building it.**

Prisma can't express a `WHERE` on a unique index, so I checked empirically before committing to the design: it neither manages nor complains about the partial index, and with `@@unique([flightId, seatNumber])` removed from the schema, `migrate diff` reports no drift. Leaving that line in would have had Prisma recreate exactly the constraint being removed.

Splitting the release out of the status made the two capable of disagreeing — a `CANCELLED` booking still holding seats became representable, which the old join made impossible. Four existing tests failed on precisely that, by cancelling via a status write. Rather than patch them, I put the invariant where slice 1 put the other one: a trigger releases held seats when a booking moves *into* `CANCELLED`, and deliberately not into `DISRUPTED`, which keeps its seat until the customer chooses. That's the policy you approved, now enforced by the schema rather than by whoever remembers.

One consequence I called out in the tests: forgetting the occupancy rule is *more* dangerous now. A released row holds a seat number that looks completely real, where the old placeholder could never match one — so a reader that skips `heldSeats()` silently reads a free seat as taken.

The migration's reversal is knowingly lossy and says so — the old index can't be recreated while two rows share a seat number, so reversing has to reimpose the placeholder and discard the real seat numbers again. It's the one migration here where reversing destroys something reversing can't restore, which is why I asked the verifier to actually run it.

Locally: lint clean, 683 unit, 78 database, build, Playwright 30/30, and both mutants dead — making the index unconditional kills two tests, firing the release trigger for `DISRUPTED` kills another. I'll report what the two agents find.

# Suggestions

## 2. The seat cell fails WCAG AA contrast

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx:359` — `color: 'rgba(255,255,255,0.4)'` at `0.75rem`. Measured in page: `Grace (Released)` composites to **3.80:1** against `rgb(13,12,20)`; AA needs 4.5:1 for 12px regular. Same for `Ada (11A)`. Pre-existing colour, but "Released" is now the sole carrier of the seat's state, so it is worth raising to ~0.62 alpha or `#9ca3af`. Seen at all three viewports (`bookings-desktop.png`, `bookings-tablet.png`, `bookings-phone.png`).

## 3. "Released" is not conveyed as seat information

ARIA snapshot of the row (desktop):

```
row "One way Mona Airways MA405 Grace (Released) Paris, France → Chicago, USA 8/10/2026 $950 Cancelled":
  cell "One way Mona Airways MA405 Grace (Released)"
```

There is no "Seat" word anywhere — visible or accessible — in that cell; the happy path reads `Ada (11A)`, equally unlabelled. A screen reader user hears "Grace (Released)" and gets no signal that the parenthetical is about a seat. Pre-existing and symmetric across both states, so not a regression, but it is the answer to the accessibility question asked: no. `ProfileClient.tsx:361` builds the string as `${p.firstName} (${seatFor(...)})`. The boarding pass already has the pattern to copy — the visually-hidden caption `CAPTION_FOR_SCREEN_READERS` in `components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx`.

Non-colour indication of the cancelled row: **present** at tablet and desktop. The status cell renders the literal word "Cancelled" and the Change Seats/Cancel buttons disappear. Colour is not the only carrier.

## 4. At phone width the "Cancelled" status is scrolled out of view, leaving a bare "Released" as the only visible difference

At 390x844 the bookings table's `overflow-x-auto` wrapper (`ProfileClient.tsx:319`) is 316px wide holding 490px of content. The Status cell sits at x 376–462 — entirely past the wrapper's visible right edge of 353. `bookings-phone.png` shows two MA405 bookings that look identical except one says `Alan (11A)` and the other `Grace (Released)`: no "Cancelled", no visible absence of buttons.

The wrapper has no `tabindex` and no `role`, so a keyboard-only user cannot scroll it to reach the status at all (WCAG 2.1.1 for scrollable regions).

This is pre-existing layout, not introduced here, but it is the concrete answer to "does the row communicate its status clearly enough that a bare 'Released' is not confusing": at phone width, no — "Released" carries it alone, at 3.8:1, unlabelled.

## 5. Wording

Beside a visible "Cancelled" (tablet, desktop) "Released" reads correctly and does not look like an error state. Alone (phone, per finding 4) it is airline jargon a customer could read as a failure. content.text:
`ui-review` found one blocking bug, and it was mine.

**The admin passenger manifest printed a released seat as live.** `AdminFlightsTable.tsx:309` tested `startsWith('CANCELLED')` — my grep for `CANCELLED-` missed it, because the check omits the hyphen. With the placeholder gone, that branch can never fire, so the manifest showed:

```
Grace Hopper — Economy / Seat 11A — Cancelled
Alan Turing  — Economy / Seat 11A — Confirmed
```

Two travellers in seat 11A on the screen a gate agent uses, with only a coloured status word in another column separating a live claim from a dead one. That's precisely the defect the profile fix exists to prevent, on a worse screen — and the existing component test was green while feeding `seatNumber: 'CANCELLED-p2'`, a value the database can no longer produce.

Fixed: `releasedAt` is carried through `passengersSeatedOnLeg`, selected by the admin query, and read by the manifest. The fixture now uses a real `12A` with a release date — the *same* seat the confirmed traveller holds, which is the reused-seat case — and reverting the component to the prefix check fails the test, which the old fixture could never do.

I also removed `CANCELLED_BOOKING`, which this slice left with no consumer outside its own test; it's redundant with the generated `BookingStatus` now.

Three pre-existing findings went to **#229** rather than into this PR: at phone width the Status column is scrolled out of view (and the wrapper isn't keyboard-scrollable), so "Released" is the only visible difference between a cancelled and a live booking; that cell measures 3.80:1 against AA's 4.5:1; and nothing conveys "Seat" to a screen reader in either state.

683 unit green and types clean after the fixes. The verifier is still running — it's likely exercising Playwright and the database right now, so I'm not starting a competing run. Once it reports I'll re-verify the manifest change, since it began before that fix existed.

## Findings

### 1. Regression — admin manifest read the `CANCELLED-` prefix (fixed mid-run, now verified)

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/app/admin/flights/AdminFlightsTable.tsx:309` was:

```tsx
{passenger.seatNumber.startsWith('CANCELLED') ? 'Released' : `Seat ${passenger.seatNumber}`}
```

and `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/app/admin/flights/page.tsx` selected only `{ passengerId, seatNumber, cabinClass }`. Once a cancelled booking keeps its real seat number, the boarding manifest printed `Seat 12A` for the cancelled traveller **and** `Seat 12A` for the live one who now holds it. Two people in one seat, on the tool ops uses to board a flight. This was the answer to "does anything still depend on the `CANCELLED-` convention" — one live code path did.

Its test passed vacuously: the fixture in `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/__tests__/components/AdminFlightsTable.test.tsx` hardcoded `seatNumber: 'CANCELLED-p2'`, a value the application can no longer produce, so `expect(screen.getByText('Released'))` asserted a dead branch. I confirmed by substituting the shape the app now produces — the test failed.

The current tree fixes both sides (`passenger.releasedAt ? 'Released' : ...`, `releasedAt` selected, carried through `passengersSeatedOnLeg`, and the fixture rewritten to give both travellers `12A`). Verified green above. This is the only reader I found that neither filtered `releasedAt` nor called `heldSeats()`.

### 2. Coverage gap — the "only place that knows the rule" guard is now vacuous

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/__tests__/lib/seatOccupancy.test.ts` still greps for the old shape:

```ts
.filter((file) => /booking:\s*\{\s*status:\s*\{\s*not:/.test(fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8')))
```

That pattern no longer exists anywhere in `app`, `lib` or `components`, and it is no longer a pattern anyone could plausibly write. The re-inlining that is now possible — `where: { flightId, releasedAt: null }` in place of `heldSeats({ flightId })` — slips straight past. The guard fires on nothing. A regex over `releasedAt:\s*null` (excluding `lib/seatOccupancy.ts`) would be meaningful and green today: I checked, and `releasedAt: null` occurs exactly once across `app`, `lib` and `components`, at `lib/seatOccupancy.ts:21`.

Related: `CANCELLED_BOOKING` has been dropped from `lib/seatOccupancy.ts` and is now referenced nowhere in the repository. Intentional or not, it means the file's remaining prose about `DISRUPTED` no longer sits next to anything that enforces it.

### 3. Coverage gap — nothing joins the database fact to the customer-facing label

Mutation: delete `releasedAt: true` from the select in `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/app/profile/page.tsx`. It **survives** `tsc --noEmit` and all 683 unit tests. The result would be a profile page printing the real seat number of a seat the customer no longer holds — precisely the bug #76 exists to prevent. The ProfileClient test supplies `releasedAt` in its own fixture, so it can never catch a page that fails to select it; Playwright's cancel flow (`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/e2e/booking.spec.ts:198-215`) asserts the Cancelled badge and the points deduction, never the seat label.

The admin fix in finding 1 has now introduced the identical unguarded seam at `app/admin/flights/page.tsx`.

### 4. Coverage gap — `cancelBookingAction` is never exercised against a real database

The unit assertion is now purely negative (`expect(mockTx.seatAssignment.updateMany).not.toHaveBeenCalled()`), and `seatRelease.database.test.ts` drives `prisma.booking.update` directly rather than the action. Both halves are covered; the seam is not. Risk is low — I confirmed `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/app/actions.ts:450` is the **only** writer of `Booking.status = CANCELLED` in the repository, and the trigger is row-level `AFTER UPDATE OF status`, so it would fire for `updateMany` or raw SQL too.

### 5. Mutation results

| Mutation | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Drop the release trigger | **dies** — 7 tests, 4 suites |
| Trigger body without `AND sa."releasedAt" IS NULL` | **dies** — exactly 1: `what releases a seat › once, keeping the time it was first let go` |
| Drop `SeatAssignment_flightId_releasedAt_idx` | **survives** (expected — pure performance index) |
| Drop the partial unique index | **dies** — 3 tests, 2 suites |
| `heldSeats()` returns `{}` | **dies** — 4 unit + 4 database |
| Delete the backfill `UPDATE` from the migration | **survives all tests**, but the migration's own guard rejects the deploy (see 6) |
| Remove `releasedAt: true` from the profile page select | **survives everything** (finding 3) |

My first attempt at the trigger-body mutation appeared to survive; it had not applied (`docker exec` without `-i`). I verified `prosrc` before and after every subsequent database mutation. Everything was restored: the dev database has all four expected indexes, both triggers, the guard clause back in the function, and no drift.

### 6. Observation — the backfill guard is unreachable through the schema's own constraints

`SeatAssignment.legId` → `ItineraryLeg(id, flightId)` FK; `ItineraryLeg.bookingId` is `NOT NULL` FK to `Booking`; `Booking.createdAt` is `NOT NULL`. The `COALESCE` fallback therefore cannot return NULL and `stranded` cannot exceed 0. I could only make it fire by dropping `SeatAssignment_legId_flightId_fkey` first. Belt-and-braces is defensible, but note the message is the wrong diagnosis for the failure mode that *can* actually reach it: when I deleted the backfill `UPDATE`, the guard correctly refused the deploy but reported *"Their legs have no booking, which should be impossible"* for two rows whose legs were perfectly fine.

### 7. Concurrency — safe, and I proved it rather than reasoning about it

`lockFlightForUpdate` still covers the new path. All four seat-mutating entry points take the `Flight` row lock, including `cancelBookingAction`, and the trigger's `UPDATE` runs inside that same locked transaction — so the release is at least as well serialised as the old rename. The lock coverage is in fact *stronger* than before: the fact now lives on the row the index covers, rather than on a `Booking` row that the flight lock never protected.

Three interleavings driven directly against Postgres at READ COMMITTED, bypassing the application lock entirely:

- **Cancellation commits between a rival's occupancy check and its insert** — the rival's insert is accepted. Correct: the seat genuinely is free. The stale read said "occupied", so the application would have refused — a spurious rejection, never a double sale.
- **Two rivals both take the freshly released seat** — T2's insert blocks on the partial index while T1 is uncommitted, then fails `23505 duplicate key value violates unique constraint "SeatAssignment_flightId_seatNumber_held_key"`. Exactly one held row survives.
- **Rival inserts while the cancellation is still uncommitted** — T2 blocks; T1 rolls back; T2 is correctly rejected `23505` and the original holder keeps the seat. No phantom, no lost release.

The partial index behaves identically to the unconditional one over the held-row set. This is the load-bearing result and it holds.

**But** the E2E contested-seat test tests the lock, not the index. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/e2e/booking-authority.spec.ts:33` starts from an empty flight; with the flight lock held, the loser's occupancy check alone rejects it, so the test would pass with no unique index at all — consistent with the partial-index mutation killing only Jest database tests, none of the E2E. Its comment ("SeatAssignment's unique index is now the sole guard against selling a seat twice") overstates what it verifies. And no test anywhere contests a seat that a cancellation just freed — the race this change actually creates.

### 8. The reversal works, with one undocumented hazard

Verified end to end against a database holding both a released `14B` and a live `14B` on the same flight: reversal succeeded, reimposed the placeholders (`14B` → `CANCELLED-p4`, lossy as documented), recreated the unconditional index, and `migrate deploy` re-applied cleanly afterwards, re-deriving correct release dates from `BookingStatusChange`.

Not documented: `'CANCELLED-' || "passengerId"` is only unique per flight if a passenger holds at most one released assignment per flight. An itinerary with two legs on the same flight would produce a duplicate and the `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` would fail. The `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` wrapper makes that safe — the whole reversal rolls back — but it is worth a line in the header comment, since the reversal is the one place the header promises to have thought this through.

### 9. Vacuity review

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/__tests__/lib/seatRelease.database.test.ts` — no vacuous assertions found. All five tests are load-bearing: three die when the index is dropped or weakened, two when the trigger is dropped or its idempotence clause removed. The `rejects.toThrow(/Unique constraint|duplicate key/i)` assertions are pinned to the right error rather than to any throw. Its only limitation is the one in finding 4: it drives `prisma.booking.update`, not the action.

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/__tests__/lib/seatLayoutGuard.database.test.ts` — the rewritten fixture does test what its comment claims, and claims correctly. The comment says a forgotten rule now reads `20F` back as occupied; the fixture asserts `released.seatNumber === '20F'` and `releasedAt !== null` before calling `updateFlightSeatingLayout`, so the layout change is genuinely being asked to ignore a row carrying a real, interpretable seat number. This is one of the two tests killed by making the index unconditional, so it has teeth. Building the state via `booking.update` + trigger rather than a hand-written placeholder is also what makes it match reality now.

### 10. Housekeeping — transient, resolved

During the run two untracked files appeared at the repository root, `scratch-admin-ui.ts` and `scratch-totp.ts`, apparently from the `ui-review` agent; the latter contained a hardcoded TOTP secret. Both are typechecked (`tsconfig.json` includes `**/*.ts`) and both would have been swept in by a `git add -A` during that window. END $$;

Slice 2 of 5 for #76. The [decision record](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/76#issuecomment-5235526479) has the plan.

## The problem

Cancelling a booking overwrote each seat number with `CANCELLED-<passengerId>`. Nothing
wanted that string. It existed only to stop `UNIQUE (flightId, seatNumber)` holding the
seat forever, because the index could not tell a held seat from a released one — so the
fix for an index that was too strict was to **destroy the data it indexed**. Which seat
somebody sat in before cancelling is unrecoverable for every booking cancelled before
this, and this migration cannot put it back.

It also leaked outward. Every reader had to know the convention: `seatLabel` translated
the placeholder into "Released" so it never reached a customer, and "is this seat taken"
needed a join to the booking's status because the seat row could not say.

## A partial unique index

`(flightId, seatNumber) WHERE "releasedAt" IS NULL`. Uniqueness applies to held seats
only, so a released row keeps the real number and the seat is free for the next
customer.

**Prisma cannot express a `WHERE` on a unique index**, so `@@unique([flightId, seatNumber])`
is removed from the schema rather than replaced — leaving it would have Prisma recreate
exactly the constraint being removed. I checked this on a scratch database before
committing to the design: `migrate diff` reports no drift and does not try to drop the
partial index, because Prisma ignores what it cannot represent. The consequence is that
the index lives and dies with the migration file, which the header says.

Three things collapse into it: `heldSeats()` is a column check instead of a join,
`seatLabel()` reads the release instead of a string prefix, and `cancelBookingAction`
no longer touches seat assignments at all.

## The invariant that splitting them broke

A `CANCELLED` booking still holding seats became representable — the old join made it
impossible. Four existing tests failed on exactly that, by cancelling via a status
write. Rather than patch them, a trigger releases held seats when a booking moves *into*
`CANCELLED`, and deliberately **not** into `DISRUPTED`, which keeps its seat until the
customer chooses between a refund and a rebooking. That is the policy from the decision
record, enforced by the schema rather than by whoever remembers.

## What review caught

**`ui-review` found a live regression I had missed.** `AdminFlightsTable.tsx:309` tested
`startsWith('CANCELLED')` — my grep for `CANCELLED-` missed it because the check omits
the hyphen. With the placeholder gone that branch can never fire, so the passenger
manifest rendered:

```
Grace Hopper — Economy / Seat 11A — Cancelled
Alan Turing  — Economy / Seat 11A — Confirmed
```

Two travellers in seat 11A on the screen used to board a flight, separated only by a
coloured word in another column. Its test was green on `seatNumber: 'CANCELLED-p2'`, a
value the database can no longer produce. Fixed by carrying `releasedAt` through
`passengersSeatedOnLeg` and reading it; the fixture now gives both travellers `12A`, and
reverting the component fails the test.

**The `verifier` proved the concurrency rather than reasoning about it.** Three
interleavings driven straight at Postgres at READ COMMITTED: a cancellation committing
between a rival's occupancy check and its insert (accepted — the seat genuinely is
free), two rivals taking a freshly released seat (one wins, other gets `23505`), and a
rival inserting while the cancellation is uncommitted (blocks, then correctly rejected).
It also found the existing contested-seat E2E test proves the *flight lock*, not the
index — it would pass with no unique index at all — so its comment is corrected and a
real race for a just-released seat is now driven in `seatRelease.database.test.ts`.

Two coverage gaps it found are closed: dropping `releasedAt: true` from either page's
select **survived `tsc` and all 683 unit tests** while printing a seat the customer no
longer holds, so the profile and admin journeys now assert the rendered label; and the
"only place that knows the rule" guard was still grepping for the old join shape, so it
was firing on nothing while the re-inlining that is *now* possible went straight past.
Both mutations were confirmed to fail after the fix.

Three pre-existing UI findings went to **#229** rather than into this PR: at phone width
the Status column is scrolled out of view and the wrapper is not keyboard-scrollable, the
seat cell measures 3.80:1 against AA's 4.5:1, and nothing conveys "Seat" to a screen
reader.

## Reversal

Documented, transactional, and **knowingly lossy** — the old index cannot be recreated
while two rows share a seat number, so reversing has to reimpose the placeholder and
discard the real seat numbers again. It is the one migration here where reversing
destroys what reversing cannot restore. The verifier ran it end to end against a
database holding both a released and a live `14B`: it succeeded, left a working schema,
and `migrate deploy` re-applied cleanly afterwards.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 683 unit + 79 database, `npm run build`,
Playwright 30/30, no drift. The verifier additionally applied the migration to databases
holding real `CANCELLED-%` placeholders, confirmed the backfill dated them from
`BookingStatusChange` (or the booking's creation for pre-#228 rows), and confirmed the
guard fires and rolls back whole.

Both reviews earned their keep, in different ways.

**`ui-review` found a live regression I'd missed.** The admin manifest tested `startsWith('CANCELLED')` — no hyphen — so my grep for `CANCELLED-` walked straight past it. With the placeholder gone that branch can never fire, and the manifest listed two travellers in seat 11A on the screen used to board a flight. Its test was green the whole time, feeding a value the database can no longer produce.

**The verifier proved the concurrency instead of arguing about it** — three interleavings driven at Postgres directly, including a cancellation committing between a rival's occupancy check and its insert. It also caught that the existing contested-seat E2E test proves the *flight lock*, not the index: it would pass with no unique index at all. One thing worth your attention: **this migration's reversal is knowingly lossy.** The old index can't be recreated while two rows share a seat number, so reversing has to reimpose the placeholder and discard the real seat numbers again — the only migration here where reversing destroys what reversing can't restore. It's transactional and the verifier ran it end to end, but it's a one-way door in practice.

input.content:
-- Record what a status change refunded, and put the history in order (#76).
--
-- Two additions to `BookingStatusChange`, both needed by the cancellation
-- rules that arrive with them.
--
-- `refundCents` is the amount owed back, decided by `lib/cancellationPolicy.ts`
-- at the moment of the change and recorded beside it. No money moves: real
-- payments are #75, which lands after this, and it will have a figure to refund
-- against rather than having to re-derive one from rules that may have changed
-- since. Null means the change was not one that refunds -- most of them.
--
-- `sequence` exists because `createdAt` cannot order two changes made in one
-- transaction. `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` is transaction start time, so a booking
-- disrupted and then cancelled in the same transaction carries two rows with
-- the same instant and a random uuid each, leaving "the latest status change"
-- unanswerable by ORDER BY and recoverable only by chaining `from` to `to`.
-- Nothing did that until now, and this slice does.
--
-- To reverse:
--
--     BEGIN;
--     DROP INDEX "BookingStatusChange_bookingId_sequence_idx";
--     ALTER TABLE "BookingStatusChange" DROP COLUMN "sequence";
--     ALTER TABLE "BookingStatusChange" DROP COLUMN "refundCents";
--     CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION "record_booking_status_change"() ... -- restore the
--         -- body from 20260810040000, which does not mention either column
--     DELETE FROM _prisma_migrations WHERE migration_name = '20260810060000_record_cancellation_refunds';
--     COMMIT;
--
-- The function has to be restored, not just the columns dropped: the version
-- below names both, and a trigger referring to a dropped column fails on the
-- next status change rather than at the moment of the drop. Reversing discards
-- the recorded refunds, which is the same decision as reversing the history
-- table itself.

SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s';

-- What the change owed back, in minor units. Null where the change did not
-- refund; zero is a real answer, and a different one -- a cancellation inside
-- the cut-off refunds nothing and says so.
ALTER TABLE "BookingStatusChange" ADD COLUMN "refundCents" INTEGER;

-- Monotonic across the whole table, which is all the ordering needs: rows are
-- only ever compared within one booking, and a sequence shared with other
-- bookings still orders those correctly.
ALTER TABLE "BookingStatusChange" ADD COLUMN "sequence" BIGSERIAL NOT NULL;

-- Existing rows were numbered by the sequence as the column was added, in
-- physical order. That is the best available: for every booking with more than
-- one change today they were written in separate transactions, so `createdAt`
-- already ordered them and the two agree.
CREATE INDEX "BookingStatusChange_bookingId_sequence_idx"
    ON "BookingStatusChange"("bookingId", "sequence");

-- The trigger learns one more setting, on the same transaction-local channel as
-- the reason and the actor. See 20260810040000 for why `true` is not optional.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION "record_booking_status_change"()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
DECLARE
    reason TEXT := nullif(current_setting('app.booking_status_reason', true), '');
    actor TEXT := nullif(current_setting('app.booking_status_actor', true), '');
    refund INTEGER := nullif(current_setting('app.booking_refund_cents', true), '')::INTEGER;
BEGIN
    IF TG_OP = 'INSERT' THEN
        INSERT INTO "BookingStatusChange"
            ("id", "bookingId", "from", "to", "reason", "actorUserId", "refundCents", "createdAt")
        VALUES
            (gen_random_uuid()::TEXT, NEW."id", NULL, NEW."status", reason, actor, refund,
             NEW."createdAt");
    ELSIF NEW."status" IS DISTINCT FROM OLD."status" THEN
        INSERT INTO "BookingStatusChange"
            ("id", "bookingId", "from", "to", "reason", "actorUserId", "refundCents", "createdAt")
        VALUES
            (gen_random_uuid()::TEXT, NEW."id", OLD."status", NEW."status", reason, actor, refund,
             CURRENT_TIMESTAMP);
    END IF;

    RETURN NULL;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

transition for the same route.

status points for a trip they took — and no refund was ever calculated.

## The rules

| Cabin | Before the cut-off | Inside it | Departed |
|---|---|---|---|
| First, Business | Full refund | Cancel, no refund | Refused |
| Premium Economy, Economy | Refund less a fifth | Cancel, no refund | Refused |

cut-off at nothing back, because refusing strands the customer with a booking they
cannot act on and keeps a seat held that could still be resold.

**Mixed cabins are apportioned.** Each traveller's share of what was actually charged
comes from the same fare model the booking was priced with, floored — so a Business
traveller pays no fee because somebody else on the booking flew Economy, and the parts
can sum to less than the whole but never more.

**The amount is recorded, not moved.** #75 owns payments and lands after this; it will
have a figure to refund against rather than re-deriving one from rules that may have
changed since. It goes on the status-history row via the same transaction-local channel
as the reason and the actor, alongside a monotonic `sequence` — `createdAt` is
transaction start time and cannot order two changes made together.

scale produced no over-refund, no negative, and no float leak — and then found six real
defects around it. All are fixed:

  cost" two different ways. Both use `bookingTotalCents` now.
- **A leg with no seat assignments** produced a refund of zero under an audit note
  reading *"refunded in full"*. The note keyed on the fee rather than the refund; and the
  adapter now assumes one Economy traveller, the same fallback the manifest makes and the
  least generous reading, so a wrong guess errs towards the airline.

  matching insertion order once the heap reuses freed space — which this table does on

Merged. `main` is at `f6928c6`, clean.

Slice 3 of #76 is in — your policy table is now enforced, and the two defects it was written to close are closed: cancelling a departed flight is refused, and every cancellation records what it owes.

**Session total: five PRs merged.**

| PR | What |
|---|---|
| #226 | Codex removed from the workflow |
| #227 | #213 closed — test infrastructure finished |
| #228 | #76 slice 1 — booking status typed, history recorded |
| #230 | #76 slice 2 — seat release without renaming |
| #231 | #76 slice 3 — cancellation eligibility and refunds |

Filed along the way: **#225** (`e2e/` and `__tests__/` unlinted), **#229** (profile bookings table: status hidden at phone width, 3.80:1 contrast, seat not announced), and a note on **#84** for the departure-time defect.

**Two slices left on #76**, and slice 4 is the one that makes the rest real:

**Slice 4** — staff cancel moves bookings to `DISRUPTED` instead of leaving them `CONFIRMED`, plus the customer's refund-or-rebook choice. Right now a staff-cancelled flight only sends a notification, so a customer keeps a valid-looking boarding pass and, if they cancel themselves, pays the 20% fee for the airline's decision. input.prompt:
Review the rendered UI of branch `feat/flight-disruption` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app (AGENTS.md step 6). Postgres and Mailpit are running. Playwright's config refuses to reuse a dev server, so start `npm run dev` yourself if you want the app running and stop it when done; do not run `npx playwright test` while your dev server is up. Do not create scratch files in the repository root — use your scratchpad.

## What is new

A staff member cancelling a flight now moves its bookings to a new state, `DISRUPTED`, instead of leaving them `CONFIRMED`. The seat stays held and the customer chooses. This is the first time a booking can be in a state other than confirmed or cancelled, so the profile has a third row appearance.

In `components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx`:
- The status cell reads "Flight cancelled by airline" in amber (`#fbbf24`), versus red "Cancelled" and green "Confirmed".
- Below it, a line: "Your seat is held. Cancel for a full refund, with no cancellation fee."
- The "Change Seats" button is hidden for a disrupted booking; "Cancel" remains.
- The cancel confirmation reads "Cancel your booking for flight X and take a full refund?" instead of the seat-releasing warning.

The notification a customer receives also changed: cancelling a flight now sends "…has been cancelled by the airline. Your seat is held while you decide; cancel the booking from your profile for a full refund."

## How to reach the state

Sign up, book a flight, then as an admin with staff MFA set that flight's status to Cancelled from `/admin/flights` — or set the booking's status directly with Prisma if that is faster. Then view the customer's `/profile`.

## What I want checked

1. **Does the disrupted row read correctly** at 390x844, 768x1024 and 1440x900? Particularly: is the amber distinguishable from the red and green, does the explanatory line wrap sanely at phone width, and does it push the layout around?
2. **Is the state legible without colour?** Note #229 already records that at phone width the Status column is scrolled out of the visible area entirely — check whether that hides this new state too, because if so a disrupted booking may look identical to a confirmed one on a phone.
3. **Accessibility of the new state**: is "Flight cancelled by airline" and its explanation announced usefully, is the amber on the dark background above 4.5:1, and does hiding "Change Seats" leave a sensible focus order?
4. **The wording.** "Flight cancelled by airline" sits in a column headed Status alongside "Confirmed" and "Cancelled". Does it read as a status? Is the distinction between "Cancelled" (mine) and "Flight cancelled by airline" (theirs) clear to someone who has not read this description?
5. **The notification** in the bell drawer for the same event — does it read well and is it actionable?

Capture screenshots at each viewport. Where a finding is pre-existing rather than introduced here, say so. If something is not applicable, give the concrete reason.

Verify branch `feat/flight-disruption` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app (AGENTS.md step 7). Slice 4 of 5 for #76 — `gh issue view 76 --comments` has the decision record. Postgres and Mailpit are running. A `ui-review` agent may be running and may hold port 3000; wait rather than killing it, and do not run Playwright beside it.

## What the change is

A staff flight cancellation used to change only the flight. The bookings stayed `CONFIRMED` holding their seats, so a customer kept a boarding pass for a flight that was not operating — and cancelling it themselves cost them the 20% Economy fee for the airline's decision.

`updateFlightStatusAction` now does the status and its consequences together under the flight's lock:
- To `CANCELLED`: bookings with a leg on that flight and status `CONFIRMED` move to `DISRUPTED` (not `CANCELLED` — the seat stays held and the customer keeps the choice). One cancelled leg disrupts the whole itinerary.
- To `ON_TIME`/`DELAYED`: bookings that are `DISRUPTED` on that flight return to `CONFIRMED`, unless another leg of theirs is still on a cancelled flight, and never if the customer has cancelled in the meantime. This is what makes a staff cancellation reversible rather than a one-way door.
- The actor and a reason go on every history row via the transaction-local settings.
- The notification for a cancellation now tells the customer their seat is held and that cancelling gives a full refund.

`cancelBookingAction` now **re-reads and re-decides the policy under the flight locks**. This slice introduces the first writer of `DISRUPTED`, which makes the TOCTOU I noted in slice 3 real: staff cancelling between the pre-lock read and the lock would otherwise charge the customer a fee they are exempt from. A `BookingDepartedError` thrown inside the transaction rolls it back and becomes the same refusal the early check gives.

`ProfileClient` renders the new state and hides "Change Seats" for it.

New test file `__tests__/app/flightDisruption.database.test.ts` (8 tests). No migration in this slice.

## What I already ran

## What I want from you

- **Concurrency, which is the point of this slice.** Prove the re-decide under the lock actually holds: construct staff cancelling a flight concurrently with a customer cancelling their booking on it, in both orders, and check the refund recorded is right in each case and that no interleaving produces a `CONFIRMED` booking on a cancelled flight or a `DISRUPTED` booking on a live one. Check the lock ordering in `updateFlightStatusAction` against `FlightBookingService` and `cancelBookingAction` — the first locks one flight, the others lock several in ascending id order. - **Does anything else read `Booking.status` and assume two values?** Grep every reader — points, the admin manifest counts, the flight board, seat occupancy, `PointsActivityService` — and say what each does with `DISRUPTED`. Points is the one I am least sure of: a disrupted booking should presumably still count until it is cancelled.

Slice 4 is implemented and green locally; both reviews are running.

**What it does.** Cancelling a flight from `/admin/flights` now moves its bookings to `DISRUPTED` in the same locked transaction as the flight's own status. The seat stays held, the customer keeps the choice, and a cancelled leg disrupts the whole itinerary since half a trip isn't usable.

**Reinstatement is the part that justifies the design.** Setting the flight back to on-time returns those bookings to `CONFIRMED` — but not if another leg of theirs is still cancelled, and never if the customer already cancelled in the meantime. That's what makes a staff cancellation reversible instead of a one-way door, which was the main argument for `DISRUPTED` over auto-cancel when you approved it.

```
Mona Airways MA304   Tokyo → San Francisco   8/16/2026
```

The amber sits on MA303, which is operating. MA304, the flight the airline cancelled, carries no marking at all. The confirm dialog then says:

> `Cancel your booking for flight MA303 and take a full refund?`

Meanwhile the bell (`desktop-drawer-inbound.png`) correctly says *"Your flight MA304 … has been cancelled by the airline."* The two surfaces contradict each other, and the one the customer acts from is the wrong one. A customer who reads only the profile believes their outbound is cancelled and their return is fine — the exact inverse of the truth. The notification drawer at 390x844 renders behind the page (`document.elementFromPoint` at the notification returns `user-avatar`, not the drawer) — pre-existing, filed as **#208**. So on a phone there is currently **no path at all** by which a customer learns the airline cancelled their flight, and the seat stays held while they never act. Neither issue is caused by this diff, but this diff is what makes both load-bearing; that escalation should be recorded on #229 and #208 before this ships.

## Non-blocking

### 4. After the scheduled departure passes, the row promises a refund the server refuses

With a disrupted booking whose flight time had passed, clicking Cancel produced:

```
confirm: Cancel your booking for flight MA303 and take a full refund?
alert:   This booking cannot be cancelled because the flight has already departed.
```

The row still reads "Your seat is held. Cancel for a full refund, with no cancellation fee." and the only offered action can never succeed (`lib/cancellationPolicy.ts:205-210` checks departed before disrupted, deliberately). A customer who waits a day is left holding an uncancellable booking on a flight that never operated. Evidence: `desktop-departed-refusal.png`. The refusal itself is well-worded; it is the row's standing promise that is wrong.

### 5. Wording — it does not read as a status, and the two "cancelled"s blur

Under a column of one-word tokens (`Confirmed`, `Cancelled`), "Flight cancelled by airline" is a sentence, and at a glance it reads as *your booking is cancelled — nothing to do*. That is the opposite of the intent. The explanatory line rescues it on desktop; at tablet the label wraps to 3 lines and at phone it is not visible at all, so the rescue is unreliable.

Suggestions: a short token that reads as a state and implies action ("Cancelled by airline", or "Action needed" with the detail beneath), and on a round trip the token must name the affected leg (finding 1).

### 6. One disrupted booking reshapes the whole table

Measured with and without the disrupted `tbody`:

| viewport | Status col | Flight | Route |
|---|---|---|---|
| 768 | 91 → **116** | 100 → **91** | 127 → **111** |
| 1280/1440 | 91 → **312** | unchanged | unchanged |

The 18rem explainer widens Status for *every* row, so at tablet one disrupted booking makes the route wrap harder on all the others (`tablet-bookings.png`). Row height goes 138→285 at tablet, 93→151 at desktop, 156→285 at phone.

No defect follows from it: `document.scrollWidth === clientWidth` at 390, 768, 1024, 1280 and 1440 — the page body never scrolls horizontally, and the table wrapper does not clip at any width from 1024 up. Recorded as a suggestion only.

### 7. Change Seats disappears even when the other leg still flies

`ProfileClient.tsx:420`. The comment says "nothing to choose on a flight that is not operating" — true of the cancelled leg, not of the one beside it. With only MA304 cancelled, the customer loses the ability to change their MA303 seat on a flight they may still intend to take.

### 8. The notification tells the customer to go somewhere but does not take them there

"cancel the booking from your profile for a full refund" — the drawer item is a `div`, not a link. One `href="/profile"` would close the loop. Also "Flight Update:" understates a cancellation in the title.

Everything green after the `ui-review` fixes. Summary while the verifier finishes:

**Three blocking findings, two of them mine.**

The worst was a genuine lie to the customer: **on a round trip, the row marked the wrong leg**. The status cell renders beside leg 1, so cancelling the *return* showed "Flight cancelled by airline" against the outbound — and the confirmation prompt named the operating flight. Meanwhile the notification correctly named the cancelled one, so the two surfaces contradicted each other and the one the customer acts from was wrong. It now finds the leg whose flight is actually cancelled and names it: "GA900 cancelled by airline".

Second: **the admin manifest called a disrupted passenger "Confirmed"** in green, and counted them as confirmed. That branch was `isCancelled ? 'Cancelled' : 'Confirmed'` — correct until this slice created a third state. Staff would cancel a flight and the manifest would still report a confirmed passenger holding a live seat on it.

Third was mine too, from the fix itself: I'd hidden "Change Seats" for any disrupted booking, but on a round trip the *other* leg may still fly. Restored.

I also removed a false promise `ui-review` caught: once a disrupted flight's departure time passes, cancelling is refused, but the row still said "Cancel for a full refund" and offered a button that could only fail. It now says the flight did not operate and hides the button. That needed the server's clock passed down — computing `Date.now()` in the component is both a hydration mismatch and a React-compiler lint error, so it's read through a named helper.

**Not fixed, escalated instead.** `ui-review` established something worth your attention: at phone width the Status column is scrolled out of view (#229) *and* the notification drawer renders behind the page (#208). Between them, **a phone user currently has no way at all to learn their flight was cancelled** — the row looks identical to a confirmed one and the fallback channel is unreadable. Neither is caused by this slice, but this slice is what makes both load-bearing. I've recorded that on both issues.

Good news from the contrast check: the amber is 11.02:1, the highest-contrast of the three states, and the explanatory line 10.58:1.

Locally green: lint clean, 714 unit, 89 database, build, Playwright 30/30, and five mutants dead — including "mark leg 1 regardless" and "call a disrupted passenger Confirmed". I'll fold in the verifier's report when it lands, then open the PR.

## Findings, most severe first

### 1. REGRESSION — two flights of one itinerary changing status concurrently leave the booking `CONFIRMED` on a cancelled flight

**27 of 30** unassisted rounds — a plain `Promise.all` of two `updateFlightStatusAction` calls, no artificial blockers. With the two flight locks held and released together, 17 of 25.

Setup: booking on legs A+B, A already `CANCELLED` (booking `DISRUPTED`), B operating. Concurrently reinstate A and cancel B. Final state observed: booking `CONFIRMED`, flight B `CANCELLED`.

Mechanism, under READ COMMITTED with each transaction holding only *its own* flight's lock (`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/app/actions.ts:1053`):

- cancel-B's `updateMany` filters `status: 'CONFIRMED'`; its statement snapshot still sees the booking as `DISRUPTED`, so it does not match and is never row-locked — no blocking, no serialisation.
- reinstate-A's `updateMany` evaluates `NOT: { legs: { some: { flight: { status: 'CANCELLED' } } } }` against a snapshot where B is still `ON_TIME` (cancel-B uncommitted), so the sibling guard passes and the booking goes `CONFIRMED`.

Both commit. Sequentially, in *either* order, the outcome is correct — this only appears concurrently. The lock is correct for the flight it takes; the predicates read rows belonging to flights it does not lock. Result is precisely the defect the slice exists to remove: a live boarding pass on a flight that is not operating, no `DISRUPTED` history row, no notification, and the customer later pays the 20% Economy fee to cancel.

### 2. REGRESSION — the mirror: reinstating both legs at once strands the booking `DISRUPTED` while both flights operate

**19 of 20** rounds. Booking `DISRUPTED` on A+B, both cancelled; reinstate both concurrently: each `updateMany`'s sibling guard sees the other flight still `CANCELLED`, both skip, booking stays `DISRUPTED` with both flights `ON_TIME`.

Same root cause. Worse to recover from than #1: the admin select already reads `ON_TIME`, so no `onChange` fires and staff cannot repair it without deliberately toggling to `CANCELLED` and back. Meanwhile the profile offers the customer "Cancel for a full refund, with no cancellation fee" on two flights that are running — a real refund on an undisrupted trip.

Both #1 and #2 need two overlapping status changes on two legs of one itinerary. Each row in `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/app/admin/flights/FlightStatusSelector.tsx` has its own `useTransition` and disables only its own `<select>`, so one admin changing two rows, or two admins, is enough.

### 3. REGRESSION — a `DELAYED` flight no longer notifies anybody holding a confirmed booking

Verified against the database: `updateFlightStatusAction(flight, 'DELAYED')` on a flight with a `CONFIRMED` booking produces **0 notifications**. On `main` it produced one — the notify query was `status: "CONFIRMED"` for every status. Now (`app/actions.ts:1071`) it is `status === 'CANCELLED' ? 'CONFIRMED' : 'DISRUPTED'`, so for `DELAYED` it selects only bookings that are already disrupted. Delay notifications are the main use of that status, and nothing in issue #76's decision record asks for this.

This is locked in vacuously. `__tests__/app/actions.test.ts:1585` now asserts the `status: 'DISRUPTED'` filter, and the same test still asserts that "is now DELAYED" notifications go to `user-1`/`user-2` — but `mockTx.booking.findMany` is mocked to return those users regardless of the `where`, so the assertion passes on a query that returns nothing in reality. Green suite, dead feature.

### 4. COVERAGE GAP — the flight lock in the status action is not exercised by anything

Mutation results (each applied alone, full unit + database suite):

| Mutation | Verdict |
|---|---|
| remove the actor `set_config` | **killed** — `cancelling a flight › records who did it and why, on the history` |
| reinstatement also revives `CANCELLED` bookings | **killed** — `does not resurrect a booking the customer cancelled in the meantime` |
| disruption updates every booking, not only `CONFIRMED` | **killed** — `leaves a booking the customer already cancelled alone` |
| drop the still-cancelled-sibling guard | **killed** — `leaves a trip whose other leg is still cancelled disrupted` |
| decide the refund from the stale pre-lock read | **killed** — 1 unit test (`prices the cancellation from the read taken under the lock`); **no database test catches it** |
| **remove `lockFlightForUpdate` from `updateFlightStatusAction`** | **SURVIVES** — 712 unit + 89 database all pass |

The lock is the load-bearing half of this slice and deleting it is invisible. I did verify by construction that it works: parking the customer's transaction on leg A's lock, cancelling leg B in between, then releasing, records `refundCents = 20000` (full) where the control case records `8000` (20% kept) — but that construction lives only in my scratch harness.

### 5. Notifications: two smaller divergences (behaviour, no test)

- **Reinstatement notifies bookings it does not reinstate.** The notify set is read before the update as "`DISRUPTED` on this flight", but the update excludes bookings with another still-cancelled leg. Observed: booking stays `DISRUPTED`, customer receives "Your upcoming flight … is now ON TIME."
- **A second cancelled leg notifies nobody.** Cancel A then cancel B on the same booking: one notification, naming A only. The customer is never told B is off.
- Repeated toggling does **not** duplicate: cancelling an already-cancelled flight sends nothing (no `CONFIRMED` bookings remain), and cancel→reinstate→cancel sends one message per real transition. No `refundCents` leaks onto the disruption history rows.

### 6. `BookingDepartedError` — clean, confirmed empirically

Constructed with a flight departing 2.5s out and the transaction parked on the flight lock past that instant. Result: `{ ok: false, error: { code: 'VALIDATION_ERROR', message: 'This booking cannot be cancelled because the flight has already departed.' } }` — returned, not thrown, so no 500. Booking still `CONFIRMED`, only the `null->CONFIRMED` creation history row, 0 notifications, seat still held. **Prisma does not retry**: instrumented the callback and it entered exactly once.

### 7. Deadlock — looked for, not found

`updateFlightStatusAction` takes one lock; `FlightBookingService`, `cancelBookingAction` and `changeBookingSeatsAction` take theirs in ascending flight id. There is no cycle available from lock *order*. The residual risk was `updateMany` row-locking order across two staff transactions on two flights sharing bookings: 20 forced rounds with 6 round-trip bookings on both flights, plus 25 rounds of the mixed scenario — **0 deadlocks**. Not a proof (the plan could differ under other statistics), but nothing observed.

Customer-vs-staff on the *same* flight is properly serialised: 12/12 concurrent rounds ended `CANCELLED` with a refund consistent with the recorded path — `10000` (full) where the history shows `->DISRUPTED` first, `8000` where it does not. No interleaving produced a wrong amount.

### 8. Every other reader of `Booking.status`

- `lib/PointsActivityService.ts:39,75,141` — all three branches key off `=== 'CANCELLED'`, so a `DISRUPTED` booking still earns and still shows as a plain credit. That matches your expectation; nothing to change, but nothing tests it either.
- `lib/seatOccupancy.ts` — occupancy is `releasedAt: null`, not status, and the release trigger fires only into `CANCELLED`. `DISRUPTED` keeps its seat. Correct, and asserted by the new test.
- `app/admin/flights/AdminFlightsTable.tsx` — updated in the latest edits: separate "Disrupted" count and per-passenger "Disrupted" label. Note line 128 still counts `b.status !== 'CANCELLED'` as "active bookings" in the row summary, so a disrupted booking reads as active there.
- `lib/FlightBookingService.ts:188` and `app/actions.ts:215/245` are *flight* status, not booking status — unaffected.
- `changeBookingSeatsAction` (`app/actions.ts:594`) refuses only `CANCELLED`. Now that the newest UI deliberately keeps "Change Seats" on a disrupted round trip, the server has no leg-level guard: a customer can move their seat on the leg the airline cancelled. No test either way.

### 9. Robustness — new failure mode from moving the status change into a transaction

`updateFlightStatusAction` now waits for the flight lock *inside* a `prisma.$transaction` with the default 5s timeout. A cancellation holding that lock longer than that turns a staff status change into a thrown `P2028`, which `FlightStatusSelector` shows as an `alert`. Previously the status write never blocked. Low likelihood, worth knowing.

### 10. `renderedAt = 0` silently disables the departed guard

`components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx:111` defaults the prop to `0`, which makes `departed` false for every real date. If a caller ever omits it, the "did not operate / no cancel button" branch vanishes with no type error and no test failure — the four new ProfileClient tests that do not pass it exercise only the non-departed branch. `lib/serverClock.ts` has no test of its own.

### 11. Environment / process notes (not defects in the change)

- **The working tree moved under me.** After my first full pass, `app/admin/flights/AdminFlightsTable.tsx`, `app/profile/page.tsx`, `components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx` and two test files were edited between 10:52 and 11:05, and `lib/serverClock.ts` appeared. My **first** Playwright run overlapped those edits and is not a trustworthy signal; everything in the table above is a re-run after the tree went quiet. The slice is also no longer what your brief described — "hides Change Seats for DISRUPTED" has become "keeps Change Seats when another leg still flies."
- **Transient lint error, since fixed.** At 11:05 `npm run lint` failed with `app/profile/page.tsx:95 Cannot call impure function during render` on `renderedAt={Date.now()}`. The 11:05:09 edit introducing `serverRenderTime()` fixed it; lint is clean now. Flagging it only so you know it was real and that the fix is what I verified.
- I deleted `.next` for a clean build while a dev server held port 3000; that server restarted (new pid). If the `ui-review` agent saw an odd reload around then, that was me.
- `app/actions.ts` was restored from backup after mutation testing and verified `sha256 OK`; I never wrote any other file in the repo.

Finding 4 says the lock could be deleted tomorrow and CI would applaud. I did not fix any of them.</result>

Slice 4 of 5 for #76, implementing the second half of the [decision record](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/76#issuecomment-5235526479).

## What was broken

Cancelling a flight changed only the flight. Its bookings stayed `CONFIRMED` holding
their seats, so a customer kept a boarding pass for a flight that was not operating —
and if they cancelled it themselves they paid the 20% Economy fee for the airline's
decision. The `DISRUPTED` branch of the policy shipped in #231 had no writer at all.

## The change

Bookings on a cancelled flight move to `DISRUPTED`: the seat stays held, the customer
keeps the choice, and one cancelled leg disrupts the whole itinerary. Putting the flight
back reinstates them — never a booking whose other leg is still cancelled, and never one
the customer has cancelled in the meantime. That reversibility is why the decision record
chose this over auto-cancelling.

The customer's row names the cancelled leg and offers a full refund; the confirmation
prompt says so rather than warning about releasing seats.

## Locking the flight was not enough — two real races

Found by the `verifier`, reproduced **27 times in 30** with a plain `Promise.all`, no
artificial blockers.

What a booking should become depends on the statuses of its **other** legs — rows the
transaction does not hold. Under READ COMMITTED two concurrent status changes each read
the other's pre-image:

- **Cancel one leg while reinstating another** → booking left `CONFIRMED` on a cancelled
  flight. A live boarding pass on a flight that is not operating, no history row, no
  notification, and the customer later pays the fee to cancel. Precisely the defect this
  slice exists to remove.
- **Reinstate both legs at once** → booking stranded `DISRUPTED` while both flights
  operate, offering "Cancel for a full refund" on an undisrupted trip. Worse to recover
  from: the admin selects already read On Time, so nothing prompts staff to fix it.

Each admin row has its own transition and disables only its own select, so one person
changing two rows reaches this.

**The fix**: the bookings are what the two transactions have in common, so they are what
is locked — `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` in ascending id order, matching every other lock order
here — and each booking's new status is then decided from its own legs rather than by a
predicate over rows that may be mid-change. Two concurrency tests drive it eight rounds
each; removing `FOR UPDATE` fails both.

The explicit `lockFlightForUpdate` is gone from this action, not left untested: the
`flight.update` a statement later takes the same row's write lock and holds it to commit.

## Other regressions caught and fixed

- **A `DELAYED` flight stopped notifying anyone.** Narrowing the notify query to
  disrupted bookings silently killed delay notifications — the main use of that status.
  Worse, the test certified it: the mock returned users regardless of the `where`, so a
  query returning nothing in reality passed. Both fixed; the test now asserts the real
  query and that a delay moves nobody's status.
- **Reinstatement told customers "is now ON TIME"** when their trip was still broken by
  another cancelled leg, and a second cancelled leg notified nobody. Messages are now
  per-booking-outcome, deduplicated per person and outcome.
- **The admin manifest called a disrupted passenger "Confirmed"**, in green, and counted
  them as confirmed — on the screen used to board a flight. Found by `ui-review`.
- **On a round trip the profile marked the wrong leg.** The status cell renders beside
  leg 1, so cancelling the return showed the cancellation against the outbound, and the
  confirm prompt named the operating flight — while the notification named the right one.
  Also `ui-review`.
- **Change Seats was hidden for any disrupted booking**, but the other leg may still fly.
  Restored, with a server-side guard so a seat on the cancelled leg still cannot be moved
  — the UI is not the place for that rule.
- **The row promised a refund after departure** that the server refuses. It now says the
  flight did not operate. That needed the server's clock passed down: `Date.now()` in the
  component is both a hydration mismatch and a React-compiler error, so it is read
  through `lib/serverClock`.
- `renderedAt` is required rather than defaulted — a default of zero makes every flight
  look upcoming, switching the departed guard off with nothing to notice.

## Recorded, not fixed

**A phone user currently cannot learn their flight was cancelled at all.** At 390px the
Status column is scrolled out of view (#229) and the notification drawer renders behind
the page (#208), so a disrupted booking is pixel-identical to a confirmed one and the
fallback channel is unreadable. Neither is caused by this slice; both are now
load-bearing, and I have [said so on each](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/229#issuecomment-5244020765).

**Rebooking is not here.** It needs a constrained search, seat reselection, a fare
difference and a history decision — its own slice, [recorded on the issue](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/76#issuecomment-5244346371)
along with credit, which has no schema anywhere.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 714 unit + 91 database, `npm run build`,

rather than confirmed ones, removing the actor, deciding the refund from the stale
pre-lock read, marking leg 1 regardless, calling a disrupted passenger Confirmed, and
dropping `FOR UPDATE` from the booking lock.
