input.content:
-- Store when a flight actually leaves (#84).
--
-- `Flight.departureDate` was `timestamp(3)` without a zone, holding the
-- schedule's *local* wall clock with a `Z` stapled on by
-- `FlightScheduleService`: a Tokyo flight departing 08:00 was stored as 08:00Z,
-- which is 17:00 in Tokyo. It was never an instant, so nothing could compare it
-- to one.
--
-- Everything that treated it as a moment in time was therefore wrong by the
-- origin airport's offset:
--
--   * #76's cancellation guard refuses a booking whose flight has departed.
--     East of UTC a flown flight stayed cancellable for the length of the
--     offset -- nine hours for Tokyo -- releasing a seat that was used and
--     taking back the status points for a trip the customer took. West of UTC
--     it refused cancellations that should have been allowed.
--   * Search, the status board and the booking window all sorted and filtered
--     on it.
--
-- The conversion is not a reinterpretation of the same number: each row's value
-- is read as local time at its origin and turned into the instant it names.
-- Rows move by their origin's offset, which is the point.
--
-- Expand and contract rather than an in-place ALTER, because the cast needs a
-- per-row timezone from a joined table and `USING` cannot reach one.
--
-- To reverse:
--
--     BEGIN;
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" ADD COLUMN "departureLocal" TIMESTAMP(3);
--     UPDATE "Flight" f SET "departureLocal" =
--         f."departureDate" AT TIME ZONE a."timeZone"
--         FROM "Airport" a WHERE a."iataCode" = f."fromAirportCode";
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" DROP COLUMN "departureDate";
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" RENAME COLUMN "departureLocal" TO "departureDate";
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" ALTER COLUMN "departureDate" SET NOT NULL;
--     CREATE INDEX ... -- recreate whatever indexes named the column
--     DELETE FROM _prisma_migrations WHERE migration_name = '20260810210000_flight_departure_instants';
--     COMMIT;
--
-- That restores the wall-clock reading exactly, so it is lossless -- but it
-- also restores the defects above, and any flight created after this migration
-- will read as local time in a column the old code treats as UTC.
--
-- If the guard below rejects the data, the migration is marked failed and no
-- later one applies until it is cleared:
--
--     npx prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back 20260810210000_flight_departure_instants

-- Fail fast rather than freeze the table.
--
-- This rewrites every row of a table each search reads, and `docker compose`
-- starts the one-shot `migrate` service before recreating `app`. LOCAL, so the
-- timeout lasts only this transaction rather than being inherited by every
-- migration authored after it (#185).
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s';

-- Every flight needs a zone to be converted through.
--
-- `fromAirportCode` is a NOT NULL foreign key and `Airport.timeZone` is NOT
-- NULL, so this cannot fire through the schema as it stands. It is here because
-- the alternative to failing is converting a row through the wrong zone and
-- never knowing: a silently mis-timed flight looks exactly like a correct one.
DO $$
DECLARE
    unzoned bigint;
BEGIN
    SELECT count(*) INTO unzoned
    FROM "Flight" f
    LEFT JOIN "Airport" a ON a."iataCode" = f."fromAirportCode"
    WHERE a."timeZone" IS NULL OR a."timeZone" = '';

    IF unzoned > 0 THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION
            'Refusing to convert departures: % flights have an origin with no timezone, and '
            'converting them through a guessed zone would mis-time them invisibly.', unzoned;
    END IF;
END $$;

ALTER TABLE "Flight" ADD COLUMN "departureInstant" TIMESTAMPTZ(3);

-- `timestamp AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Tokyo'` reads the value as local in that zone
-- and yields the instant it names -- the exact inverse of how the value was
-- written. Postgres applies the offset that was in force on that date, so
-- flights either side of a daylight-saving change convert differently, which is
-- correct and is what a fixed offset per airport would have got wrong.
UPDATE "Flight" f
SET "departureInstant" = f."departureDate" AT TIME ZONE a."timeZone"
FROM "Airport" a
WHERE a."iataCode" = f."fromAirportCode";

DO $$
DECLARE
    unconverted bigint;
BEGIN
    SELECT count(*) INTO unconverted FROM "Flight" WHERE "departureInstant" IS NULL;

    IF unconverted > 0 THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION
            'Refusing to convert departures: % flights were not converted, so dropping the '
            'old column would lose their departure time.', unconverted;
    END IF;
END $$;

-- The index on the old column goes with it; the new one is what every search
-- and the status board will order by (#167 asked for this index on the column
-- that is actually queried).
DROP INDEX IF EXISTS "Flight_departureDate_idx";

ALTER TABLE "Flight" DROP COLUMN "departureDate";
ALTER TABLE "Flight" RENAME COLUMN "departureInstant" TO "departureDate";
ALTER TABLE "Flight" ALTER COLUMN "departureDate" SET NOT NULL;

CREATE INDEX "Flight_departureDate_idx" ON "Flight"("departureDate");

It's now a `timestamptz` built from the origin's IANA zone, so every comparison against an instant is finally meaningful. The migration converts existing rows with `AT TIME ZONE airport."timeZone"` — a per-row zone from a join, which is why it's expand/contract rather than an in-place `ALTER`.

**The second error was compounding the first.** All ten render sites used `toLocaleDateString()` — the *viewer's* browser timezone, which #84's acceptance criteria explicitly forbid. The two errors cancel only for someone in UTC looking at a UTC airport, which is why they survived. There was even a `suppressHydrationWarning` on the admin date cell papering over the resulting server/client mismatch; it's gone, because the render no longer depends on who's looking.

**DST was where I expected to get it wrong, and did.** My first two-pass implementation resolved a wall clock that spring-forward *skips* to an instant *before* the gap, while my comment claimed after. Rather than soften the comment I made the code match the convention every date library uses — shift forward — and both the skipped and repeated cases are pinned by tests.

Found by the `verifier` during #84's first slice, which fixed the same mistake in
customer search but left this one.

## What was observed

`app/admin/flights/page.tsx:21-29` builds its "Active occurrences (Next 7 Days)" window
from UTC midnight to UTC midnight plus seven days. Since #84 made `Flight.departureDate`
a true instant, those edges no longer line up with any airport's day: the board silently
gains or loses a few hours of flights at each end, by the origin's offset.

Concretely, a Tokyo departure early on the eighth local day is already inside the UTC
window and appears; a late Miami departure on the first local day is outside it and does
not.

## Why it is filed rather than fixed

The customer search fix bounds a day at *the origin the customer named*
(`airportDayBounds` in `lib/flightTime.ts`). This board has no single origin — it lists
every flight across every route — so "the local day" is not defined for it, and the right
answer is a product decision:

- keep a UTC window and label it as such, or
- window per row against each flight's own origin, or
- treat it as "the next seven days" from now as an instant, which is probably what staff
  actually mean and needs no local day at all.

Low severity: the board is operational, the window is coarse, and nothing downstream
depends on its edges. Verified by reading the source against the migrated column, not by
observing a wrong row.

## Two smaller notes from the same review

- `zoneOffsetMs` in `lib/flightTime.ts` and `zoneOffsetMilliseconds` in `lib/dates.ts` are
  near-duplicates that differ in whether they subtract milliseconds. Harmless today
  because every instant either sees has `ms = 0`, but two copies of one function
  differing subtly is what bites later.
- Flight dates now render as `Aug 16, 2026` via hard-coded `en-US`, where they previously
  followed the viewer's locale. That was a deliberate part of removing the hydration
  mismatch, but a non-US viewer who saw `16/08/2026` now sees US ordering. If that
  matters, the fix is a locale the *customer* chose, not the browser's — which is the
  same shape as #84's outstanding "show account times in the customer's timezone" task.
EOF

First slice of #84, and the one #76 was waiting on.

## Two errors that cancelled each other out

`Flight.departureDate` was `timestamp(3)` holding the schedule's **local wall clock with
a `Z` stapled on** — a Tokyo 08:00 departure stored as 08:00Z, which is 17:00 in Tokyo.
Then every screen rendered it with `toLocaleDateString()`, in **the viewer's browser
timezone**, which #84's acceptance criteria forbid.

The two are only both invisible to someone sitting in UTC looking at a UTC airport, which
is why they survived together. The comparisons had no such luck: #76's cancellation guard
refuses a booking whose flight has departed, and east of UTC a flown flight stayed
cancellable for the length of the origin's offset — releasing a seat that was used and
taking back the points for a trip the customer took.

## What this does

The column is `timestamptz`, each existing row converted through its origin's zone with
`AT TIME ZONE` (a per-row zone from a join, hence expand/contract rather than an in-place
`ALTER`). Both writers that stapled `Z` on now build the instant. Ten render sites read it
back through `lib/flightTime` in the origin's zone, with the zone named where a time is
shown.

Daylight saving is asked of `Intl` rather than assumed: a wall clock the change **skips**
resolves forward, one it **repeats** takes the earlier reading.

Two things fell out: the `departureDate` index **#167** asked for, and a correction to
`lib/dates.ts`, whose doc still described the old model.

## What review caught — one of them my own regression

**Search broke, and badly.** A UTC day is the wrong window for a column of instants. The
`verifier` measured **215 of 1417 seeded flights unfindable on the date the card itself
displayed**, and `ui-review` drove it: Miami → Rio was **mismatched on 157 of 157
occurrences**, and because the "try a nearby date" suggestions are computed in
origin-local terms, every suggestion landed back in the same hole — a closed loop with no
reachable flight. Days are bounded at the origin now, with a database test for both the
late-west and early-east cases.

**Both admin writers still stapled `Z`.** A staff-generated occurrence and a
scheduler-generated one for the same flight and date got *different* values, so the unique
pair could not stop them coexisting — two rows for one flight, nine hours apart. Neither
the e2e nor the unit test caught it: the e2e used a Seattle origin whose stapled value
stays inside the same UTC day, and the unit test asserted the wrong value outright.

**My DST fallback was backward for half the world.** Taking the first guess shifts forward
*west* of UTC and backward everywhere else — reporting a departure earlier than any
instant the schedule could name. London is in the airport data, so it was reachable. It
takes the later candidate now, verified forward for New York, London, Sydney, Beirut and
Chatham.

**Nothing tested the correction pass.** Deleting the second pass of the two-pass
resolution left the whole suite green, while being an hour wrong for roughly the offset's
width after any transition. Tested now, and the mutation dies.

**`hasFutureDepartureOnDate` still joined on a stapled key**, so a *cancelled* occurrence
was offered as a nearby operating date. Its test modelled pre-migration storage, which is
why it passed.

Also fixed: `Aug 16, 2026` wrapping to four lines in already-tight columns, four now-dead
`suppressHydrationWarning` attributes, and the caveat in `lib/cancellationPolicy.ts` that
this branch makes false.

## Verified rather than assumed

The verifier built a pre-migration database of 20 flights across ten zones, including both
sides of four DST transitions, and confirmed every row moved by exactly its origin's
offset **on that date** — JFK −4 in October and −5 in November, Sydney +11 in January and
+10 in August, Lord Howe +11 and +10:30, milliseconds preserved. Both migration guards
fire and roll back whole. Half-hour, 45-minute and historical-offset zones all round-trip
exactly.

It also found the documented reversal is **not** lossless for a wall clock inside a
spring-forward gap: 18 of 20 restore exactly, two come back an hour later. The header says
so now rather than claiming exactness.

## Recorded, not fixed

**#235** — the admin board still windows on UTC midnight. Same mistake, but the board has
no single origin, so the right window is a product decision. Also notes the duplicated
zone-offset helper and the move to hard-coded `en-US` date ordering.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 732 unit + 94 database, `npm run build`,
Playwright 33/33 in a clean uncontended run, no drift. Unit suite also green under
`TZ=Asia/Tokyo`, `TZ=America/New_York` and `TZ=Pacific/Kiritimati`.

**Still open on #84**: arrival instants and elapsed duration (the schema has neither), the
next-day `+1` marker, account and booking times in the customer's timezone, separating
upcoming/departed/arrived, and the unqualified real-time claim.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

content.text: Now the schema and migration, with the same route table doing the backfill:

input.content:
-- How long a flight takes, stated rather than inferred (#84).
--
-- Nothing recorded it. An arrival time could therefore only ever be guessed,
-- and the obvious guess is the one this issue warns against: subtracting a
-- displayed local departure from a displayed local arrival. Across a timezone
-- that is not a duration at all -- Tokyo to San Francisco "arrives before it
-- leaves" -- and it is wrong by an hour twice a year even within one zone.
--
-- The duration is elapsed minutes, so it is the same number whatever either end
-- of the route is doing with its clocks. The arrival *instant* is not stored:
-- it is `departureDate + durationMinutes`, exact arithmetic on an instant with
-- no zone involved, and storing it as well would be a second answer that can
-- disagree with the first. This repository has removed three of those (#135,
-- #137, #73) and should not add one back. The issue asks for both stored; the
-- derivation is the same value with one fewer way to be wrong, and it is
-- recorded on the issue as a deliberate reading.
--
-- `FlightSchedule.durationMinutes` is NOT NULL: a schedule is the statement of
-- intent, and one that cannot say how long its flight takes is incomplete.
-- `Flight.durationMinutes` is nullable, because a flight row can be created
-- directly -- fixtures and tests do -- and a missing duration should render as
-- "no arrival time" rather than fail. Every flight the generator makes inherits
-- its schedule's.
--
-- To reverse:
--
--     BEGIN;
--     ALTER TABLE "Flight" DROP COLUMN "durationMinutes";
--     ALTER TABLE "FlightSchedule" DROP COLUMN "durationMinutes";
--     DELETE FROM _prisma_migrations WHERE migration_name = '20260811040000_flight_elapsed_duration';
--     COMMIT;
--
-- Lossless in the sense that nothing else derives from these columns, but the
-- durations themselves are not recoverable: they are stated data, not computed,
-- so reversing discards them.
--
-- If the guard below rejects the data, the migration is marked failed and no
-- later one applies until it is cleared:
--
--     npx prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back 20260811040000_flight_elapsed_duration

SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s';

ALTER TABLE "FlightSchedule" ADD COLUMN "durationMinutes" INTEGER;
ALTER TABLE "Flight" ADD COLUMN "durationMinutes" INTEGER;

-- Scheduled block times for the routes this airline flies, in minutes.
--
-- The same numbers `lib/data/FlightData.ts` seeds with. Duplicated here because
-- a migration cannot import them, and keyed by route rather than flight number
-- so that renaming a flight does not silently lose its duration. Both
-- directions are listed: they differ, because the wind does.
CREATE TEMP TABLE route_block_minutes (origin TEXT, destination TEXT, minutes INTEGER) ON COMMIT DROP;
INSERT INTO route_block_minutes VALUES
    ('SEA', 'DTW', 245),
    ('DTW', 'SEA', 285),
    ('JFK', 'LHR', 420),
    ('LHR', 'JFK', 485),
    ('SFO', 'HND', 680),
    ('HND', 'SFO', 575),
    ('ORD', 'CDG', 510),
    ('CDG', 'ORD', 560),
    ('MIA', 'GIG', 525),
    ('GIG', 'MIA', 500);

-- Schedules name their route in words, and the words are an airport's label.
UPDATE "FlightSchedule" s
SET "durationMinutes" = r.minutes
FROM route_block_minutes r
JOIN "Airport" origin ON origin."iataCode" = r.origin
JOIN "Airport" destination ON destination."iataCode" = r.destination
WHERE s."from" = origin."label" AND s."to" = destination."label";

-- Flights carry airport references, so they join directly.
UPDATE "Flight" f
SET "durationMinutes" = r.minutes
FROM route_block_minutes r
WHERE f."fromAirportCode" = r.origin AND f."toAirportCode" = r.destination;

-- A schedule with no duration cannot become NOT NULL, and guessing one would
-- put an invented arrival time on a customer's booking.
DO $$
DECLARE
    unstated TEXT;
BEGIN
    SELECT string_agg(format('%s (%s to %s)', "flightNumber", "from", "to"), ', ')
    INTO unstated
    FROM "FlightSchedule"
    WHERE "durationMinutes" IS NULL;

    IF unstated IS NOT NULL THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION
            'Refusing to require a duration: these schedules fly a route with no stated '
            'block time, and inventing one would put a made-up arrival time on a '
            'customer''s booking: %. Add the route to this migration, or give those '
            'schedules a duration first.', unstated;
    END IF;
END $$;

ALTER TABLE "FlightSchedule" ALTER COLUMN "durationMinutes" SET NOT NULL;

-- A duration has to be a positive number of minutes. Zero would make an arrival
-- equal its departure, and negative would make it earlier.
ALTER TABLE "FlightSchedule"
    ADD CONSTRAINT "FlightSchedule_durationMinutes_positive" CHECK ("durationMinutes" > 0);
ALTER TABLE "Flight"
    ADD CONSTRAINT "Flight_durationMinutes_positive"
    CHECK ("durationMinutes" IS NULL OR "durationMinutes" > 0);

content.text:
Second slice of #84 is implemented and green; both reviews are running.

**The design decision worth your attention.** The issue's task says "store explicit elapsed duration **and** arrival instants". I stored only the duration and derive the arrival as `departure + durationMinutes`. That's exact arithmetic on an instant with no timezone involved, and storing both would be a second answer that can drift from the first — something this repo has deliberately removed three times (#135, #137, #73). I've asked the verifier to push back if that reading is wrong, and I'll flag it on the issue either way, because it's a departure from the literal wording.

The duration itself had to come from somewhere honest. It's now stated per schedule — nine routes, both directions, with real block times that differ by direction because the wind does — backfilled by IATA pair rather than flight number so renaming a flight can't lose it, and guarded so a route with no stated time fails the migration loudly rather than getting an invented arrival on a customer's booking.

**The day marker is the part most likely to be got wrong.** It's computed from the two *local calendar dates*, not from elapsed time — because elapsed time can't tell you: Tokyo → San Francisco takes 9h35 and lands on the same date it left, hours earlier by the clock, while a 4h05 hop leaving at 23:00 lands the next day. Both cases are tested, and computing the marker from elapsed time kills three tests.

`Flight.durationMinutes` is nullable on purpose: a flight row created outside a schedule (fixtures, tests) shows no arrival rather than failing. Every flight the generator makes inherits its schedule's.

Locally: lint clean, 739 unit, 94 database, build, Playwright 33/33, and the seeded database has 0 of 1416 flights without a duration.

One scoping note: only the status board shows arrival so far. Search, checkout and the e-ticket still show departure alone — I've asked `ui-review` whether that inconsistency is tolerable for a slice or whether one of those needs it now.

## Blocking defects

**1. The arrival never renders. The whole feature is invisible in the running app.**
`app/flights/page.tsx:86-94` selects an explicit field list that omits `durationMinutes`:

```ts
select: { id: true, flightNumber: true, airline: true, departureDate: true,
          priceCents: true, status: true, ...flightRouteInclude },
```

So `flight.durationMinutes` is `undefined` in `FlightStatusBoard.tsx:240`, `arrival` is always `null`, and no row gets an arrival line. Verified at all three viewports: every departure cell is 2 lines, no `→` anywhere (`shots/board-phone.png`, `board-tablet.png`, `board-desktop.png`). The comment above that select ("Only what the board renders") is exactly the trap — the board's needs changed and the select did not. Component tests pass props directly, so nothing caught it. User impact: the slice ships with no user-visible change at all.

Everything below I assessed by injecting the exact markup the component builds, with strings computed from the real `lib/flightTime` (`shots/preview-*.png`). The library itself is correct on all three requested routes: Tokyo→SF `→ 08:35 PDT (9h 35m)` dayOffset 0, NY→London `→ 07:30 +1 GMT+1 (7h 00m)` dayOffset 1, Seattle→Detroit `→ 15:05 EDT (4h 05m)` dayOffset 0.

**2. The duration input is white text on a white box — the typed value is invisible.**
`components/ui/flightScheduleForm.tsx:290-300`. `app/globals.css:923` scopes the dark-field styling to `.admin-card input[type="text"], .admin-card textarea`; the new field is `type="number"`, so it gets none of it. Tailwind preflight gives it `color: inherit` (white) while the UA keeps the white background. Computed: `background rgb(255,255,255)`, `color rgb(255,255,255)` — 1:1 contrast. Also no border, no radius, `padding: 0`, height 24px against 49px for its neighbours, so it is vertically misaligned in its own grid row. Seen at all three viewports; `shots/card-desktop.png` and `card-tablet.png` show a bare white bar between the correctly styled Departure and Price fields, with `245` typed into it and unreadable. An admin cannot see what they are entering, and cannot check it before submitting.

**3. `durationMinutes` is not cleared after a successful create, so the next schedule silently inherits the last one's block time.**
`flightScheduleForm.tsx:168-182` resets flightNumber, airline, from, to, departureTime, price, daysOfWeek and the seating fields — but never calls `setDurationMinutes('')`. Verified live at 1440x900: after "✅ New schedule created successfully!", every field is `""` and `durationMinutes` is still `"245"`.

This compounds with #2 and with the fact that the admin schedule list (`app/admin/flights/page.tsx:94-98`) has no Duration column and there is no edit route (only `DeleteScheduleButton`). So an admin creating a JFK→LHR schedule after a SEA→DTW one gets Seattle→Detroit's 245 minutes, cannot see it in the field, cannot see it in the list afterwards, and cannot edit it. Every generated flight on that route then carries a wrong arrival. That is the "says the true thing" failure, and it is the reason this one is blocking rather than cosmetic.

**4. At 768x1024 the board newly starts scrolling horizontally, and Price is cut off.**
Measured with and without the arrival line at each width:

| viewport | table width without | with | wrapper |
|---|---|---|---|
| 390 | 697 | 785 | 356 |
| 768 | **734** | **785** | **734** |
| 1440 | 998 | 998 | 998 |

At tablet the table fits exactly today and stops fitting once the nowrap arrival line widens the Departure column from 139px to 227px. Compare `shots/board-tablet.png` (all prices visible: $1,200, $850) against `shots/preview-tablet.png` (every price clipped to "$1,2", "$8"). A tablet user loses the fare — the thing they are comparing on — unless they discover the sideways scroll. Phone was already overflowing (pre-existing, #229/#200) and gets 88px worse; the page body itself never scrolls horizontally at any width, so the card's `overflowX: auto` is doing its job. Desktop absorbs it by shrinking every other column (Flight −15, From −18, To −20, Status −12, Price −10) and row height 87→108px; no wrapping with the seeded city labels, but the margin is thin.

## Notation (question 2) — needs rework before it ships

The line is `→ 07:30 +1 GMT+1 (7h 00m)`. Three problems, in order:

- **`+1` immediately followed by `GMT+1` is genuinely unreadable.** The task brief assumed `BST`; the app renders `GMT+1`, so the day marker and the zone label collide into "+1 GMT+1". Same for Tokyo (`+1 GMT+9`) and Rio (`+1 GMT-3`). A reader has no way to know which `+1` means "next day". This alone rules out the current arrangement. (The `GMT+n` labels rather than `BST`/`JST`/`CEST` are pre-existing from the previous slice, but they were only in one place per row before; now there are two per row and one of them sits against the day marker.)
- **The arrow is not enough, and for assistive tech it is nothing.** The column header is still "Departure" (`FlightStatusBoard.tsx:230`) while the cell now announces `Aug 11, 2026 / 19:30 EDT / → 07:30 +1 GMT+1 (7h 00m)`. `→` (U+2192) is dropped by some screen readers and read as "right arrow" by others, so the arrival can be announced as a bare second time under a header that says "Departure".
- **The bracketed duration is the least ambiguous part** — `(7h 00m)` reads as elapsed time — but sitting fourth on a line that already has two numbers and a zone, it is easy to skim past.

A clearer arrangement, keeping one row: split the column into `Departure` and `Arrival` headers, each cell `19:30 EDT` / `07:30 GMT+1` with `next day` (or `+1 day`) as a small separate marker rather than a bare `+1` adjacent to the zone, and move the duration to its own `Duration` column or under the flight number. If a second column is out of scope for this slice, at minimum: rename the header to `Departure / Arrival`, replace the bare `→` with the word `Arrives`, and separate the day marker from the zone (`Arrives 07:30 GMT+1 (next day) · 7h 00m`). Also give the arrival a different weight or colour from the departure — right now both are `rgba(255,255,255,0.5)` at 14px, so they look like one continuous fact.

## Question 3 — inconsistency

Tolerable for this slice, but wider than the brief states. The search result card (`shots/search-desktop.png`) shows only `Aug 13, 2026` — **no departure time at all**, let alone arrival. So a customer moving from the board to booking already loses the time; arrival is not the first thing missing. Because that gap is pre-existing rather than introduced here, it should not block this slice — but the search card is the surface where a time actually changes a purchase decision, and it should be the next thing to get one. File it rather than widen this slice.

## Non-blocking findings

- **The duration field has no inline error, unlike its siblings.** `from` and `to` render `<p id="...-error">` with `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` (`flightScheduleForm.tsx:247-254, 266-273`); `durationMinutes` has none. Server messages are legible and correctly worded — empty → "Please fill in all required fields." (client check, does not name the field), `0` and `-5` → "Flight duration must be at least one minute.", `99999` → "Flight duration must be shorter than three days.", `1.5` → "Flight duration must be a whole number of minutes." — but they appear only in the top banner.
- **Focus is not moved to the duration field on a validation failure.** The handler at `flightScheduleForm.tsx:153-162` is meant to focus the first bad field; after submitting `0`, `99999`, `1.5` and `-5`, `document.activeElement` was `BODY` every time. Keyboard users land at the top of the document with a banner, not on the field.
- **Focus ring is the browser default.** Price focused: purple border `rgb(139,92,246)` plus glow. Duration focused: `outline: rgb(22,22,22) auto 1px` — a near-black ring on a white box. Same cause as #2.
- **Missing input constraints.** `min={1}` only; no `max`, no `step`, no `inputMode`. Adding `max={4320}` and `step={1}` would let the browser and the spinner enforce what Zod already knows. Typing `e` into a number input yields `value === ''`, which surfaces as "Please fill in all required fields" on a field that looks filled.
- **Tab order is correct**: Departure → Duration → Price, verified at 1440x900.
- **The horizontal scroll container has no keyboard affordance** — `overflow-x: auto` with no `tabindex="0"`, `role="region"` or `aria-label` (`FlightStatusBoard.tsx:223`). Chrome makes scrollable boxes implicitly focusable so it did appear in my tab sequence, but Firefox and Safari do not. Pre-existing, newly relevant because tablet now overflows too.
- **Console is clean** — no errors or React warnings on the board at any viewport, or on the admin form through the full create journey.

## Headings with nothing to report

- **Contrast**: passes. I measured the composited row background at `rgb(23,20,31)`; the arrival line at `rgba(255,255,255,0.5)`/14px gives **5.30:1**, above AA for normal text. No contrast failure introduced on the board. (The form field is a contrast failure, but at 1:1 it is a styling bug, reported as #2.)
- **Page-level horizontal scroll**: none at 390, 768 or 1440, on either the board or the admin page.
- **Loading and empty states**: the board's four-branch empty message and the `role="status"` count line are untouched by this diff and behaved correctly.

# Verification: `feat/flight-arrival-times`

**Important context first:** the working tree changed **twice while I was verifying it**. A `ui-review` pass landed changes to `app/flights/page.tsx`, `app/globals.css`, `components/ui/FlightStatusBoard.tsx`, `components/ui/flightScheduleForm.tsx` and two test files partway through my first battery, and a further edit to `__tests__/components/flightScheduleForm.test.tsx` landed after my second. I discarded the first battery and re-ran everything. **All results below are for the final state**, which I confirmed stable (unchanged over a 30s window after the last run). There are no commits on the branch — everything is uncommitted working-tree state plus one untracked migration.

## What I ran

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `npx tsc --noEmit` | clean |
| `npm run lint` | 0 errors, 8 warnings (all pre-existing: `react-hooks/incompatible-library`, `no-img-element`) |

Build and Playwright ran against the state immediately before the final test-file-only edit; that edit touches neither the build output nor `e2e/`, so those results carry.

No flakes. Nothing failed for a reason connected to the diff.

## Migration, exercised on real pre-migration data

I built a scratch database at the pre-migration migration set and populated it with `Airport`, `FlightSchedule` and `Flight` rows lacking the column, including two schedules on routes the table does not cover (`Seattle, USA → London, UK` active, `Paris, France → Tokyo, Japan` **inactive**) and a flight on an uncovered route.

- **Guard fires**, naming both offenders including the inactive one — correct, since `NOT NULL` applies regardless of `isActive`.
- **Rollback is whole**: after the failure, neither column exists, neither CHECK exists, and the `route_block_minutes` temp table is gone.
- `P3009` on retry, `migrate resolve --rolled-back`, then a clean second run — the documented recovery path works end to end.
- **Guard passes** once the uncovered schedules are removed: all 9 schedules backfilled correctly, 3 covered flights backfilled, the uncovered flight left `NULL`, `NOT NULL` on `FlightSchedule`, both CHECKs present.
- CHECKs verified live: `0` and `-5` rejected on both tables; `NULL` accepted only on `Flight`.

## Findings

### 1. The arrival never rendered on the only page that uses the board — fixed mid-run (regression, now resolved)

`app/flights/page.tsx` picks columns explicitly and the `select` omitted `durationMinutes`. `FlightStatusBoard`'s prop is `durationMinutes?: number | null`, so TypeScript did not object, and `flight.durationMinutes ? … : null` silently produced nothing.

I measured it two ways before the fix: the page's query returned rows whose keys were `id, flightNumber, airline, departureDate, priceCents, status, from, to` with `'durationMinutes' in row === false`, and the live rendered `/flights` had **27 flight rows and 0 arrival markers**. The entire user-visible half of the slice was dead.

This was fixed while I was verifying, together with a test in the direction the existing pinned-select test could not see. I re-verified on the final state: **27/27 rows now render an arrival, 12 with a next-day marker**, header `Departure / Arrival`. Spot-checked against the destination zone — all nine routes correct, e.g. `Tokyo → San Francisco 15:00 GMT+9 → Arrives 08:35 PDT, 9h 35m` (no marker) and `Chicago → Paris 17:45 CDT → Arrives 09:15 GMT+2 (next day), 8h 30m`.

Flagging it because the parent agent should know the seam existed: a component test hands props directly, so a page that stops selecting a field the component reads fails nothing. The new `__tests__/app/flightsPage.test.ts` case closes it, and I confirmed removing `durationMinutes: true` from the page now kills 2 tests.

### 2. The duration requirement is enforced at three layers and tested at none (coverage gap)

You asked whether a schedule can still be saved without a duration. It cannot — but nothing proves it, so nothing will notice when it can again. Three mutations, all surviving 743/743:

- `lib/validation.ts` — appending `.optional()` to `durationMinutes`: **survives**.
- `lib/validation.ts` — deleting `.int(…)`, `.min(1, …)` and `.max(3 * 24 * 60, …)` outright: **survives**. All three custom messages are unreachable from any test.
- `components/ui/flightScheduleForm.tsx` — removing `!durationMinutes` from the required-fields check: **survives**.

Every new test supplies `durationMinutes: 245`; none omits it, none goes out of range. Note also that the action's own server-side guard at `app/actions.ts:752` (`if (!data.flightNumber || … || !data.price)`) does not include `durationMinutes`, so Zod is the only thing standing there.

### 3. `FlightScheduleService` can stop inheriting the duration and nothing fails (coverage gap)

Deleting `durationMinutes: schedule.durationMinutes` from the `flight.create` in `lib/FlightScheduleService.ts:114`: **743 unit + 94 database tests all pass**. This is the path the seed and the horizon generator use — it produced all 1416 seeded flights. Its twin in `generateFlightOccurrencesAction` (`app/actions.ts:1007`) *is* covered: the same deletion there kills a test. The asymmetry is worth closing, since the service is the higher-volume path.

### 4. Both CHECK constraints can be dropped with no test failing (coverage gap)

Dropped `FlightSchedule_durationMinutes_positive` and `Flight_durationMinutes_positive` from a freshly seeded database and ran the database project: **94/94 pass**. The constraints work — I verified directly — but nothing observes them. Combined with finding 2, if the Zod bounds regressed, a non-positive duration would be caught only by Postgres, and only in production.

### 5. The negative day marker is unreachable by any test (coverage gap)

`LocalArrival`'s doc says "a westbound crossing of the date line can be negative", and the board now renders `(previous day)` for it. Removing that branch: **743/743 pass**.

It is reachable from admin-authored data: Tokyo → San Francisco departing before roughly 06:25 JST. I confirmed `00:30 JST + 9h35 → Aug 16, 18:05 PDT, dayOffset = -1`. The seeded 15:00 JST departure gives 0, so the seed never produces it. This is the row a reader most needs the marker on — the arrival appears to be on an earlier date than the departure.

### 6. The guard's suggested remedy is impossible to follow (migration)

> `Add the route to this migration, or give those schedules a duration first.`

The second half cannot be done. When the guard fires, `FlightSchedule.durationMinutes` does not yet exist — the migration creates it — so there is nowhere to put a duration. I tried the obvious workaround (add the column by hand, backfill, re-run) and the migration fails at its own `ADD COLUMN`:

```
Database error code: 42701
ERROR: column "durationMinutes" of relation "FlightSchedule" already exists
```

The only workable remedies are adding the route to the table, or removing/retiring the offending schedules. The first clause is correct; the second sends an operator down a path that leaves them with a second failed migration to unwind.

### 7. Editing a schedule's duration does not reach flights already generated (behaviour, pre-existing pattern)

`saveFlightScheduleAction` skips any occurrence that already exists, so a corrected `durationMinutes` reaches only future generations. Identical to how `priceCents` behaves, so it is a pre-existing pattern rather than something this change invented — but the consequence is new and larger: at 157 rows per route across the booking horizon, a duration typed wrong once puts a wrong arrival time on every one of them, and there is no Duration column in the admin schedule list and no page wiring `initialSchedule` into the form, so nothing surfaces it. The comment added to the form-reset test acknowledges exactly this. Worth an issue rather than widening the slice.

## On the derivation decision — your reading is right

Deriving is defensible, and I could not find anything that needs a stored arrival instant.

- **Nothing today filters or sorts by arrival.** I grepped every Prisma call; no `where` or `orderBy` touches it, and no raw SQL does.
- **The obvious future caller is expressible in SQL.** #84's task 8 ("separate upcoming, departed, **arrived**, delayed, cancelled") needs "has it landed", which is `"departureDate" + make_interval(mins => "durationMinutes") <= now()`. Prisma's query builder cannot express that, so it would need `$queryRaw` — but Postgres will also accept it as `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (…) STORED`, since `timestamptz + interval` is immutable, and that column is indexable. A derived arrival therefore does not corner the design; it defers the choice rather than foreclosing it, and a generated column is still one answer rather than two.
- **One caveat for whoever writes that predicate**: `Flight.durationMinutes` is nullable, so it needs an explicit NULL policy — a flight with no stated duration can never be "arrived", and `NULL` in that comparison yields unknown, which silently drops rows from both sides of a naive split.

The precedent you cite (#135, #137, #73) is the right one, and the reasoning is recorded in the migration header and the schema comments where the next reader will find it. I would not store the instant.

## Edge cases: I could not break `flightArrival` or `calendarDaysBetween`

Every case you named, exercised against the real airport data. All correct:

- **Date line westbound** SFO→HND 11:00 PDT → `+1`; departing 23:59 PDT → `+2`, correctly printed as `(+2 days)`.
- **Date line eastbound** HND→SFO 15:00 JST → same date, `0`; 00:30 JST → `-1`; 23:59 JST → `0`.
- **Landing exactly at local midnight** SEA→DTW departing 16:55 PDT → `00:00 EDT`, `dayOffset 1`. One minute earlier → `23:59 EDT`, `0`. No off-by-one at the boundary.
- **Departing exactly at local midnight** → `07:05 EDT`, `0`.
- **DST at the destination mid-flight**, both directions: SEA→DTW over the 2026-11-01 fall-back → `04:35 EST`, `+1` (wall-clock difference 6h05, elapsed still 4h05); over the 2027-03-14 spring-forward → `05:35 EDT`, `+1`; JFK→LHR over the 2026-10-25 UK fall-back → `06:30 GMT`, `+1`. The marker stays right because it never touches elapsed time.
- **DST at the origin**: a departure inside the skipped hour (02:30 PDT) lands past the gap at 03:30 — pre-existing documented behaviour, and the arrival follows correctly.
- **Same-zone routes** SEA→SFO (both `America/Los_Angeles`) 23:00 + 2h → `+1`; JFK→MIA (both `America/New_York`) across the fall-back → `0`.
- **No-DST destination** MIA→GIG and GIG→MIA both correct.
- **`calendarDaysBetween`** is sound: both dates are parsed as UTC midnights and `Math.round`ed, so DST cannot perturb it and negatives work.

The two mutations you already killed, I re-confirmed on the final state: reading the arrival in the origin's zone kills 5 tests, computing `dayOffset` from elapsed time kills 4.

**Nothing infers a duration or an arrival by subtracting local times.** I grepped `app/`, `lib/` and `components/` for `getTime()` subtraction, `getHours`/`getMinutes`, and `HH:MM` splitting. The seven hits are unrelated (date-range width, points-month sorting, rate-limit backoff, the cancellation policy's hours-to-departure). No `split(':')` does time arithmetic.

All ten entries in the migration's `route_block_minutes` match `lib/data/FlightData.ts` exactly. Both directions are present for all five routes, and every eastbound leg is shorter than its westbound pair — SEA/DTW 245 vs 285, JFK/LHR 420 vs 485, HND/SFO 575 vs 680, ORD/CDG 510 vs 560, GIG/MIA 500 vs 525 — which is what prevailing winds do. All are within about 20 minutes of real-world block times.

Two notes: `GIG → MIA` is in the migration table but `FlightScheduleData` has no Rio → Miami return schedule, so the entry is unused (harmless, and the asymmetry is pre-existing in the seed). And nothing keeps the migration's table and `FlightData.ts` in sync — the header says they are the same numbers, but no test asserts it, unlike the `AirportData` ↔ `Airport` drift test. Low severity, since a migration is one-shot.

`saveFlightScheduleAction` (`app/actions.ts`) pre-generates occurrences and skips any

  overwrites it. (That last one is fixed in the slice; the other two are not.)

   nothing routes to it.

   is not obviously right — a flight somebody has booked has a departure and an arrival
   they were told — so this is a product decision, not just a missing update. It is the

## Related

- #84 — where the duration came from
- #235 — the other admin-board item from the same review

gh pr create --base main --head feat/flight-arrival-times --title "feat(flights): state how long a flight takes, and show when it lands" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Second slice of #84.

## Why a duration had to be stored

Nothing recorded one, so an arrival time could only be guessed — and the obvious guess is
the one this issue warns against: subtracting a displayed local departure from a
displayed local arrival. Across a timezone that is not a duration at all. Tokyo → San
Francisco takes 9h35 and lands **earlier by the clock** than it left; a 4h05 Seattle hop
leaving at 23:00 lands the next day. Elapsed minutes are the same number wherever either
end of the route is.

Schedules now state it, flights inherit it, and existing rows are backfilled from a route
table keyed by IATA pair — not flight number, so renaming a flight cannot lose it. A route
with no stated block time **fails the migration** rather than getting an invented arrival
onto somebody's booking.

## The design decision, and the pushback I asked for

The issue's task says "store explicit elapsed duration **and** arrival instants". I store
only the duration and derive `departure + durationMinutes` — exact arithmetic on an
instant, no zone involved — because a second stored answer can only disagree with the
first, and this repository has removed three of those (#135, #137, #73).

I asked the `verifier` to argue the other side. It confirmed nothing today filters or
sorts by arrival, and that the obvious future caller — #84's "separate upcoming,
departed, **arrived**" — is expressible either as raw SQL or as a `GENERATED ALWAYS AS`
column, which is still one answer rather than two. So the derivation defers that choice
rather than foreclosing it. Recorded on the issue.

The day marker is counted between the two **local calendar dates**, never from elapsed
time, which cannot tell you which day it is.

## What review caught — the slice rendered nothing at all

`app/flights/page.tsx` selects an explicit column list, and it did not include
`durationMinutes`. So `arrival` was always null and **not one row rendered an arrival
line**: 27 flight rows, 0 arrival markers. The entire user-visible half of the change was
dead on arrival.

Worse, there *was* a test pinning that select — it just pinned it in one direction,
catching a column arriving that nothing reads while being blind to the board growing a
field the select never adds. Both directions are covered now. This is the same seam that
hid a released seat in #230; a component test hands props directly, so the page can stop
selecting a field and nothing fails.

Three more from `ui-review`:

- **The duration input was white text on a white box** — 1:1 contrast, invisible. The
  admin dark-field CSS is scoped to `input[type="text"]`.
- **The form never cleared it after a create**, so the next schedule on a different route
  silently inherited the last one's block time — with no Duration column in the list and
  no edit form to notice with.
- **`→ 07:30 +1 GMT+1` was unreadable**: the day marker sat against a `GMT+1` zone label
  with no way to tell which `+1` meant "next day". It now reads
  `Arrives 07:30 GMT+1 (next day)` with the duration on its own line. The arrow is gone —
  a screen reader either drops `→` or says "right arrow", leaving a bare second time under
  a heading that said "Departure". That heading now says "Departure / Arrival".

It also measured that the nowrap arrival line pushed the tablet board into horizontal
scroll and clipped the Price column; letting it wrap fixes that.

The `verifier` then found five coverage gaps in one shape — the enforcement exists, the
test does not. The duration requirement was enforced at three layers and asserted at
none; the higher-volume generator could stop inheriting it; both CHECK constraints could
be dropped; and the negative day marker — the row a reader most needs it on, where the
arrival looks like a mistake — was unreachable. All five now have tests, and each
mutation dies.

It also caught that the migration guard suggested a remedy that **cannot be followed**:
"give those schedules a duration first" names a column the migration has not created yet,
and adding it by hand makes the migration fail on its own `ADD COLUMN`. Reworded.

## Verified rather than assumed

The verifier built a pre-migration database including two schedules on uncovered routes —
one of them inactive — and confirmed the guard names both, rolls back whole, and recovers
through the documented `migrate resolve` path. It could not break `flightArrival`: date
line in both directions, departures at 23:59 and at local midnight, landings exactly at
local midnight, DST transitions mid-flight at either end, same-zone routes, and
no-DST destinations all came out right.

Seeded block times check out too: both directions present for every route, every
eastbound leg shorter than its westbound pair, all within ~20 minutes of real-world times.

## Recorded, not fixed

**#237** — editing a schedule never reaches occurrences already generated. Pre-existing
for `priceCents`, but now a duration typed wrong once puts a wrong arrival on all 157
occurrences of a route, and there is no Duration column and no edit path to notice with.
Whether existing flights *should* be updated is a product decision.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 750 unit + 96 database, `npm run build`,
Playwright 33/33, no drift. Seeded database: 0 of 1416 flights without a duration.

**Still open on #84**: the arrival-in-destination display beyond the board (search,
checkout and the e-ticket still show departure only — and search shows no time at all),
account times in the customer's timezone, the upcoming/departed/arrived split, and the
real-time claim.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -3

Done, and **#238 is merged** — the duration slice is in.

**[PR #239](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/pull/239)** records the split in AGENTS.md so it survives this session:

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| Main agent, freely | lint, `tsc`, the whole unit project — ~18s, needs nothing running |
| Main agent, focused | database tests for the change, the one Playwright spec that changed |
| Verifier alone | full database project, `npm run build`, full `npx playwright test` |

Beyond the wasted minutes, running them in both places has actively cost us: the verifier reported on both #232 and #236 that its results were polluted by my concurrent runs competing for port 3000 and the shared database, and it had to discard and redo a full battery each time.

**One thing I found while writing this that you'll want to know.** `npm run test:unit -- <path>` doesn't filter — it silently runs all 732 tests:

```
$ npm run test:unit -- flightTime
Tests: 732 passed, 732 total
```

The script ends in `--selectProjects unit`, which takes a *list*, so the path is read as another project name and ignored. `--testPathPattern` works and cuts it to 15 tests in 1.3s. `npm run test:database -- <path>` *does* filter, because `--runInBand` sits between the project list and the path — which is precisely why the difference is invisible.

So every "focused" unit run I did this session was actually a full run. Nothing was wrong with the results; the cost was just hidden. Both facts are now in the Gotchas, and the Commands line shows the form that works.

I also hit a related snag switching branches: the generated Prisma client was still the arrival-times one, so `tsc` reported errors that were purely stale-artifact. Regenerating fixed it — worth remembering when a branch switch crosses a schema change.

content.text:
Closed #167 — #236 fixed it in passing, since converting the column forced both indexes to be recreated.

**My recommendation: the phone cluster, #229 + #208.** Together they mean a customer on a phone **cannot find out their flight was cancelled** — the Status column is scrolled out of the visible area, so a disrupted booking is pixel-identical to a confirmed one, and the notification drawer renders *behind* the page, so the fallback is unreadable too. Neither is new, but #76 and #84 just made them load-bearing: we shipped a whole disruption flow that a phone user can't see. Both are small — a column layout and a stacking-context fix — and the impact is disproportionate to the work.

Two strong alternatives:

**#84's next slice — times on the booking surfaces.** `ui-review` was pointed about this: the search result card shows **no departure time at all**, let alone an arrival. That's the screen where a time actually changes a purchase decision, and `flightDeparture()`/`flightArrival()` now hand it over for free. Checkout and the e-ticket are the same story.

**#74, inventory holds** — next in the #143 plan order, and #75 (payments) sits behind it. #143's own reasoning: without holds, a checkout dying between commit and capture strands a seat, and #75's analysis proposes a throwaway sweeper to compensate that landing #74 first deletes.

I'd sequence it: phone cluster → #84 booking-surface times → #74. The first two are hours, not days, and they close gaps in work already shipped rather than opening new ground.

Notification drawer is clipped to 16 visible pixels on phone

Found during the `ui-review` for the test-infrastructure cleanup. **Pre-existing**, measured against running code at 390x844.

## Where

`components/ui/titlebar.tsx:201-311` renders the drawer `position: absolute` inside `header nav ul li`. At `max-width: 600px`, `app/globals.css:887-891` sets `header nav { overflow-x: auto }` — and per spec that forces `overflow-y: auto` too, so the drawer is clipped by the 56px-tall nav.

## What was observed

```
nav:    clientHeight 56, scrollHeight 429, overflowX auto, overflowY auto
drawer: height 389 (top 96, bottom 485)
visible drawer height: 16px
```

`document.elementFromPoint` at the drawer's centre returns the hero `H1`, not the drawer. A signed-in user with 5 unread taps the bell and sees a bare sliver — no notification text, no "Mark all read", no empty state. Same on the admin header.

## Why it matters

The clicks still land (the badge counted down when they were forced), so this is a paint/clip failure rather than a dead control — which is worse, because a user cannot see what they are tapping. The whole feature is unusable on a phone.

Belongs to #79 (P3.2 responsive layouts).

Review the rendered UI of branch `fix/phone-status-and-drawer` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app (AGENTS.md step 6). Postgres and Mailpit are running. This change exists **because of your findings** on #229 and #208, so you are the right check on whether they are actually fixed. Both were pre-existing and both became load-bearing when #76 shipped the disruption flow: together they meant a phone user could not learn their flight had been cancelled at all.

## What changed

**#208 — the notification drawer.** It was `position: absolute` inside `header nav ul li`, and `header nav { overflow-x: auto }` at phone width forced `overflow-y: auto` too, clipping a 389px panel to 16 visible pixels. It is now rendered through `createPortal` into `document.body` as `position: fixed`, anchored by measuring the bell's `getBoundingClientRect()` on open and on scroll/resize. Width is `min(320px, calc(100vw - 16px))` and height `calc(100vh - top - 16px)`. The outside-click handler now checks both the trigger and the panel.

**#229 — the profile bookings table.**
- The Status column still sits past the right edge at 390px, so the status is now *also* rendered beside the flight number in the first cell, `sm:hidden` so it does not duplicate at wider widths. It carries `aria-hidden="true"` because the column already conveys it to assistive technology.
- The scroll wrapper gained `tabIndex={0}`, `role="region"` and an `aria-label`.
- The seat line went from `rgba(255,255,255,0.4)` to `0.72` — you measured the old one at 3.80:1.
- `seatLabel` now says `Seat 11A` / `seat released` / `No seat assigned`, matching the admin manifest, because the word "Seat" appeared nowhere, visible or accessible.

1. **Is the drawer actually usable on a phone now?** Open it with several notifications and with none. Check it is fully visible, scrollable if long, does not cover the bell, closes on an outside click, and that "Mark all read" works. Measure the visible height against the panel height — that was 16px of 389px.
2. **Does the drawer still behave at tablet and desktop**, and does it stay anchored when the page scrolls? It is `fixed` now, so a stale anchor would show as drift.
3. **Can a phone user tell a cancelled or disrupted booking from a confirmed one without scrolling sideways?** That is the whole point. Check the status copy does not duplicate visibly at ≥640px, and that it does not wreck the first cell's layout.
4. **Contrast** of the seat line at its new alpha, and of the new phone status copy in all three colours (green/amber/red).

content.text:
Both reviews are running, and this is the first slice under the new split — I ran lint, `tsc`, the full unit project (750 green) and the two Playwright specs whose journeys changed, and handed the rest over.

**What the fixes do.**

**#208** — the drawer was `position: absolute` inside `header nav ul li`, and `overflow-x: auto` at phone width forces `overflow-y: auto`, clipping a 389px panel to sixteen visible pixels. The clicks landed and the badge counted down, so it wasn't dead — just invisible, which is worse. It's now portalled into `document.body` as `position: fixed`, anchored by measuring the bell on open and on scroll or resize, and clamped to the viewport. I moved it out of the clipping subtree rather than trying to out-manoeuvre the clip, because the header's `backdrop-filter` makes it a containing block and a plain `position: fixed` would likely still have been clipped by the nav in between.

**#229** — the status now also appears beside the flight number at phone width, since the column genuinely sits past the right edge; the scroll wrapper is focusable and named, which is WCAG 2.1.1; the seat line went from 3.80:1 to a passing contrast; and a seat now says it's a seat — `Seat 11A`, matching what the admin manifest already did.

Two judgement calls worth flagging. The phone status copy is `aria-hidden`, because the column already conveys it to assistive technology whether or not it's scrolled into view — otherwise a screen reader would hear it twice. And it duplicates in the DOM at every width, which made two e2e assertions ambiguous; they now filter on visibility rather than guessing an index, since which copy is visible depends on the viewport.

I've asked the verifier specifically to challenge the portal — SSR, listener cleanup, signing out with the drawer open — and to expect that some of this is CSS-level and may not be assertable in jsdom, so I get told which mutations survive rather than a clean bill.

## How I exercised it

The MCP browser wanted Chrome at `/opt/google/chrome/chrome`, which isn't installed, so I drove the repo's bundled Chromium through Playwright scripts instead (headless, DPR 2). I seeded a real user with a confirmed round trip (2 passengers), a **disrupted round trip whose return leg is the cancelled one**, a cancelled booking with a released seat, an unseated booking, and 8 notifications. Screenshots are in
`/tmp/claude-1000/-home-scottdensmore-Developer-scottdensmore-travel-app/94121201-47c3-4281-aeff-7838379a510d/scratchpad/shots/`.

## Both issues are genuinely fixed

**#208 — yes.** At 390x844 the panel is **419px tall and 419px of it visible**, fully inside the viewport, not covering the bell (bell bottom 106, panel top 116), list scrolls (853px into 340px), outside click closes, item click does not, "Mark all read" clears the badge and leaves the panel open (`drawer-390-open.png`, `drawer-390-empty.png`). Anchoring holds: page scroll to 600 moved it 116→114, tracking the header's own shrink; scrolling the phone `header nav` sideways — the exact overflow that caused #208 — put the panel's right edge at 244.6 against a bell right edge of 244.6, exact. Tablet and desktop are clean (`drawer-768-unread.png`, `drawer-1440-unread.png`). At 844x390 landscape the outer `maxHeight` binds correctly: 283px panel, list shrinks to 204 and scrolls. No console errors or React warnings on `/`, `/book`, `/flights`, `/travelguide`, `/profile` with the drawer opened at each.

**#229 — yes.** At 390 the phone copy is visible in the first cell for all three states, no sideways scroll needed (`bookings-390.png`). At 768 and 1440 the `sm:hidden` copy is `display:none` and only the column renders — no visible duplication (`bookings-768.png`, `bookings-1440.png`). No page-level horizontal scroll at any of the three widths. Contrast all passes: seat line **9.82:1** (from 3.80), green 9.57, amber 11.02, red 6.65. The region's focus ring is real — pixel-diffed white (255,255,255) against rgb(24,20,32), maxDelta 235.

## Blocking

**1. Portalling the panel broke keyboard and screen-reader order** — `components/ui/titlebar.tsx:258,375` — 390/768/1440, drawer open.
The panel paints under the bell but its DOM home is the end of `document.body`. Measured tab sequence after opening with the keyboard at 390: avatar link → Sign Out → bookings region → Change Seats → Cancel → Change Seats. "Mark all read" is never reached; it is the last focusable element in the document. Escape does not close it (verified: still open after `Escape`). The bell carries no `aria-expanded`, `aria-haspopup` or `aria-controls`, the panel has no role or accessible name, and focus is neither moved in nor restored. Before this change the panel sat immediately after the bell in the same `li`, so tab order was bell → Mark all read. A keyboard user now opens a drawer and has to traverse the entire page to reach its one control, with no way to dismiss it except a mouse click elsewhere. WCAG 2.4.3. Fix together: `aria-expanded`/`aria-controls` on the bell, `role="dialog"` + `aria-label` on the panel, an Escape handler, focus into the panel on open and back to the bell on close.

**2. The bell has no visible focus indicator** — `components/ui/titlebar.tsx:232` (`outline: 'none'`) — all viewports.
Computed styles are byte-identical focused and unfocused (`outline: ... none 3px`, same box-shadow). Pre-existing, not introduced here, but it is the entry point to the feature this change exists to fix and it is in the changed file: keyboard users cannot see where they are when they arrive at the bell. WCAG 2.4.7.

## Non-blocking findings

**3. A phone user can now learn about the disruption but still cannot act on it** — `components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx:345-354,485` — 390x844.
Measured: the Status column starts at x=380 and every Change Seats/Cancel button spans x=471–633, all beyond the region's right edge at 353. So the inline copy says "UIR400 cancelled by airline", but "Your seat is held. Cancel for a full refund, with no cancellation fee." and the Cancel button stay behind a horizontal scroll with no visible affordance — `offsetHeight === clientHeight` (no scrollbar gutter), and `app/globals.css:1146` paints the thumb `#2b2640` on a `#0d0c14` track, roughly 1.4:1, invisible even where a scrollbar is drawn. The slice's goal is met; the follow-through is not. Worth filing rather than widening the slice.

**4. The scroll region is a tab stop that lies at ≥640** — `components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx:345-354` — 768 and 1440.
Measured `scrollWidth === clientWidth` (662 and 997): nothing scrolls, yet `tabIndex={0}` still creates a stop and the landmark is still named "Your bookings, scrollable". Condition both on real overflow (ResizeObserver), or drop "scrollable" from the name. At 390, where it does overflow, the order is good: it lands after Sign Out and before the row buttons.

**5. Stale-anchor flash on reopen** — `components/ui/titlebar.tsx:116-136,258`.
`anchor` survives close and `place()` runs in `useEffect`, i.e. after paint. With the bell moved (nav scrolled sideways) while closed, reopening painted the panel at the previous position (right 355.6) for two frames before settling at 244.6. `useLayoutEffect`, and clearing `anchor` on close, removes both.

**6. The 340px list cap now fights the measurement that was just added** — `components/ui/titlebar.tsx:317`.
At 768x1024 and 1440x900 the panel is 388px tall with 600+px of free viewport, showing 3 of 8 notifications while the badge says 8 — and with the scrollbar styling above, nothing indicates more exists. Let the outer `maxHeight: calc(100vh - top - 16px)` govern.

**7. `seat released` is the odd one out, and the comment's premise is wrong** — `lib/bookingItinerary.ts:90-98`.
"Ada (Seat 11A)" and "Alan (No seat assigned)" read well; "Bob (seat released)" beside them reads like a typo, and it is the only lowercase form. The comment says it matches the admin manifest, but `app/admin/flights/AdminFlightsTable.tsx:320` renders `Released` — the two surfaces now disagree on this exact string. "Seat released" in both, or have admin call `seatLabel`, would make the claim true.

**8. 0.4-alpha text still in the drawer this change rewrites** — `components/ui/titlebar.tsx:347` (timestamps, measured **3.78:1**) and `:368` ("You're all caught up!", same alpha). That is the same defect just corrected on the seat line (3.80 → 9.82), one file over, in the panel this change moved.

**9. The status expression is written twice** — `components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx:433-437` and `:463-467`. Identical conditionals that must always agree; an edit to one is precisely the "names one flight while listing another leg's data" failure mode. Extract to a single variable above the return.

## Nothing to report

- **Layout / horizontal scroll**: `documentElement.scrollWidth === clientWidth` at all three widths, on all five routes.
- **Console**: zero errors and zero React warnings across the whole journey.
- **Contrast of everything this change touched**: all pass AA, most pass AAA (numbers above).
- **Status duplication at ≥640**: does not occur; the phone copy is `display:none` and correctly `aria-hidden`, so assistive technology hears the status once.
- **First-cell layout**: not wrecked. It is cramped at 390 — the column is 83px, so "UIR400 cancelled by airline" wraps to three lines — but that is the pre-existing table cramping, and the wrapping is legible.

## Gaps in this review

- Headless Chromium only. Real-device touch behaviour was not exercised: iOS overlay scrollbars, and whether a tap reliably synthesises the `mousedown` the outside-click close depends on (`titlebar.tsx:152`).
- The admin header variant (`pathname.startsWith('/admin')`, white text) was not exercised — the fixture user is not staff and staff access gates on TOTP enrollment. The drawer markup is shared, so I expect parity, but I did not see it.
- No pre-change measurement of the 16px-of-389px state: confirming it would have meant stashing your uncommitted work. The "before" numbers are from #208 and #229; every "now" number above is measured.
- The `e2e/*.spec.ts` edits were read, not run — you asked me not to start Playwright while my dev server was up. The `.filter({ visible: true })` additions are the right shape for a 1280-wide default viewport where the phone copy is in the DOM but hidden; proving that is the verifier's pass.</result>

is not proving it — and the failure mode is the wrong direction, reporting that startup
*succeeded* when it should have thrown.

assertion depends on `instrumentation.ts` not having been imported already with a valid
environment.

deliberately. It would be worth deciding whether the suite should run randomised in CI —
this is exactly the class of bug that ordering hides, and it is the second one found this
week (the drawer tests in the branch that surfaced this were also passing only because a
sibling had signed a user in).

fix(profile): let a phone see that a flight was cancelled

Two pre-existing defects that #76 made load-bearing. Together they meant a
phone user could not learn their flight had been cancelled at all: the
profile's Status column sits past the right edge of a scrolling region, so
a disrupted booking was pixel-identical to a confirmed one, and the
notification drawer was clipped to sixteen visible pixels of a 389px panel,
so the fallback could not be read either. The drawer's clicks landed and
its badge counted down, which is why nothing failed.

The drawer is portalled out of the header and positioned from the bell's
measured rect. `position: fixed` alone would have escaped today's clip;
the portal removes the dependency on nothing in that subtree ever gaining
a containing block, and its cost -- the panel becoming the last thing in
the document -- is paid back with dialog semantics, Escape from anywhere
and focus moved in and returned.

The status is repeated beside the flight number when, and only when, the
Status cell is out of reach. That is measured rather than guessed: a
breakpoint cannot answer it, because the crossover moves with the widest
row's content, and asking whether the region merely scrolls showed the
duplicate for another 190px, since Status is not the last column.

Also: the seat line went from 3.80:1 to passing, and a seat now says it is
a seat -- "Seat 11A" -- through one function both the profile and the admin
manifest read, so the two cannot drift.

Fixes #229 and #208.

Merged. `main` is at `fb3a691`, clean. **#229 and #208 are both closed** — a phone user can now see that their flight was cancelled, and read the notification that says so.

**Ten PRs merged this session:**

| PR | What |
|---|---|
| #226 | Codex removed from the workflow |
| #227 | Test infrastructure finished (#213) |
| #228, #230, #231, #232, #233 | #76 in five slices — cancellation, disruption, refunds |
| #236, #238 | #84 slices 1–2 — departures as instants, arrival times |
| #239 | Verifier owns the slow checks |
| #243 | The phone cluster (#229, #208) |

Six issues closed, and these filed along the way: **#225**, **#234**, **#235**, **#237**, **#240**, **#241**, **#242**.

**Two things I'd genuinely act on next, both about how we're working rather than what we're building.**

**#242 and the ordering problem.** Two order-dependent tests surfaced today — my drawer tests passing only because a sibling had signed a user in, and `instrumentation.test.ts` failing 1 run in 3 under `--randomize`. That second one guards a fail-closed boot check, and it fails in the *wrong direction*: reporting startup succeeded when it should have thrown. `npm test` doesn't randomise, so neither was visible. Making CI randomise is a small change that catches this class permanently.

**#225 — `e2e/` and `__tests__/` have never been linted.** Several of today's bugs were in test code: a locator that matched the wrong element, an edit that silently no-op'd, assertions that passed by viewport accident. Lint wouldn't have caught all of that, but it's the one tree with no static checking at all, and it's where a growing share of the defects now live.

On the product side, **#84 has four tasks left** — the biggest being times on the booking surfaces, where search currently shows no departure time at all. And **#74 (inventory holds)** is still next in the #143 plan, with #75 behind it.

Thinking through our main agent vs sub agent verifier. I want to keep the main agent context as clean as possible. We are
  doing tdd so we have to build and run tests. We also are doing user journey testing. How should we handle this? have the
  main agent run the one and the verifier run the entire suite?

Yes to that split — it's what #239 already encodes. But I'd push back on the premise: **running tests is not what costs context.** Filtering the output is, and we already do it.

Concretely, from today: a full unit run is `npm run test:unit | grep -E "^Tests:"` — about 50 tokens for 765 tests. I ran it perhaps forty times. That's negligible. What actually consumed context was:

1. **Review reports.** Twelve verifier/ui-review passes, each returning 3–5k tokens. Call it 50k. Easily the largest line item.
2. **Failure debugging.** A failing Playwright test dumps call logs and locator resolutions; a failing Jest test dumps a DOM tree. Each investigation round is 500–2000 tokens, and today had a lot of rounds.
3. **Edit churn.** Reading files to find anchors, re-reading after a `python` edit silently no-op'd.

So moving whole-suite runs to the verifier saves *wall clock and CPU contention*, which is worth doing. It barely touches context.

**The division I'd keep:**

| Main agent | Verifier |
|---|---|
| TDD inner loop — one file, `--testPathPattern` | Full unit + database projects |
| The **red** step (confirm it fails for the right reason) | `npm run build` |
| Full unit project once, when a slice is done | Full `npx playwright test` |
| lint, `tsc` | Migration against fresh *and* populated databases |
| The single journey spec being written | Cross-file regression sweeps |
| Mutation testing | Re-running the mutation battery independently |

Two things can't move. The **red step is a design check, not a verification** — "does this fail for the reason I intended" needs the intent, so a subagent can't do it. And **fixing findings is always mine**, which is the expensive part and can't be delegated.

**Three rules that would save more context than the split:**

**Never launch the verifier until the tree is settled.** I broke this twice today and it cost a full battery each time — it snapshotted, I edited underneath it, and everything it reported certified a state that no longer existed. That's pure waste on both sides.

**Prefer one thorough verifier pass to several narrow ones.** This branch had five. Each found real things, so they weren't wasted — but three of them existed only because I'd fixed one round's findings and had to re-verify. Batching the fixes would have cut it to two or three.

**Cap failure triage.** Grep to the assertion and the expected/received first. If two rounds don't explain it, delegate the investigation rather than reading progressively more output — that's the pattern that ate context today when the phone-width test kept passing against mutations.

One optional addition worth considering: when a *journey* test fails for an environmental reason — the stale `.next` 404s, a port collision — that's pure noise for me to diagnose. Those could go straight to a subagent with "tell me if this is real."

Want me to fold the table and the three rules into AGENTS.md step 7? It's a small edit to what #239 already put there, and it'd make the red-step constraint explicit, which the current text doesn't say.
Yes lets add your recommendations

You verify and report. You do not fix: you have no editing tools, and that is

## Scope the run to the change

Read `git diff main...HEAD` plus staged, unstaged and untracked files, then pick
the checks that can actually catch a regression in it. Justify anything you skip.

## The checks

```bash
npx tsc --noEmit            # typecheck; covers tests too, they are in tsconfig
npm run lint                # eslint app components lib
npm test                    # Jest; needs Postgres running
npx playwright test         # E2E; auto-starts the dev server
npm run build               # never bare `next build` - the sanitize step matters
```

Database work additionally needs proof the migration applies to an *empty*
database, not just the already-migrated dev one:

```bash
docker compose up -d db mailpit          # podman/podman-compose if Docker is absent
npx prisma migrate deploy && npx prisma db seed
```

Create a scratch database and run `migrate deploy` against it. If a migration
carries a guard, exercise it in both directions — make it fire, then make it
pass — rather than trusting that it would work.

## Environment traps that produce false results

- Jest and Playwright need Postgres up; `*.database.test.ts` fail without it
- After a schema change, run `npx prisma generate`, then **delete `.next`**.
  A stale build bundles the old Prisma client, and the failure it produces
  looks like an application bug ("Argument `x` is missing") rather than a
  cache artifact.
- A stale dev server holding port 3000 makes Playwright time out on startup
- Playwright runs `workers: 1, fullyParallel: false` on purpose; do not
  parallelise it

## Flakes are findings

A test that passes on retry has not passed. When something fails:

1. Determine whether it fails for a reason connected to the diff
2. Re-run it in isolation and as part of the suite — order-dependence and
   cold-start timing are common here
3. Report the mechanism, not just "flaky"

Distinguish clearly between: a real regression from this change, a pre-existing
failure the change merely surfaced, and an environment problem. Getting this
wrong wastes the most time of anything you do.

## Coverage

Note behaviour the change introduces that no test would catch. Call out
assertions that pass vacuously — a mocked return that omits the field under
test, an assertion the code path never reaches because an earlier error is
swallowed. A green suite that never exercises the change is a finding.

## Report

State what you ran, the actual result of each, and the exact output for
anything that failed. Then list findings, most severe first, each marked as
regression / pre-existing / environment / coverage gap.

Never report success you did not observe. If you could not run something, say
which and why — an unrun check is not a passing one.

The second pass found something that indicts my own testing, not just the test:

**My guard was very nearly vacuous, and my mutation testing hid it.** Five of the eight assertions were satisfied by prose that assigns nothing — `npm run build` and `npx playwright test` appear in the Commands block, in Gotchas, and worst of all in the verifier's own sentence describing what the *main agent* skips. A verifier definition that never once told it to build would have gone green.

The part worth sitting with: I ran three mutants and all three hit the load-bearing assertions. The two that would have exposed the vacuity — delete the `npm run build` row, delete the Playwright row — I didn't attempt. I picked mutants that confirmed the test worked rather than ones that could show it didn't. That's the same failure as #231 wearing a different hat, and "I mutation-tested it" is exactly the sentence that made it feel covered.

Fixed by anchoring both sides to the passage that actually assigns work: the verifier *column* of the table, and the definition from `## The checks` onward. All four mutants now die, including moving a check to the main agent's column — which whole-file matching could never have seen.

Also this round: the "you have no editing tools" claim was false as stated (Bash can `sed -i`), so it's now phrased as the rule it is; both tooling traps you and I have been bitten by are in the verifier's environment section; and it's told that silence is a finding — a behavioural change arriving with no mutant named means either nothing was done or nothing was passed on, and it can't tell which.

The third pass asks it to attack the two extraction helpers adversarially. `indexOf` returning -1 slices from the end of a string rather than throwing, so a renamed heading could make the test fail open — green while the ownership claim is gone. I'd rather know that now than ship a guard with the same flaw as the one it replaced.
